confirmed.title: Every context marked in a transaction stays valid, so the app role can reinstall a co-signer's context with set_config and attribute any write to that person
confirmed.description: set_actor_context adds a marker (xact, pid, sha256(ctx)) for every context it installs. It prunes only markers from earlier transactions and never removes the markers of the current one. actor_context_validated (lines 170-172) accepts whatever context ebmr.ctx holds if any marker of this transaction matches it. When module code switches context and then switches back, the temporary context stays valid until commit, and the app can bring it back with set_config('ebmr.ctx', ...). esig.sign (0230 line 483) does exactly this for every co-signature: iam.set_internal_actor(v_actor || {person_id: signer, account_id, role_code, auth_event_id, legal_name}) writes both the kernel marker and the iam.command_log row, then set_actor_context(v_actor) restores the performer's context. The app can rebuild the co-signer's context exactly: its own context plus the actor object in the esig.signature INSERT audit event, which it can SELECT. kernel.current_actor(), iam.assert_validated_actor() and the audit trigger then accept that context. It pairs the co-signer's person with the performer's session, a combination begin_command would reject (EBMR-IAM-111), and it consumes no fresh authentication event. ADR-0016 claims a validated command cannot swap in another person's context. The attribution test only tries a context that was never marked.
confirmed.failure_scenario: I reproduced this with the real stack: a vitest file in my scratchpad ran against a fresh template DB with seeded SHARED-device actors. As ebmr_app: BEGIN; select kernel.begin_command(<performer ctx with fresh badge event>); select esig.sign(<co-signature challenge naming the verifier>, <verifier's SIGNATURE auth event>, 'OPEN', null, false); select esig.seal_signature(...); select payload->'actor' from kernel.audit_event where table_name='esig.signature' and record_id=<sig id>; select set_config('ebmr.ctx', <performer ctx overlaid with the verifier's person_id, account_id, role_code, auth_event_id, legal_name>, true); insert into esig.stub_signable (kind,title,value,unit) values ('STEP','forged entry','99','kg'); COMMIT. Result: iam.assert_validated_actor() returns the verifier's context. The INSERT audit event records person=verifier, role=VERIFIER, auth_event_id=the already-consumed signature event. This is a data entry the verifier never made, on a SHARED device, with no per-command authentication (INV-40 bypass). Any definer command function gated by iam.require_permission or assert_validated_actor (approvals, publications and similar) can also be run as the co-signer, for example as a QA approver who co-signs at an operator kiosk.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Allow only one validated context per (transaction, backend) at a time. set_actor_context should delete all markers of pg_backend_pid(), including the current transaction's, before inserting the new one; a savepoint rollback undoes the delete together with the GUC. Better still, store the context in the marker row and have current_actor() read it from there instead of from the GUC. Change iam.authn_change_secret (0160:538) and iam.bootstrap_installation (0180:152) to restore through set_actor_context, not set_config. Add a bypass test: after a co-signature, reinstalling the co-signer's context in the same transaction must fail with EBMR-AUDIT-009 and EBMR-IAM-002.

2. esig.sign on a VERIFIED co-signature challenge, using the verifier's SIGNATURE event; then esig.seal_signature, which succeeded.
3. Read payload->'actor' from kernel.audit_event for that esig.signature row.
4. set_config('ebmr.ctx', performer context overlaid with the verifier's person_id, account_id, role_code, auth_event_id and legal_name, true).
5. iam.assert_validated_actor() returned the verifier's context (role VERIFIER, the performer's session_id and device, the already-consumed signature auth_event_id).
6. INSERT INTO esig.stub_signable ('forged entry', '99', 'kg'); COMMIT. It succeeded.

The committed audit event for the insert records actor person_id = verifier, role_code = VERIFIER, and auth_event_id = the signature event. That is a data entry the verifier never made, paired with a session begin_command would reject (EBMR-IAM-111), with no fresh per-command authentication (INV-40 on a SHARED device).

Why this stands as a finding:
- It is not intended behaviour. ADR-0016 ("Consequences") claims that a validated command cannot swap in another person's context mid-transaction.
- The only bypass test (packages/kernel/test/identity/attribution.test.ts:148-171) swaps to a context that was never marked, so it does not cover this path.
- It is not in PROGRESS.md "Follow-ups carried into Phase 2" and is not deferred to a later phase.
- The attack needs only the application role's credentials, which ADR-0012 assumes may leak.

Critical severity is justified: it is a forged-attribution / Part 11 bypass that the application role can exploit.

Lesser related paths come from the same root cause:
- esig.stub_complete (0250:138) and the state engine (0550:389) leave the performer's context marked with a canned reason_code.
- The app could reinstall that context to UPDATE or DELETE audited rows under a reason the user never gave. That would get past the reason requirement (EBMR-AUDIT-002).

confirmed.title: verify_chain and anchors do not bind audit_event.table_name and record_id, so rewriting them is undetectable
confirmed.description: The payload hash covers 'table' and 'record_id', but the 'indexed columns differ from the hashed payload' check compares only seq, chain_key, action, correlation_id and recorded_at. The stored columns table_name and record_id are never compared with the payload. verify_anchor and continuity.external_anchor_problems check only (chain_key, seq, hash). Several consumers read these unhashed columns: record-level audit-trail lookups (index audit_event_record), iam.record_entry_persons (0170:472; the involvement set used for segregation checks), esig integrity (0240:66,150), DI-investigation extracts (0430:77-88), time-anomaly windows (0520:332-336) and the sample record's content_version (0910:17). kernel.audit_event also has no insert-only trigger, so the rewrite needs no DISABLE TRIGGER and leaves nothing in kernel.ddl_log. That contradicts DI-23's catalog test ('change an audit row directly in the DB ... the verification job alarms and names the entry') and threat-model DB-2.
confirmed.failure_scenario: As superuser (break-glass or DBA): update kernel.audit_event set record_id = 'other', table_name = 'testgmp.reading' where chain_key = 'batch:<b>' and seq = 2; Then select * from kernel.verify_chain('batch:<b>') returns 0 rows, and verify_anchor(<anchor taken before the change>) reports nothing for that chain (reproduced). The UPDATE drops out of the record's audit trail and out of iam.record_entry_persons, so the person who entered or changed the value is no longer in the involvement set used by segregation checks. No verifier flags it.
confirmed.suggested_fix: In verify_chain, also compare r.payload->>'table' IS DISTINCT FROM r.table_name and r.payload->>'record_id' IS DISTINCT FROM r.record_id. Use IS DISTINCT FROM for all the column comparisons so NULLs cannot hide a mismatch. Consider adding a reject_mutation-style trigger on kernel.audit_event (with an owner-only purge authorisation), so even owner-level definer code cannot alter rows in place. Extend the [INV-08][DI-23] tamper test to cover these columns.

Its 'indexed columns differ from the hashed payload' check compares only seq, chain_key, action, correlation_id and recorded_at. It never compares r.table_name with payload->>'table', or r.record_id with payload->>'record_id'. The row hash is not changed, so verify_anchor (line 456), which compares only chain_key/seq/hash, cannot see the rewrite.

confirmed.title: Full-database verification enumerates chains from audit_chain_head, so deleting a head row hides a tampered chain from the verification job
confirmed.description: verifyAllChains takes its chain list from kernel.audit_chain_head only. The backup-drill verification (continuity/backup-drill.ts:480) does the same. verify_chain checks the head only 'if found', so events without a head row are never reported as inconsistent. After deleting the head row of a chain, the scheduled whole-database verification never looks at that chain's events. Even naive tampering, with no hash recomputation, goes unnoticed. Anchors catch it only if the tampered event is at or before an anchored seq of that chain.
confirmed.failure_scenario: As superuser: update kernel.audit_event set payload = jsonb_set(payload,'{body,new,value}','42') where chain_key='batch:<b>' and seq=2; delete from kernel.audit_chain_head where chain_key='batch:<b>'; Then select ... from kernel.audit_chain_head h cross join lateral kernel.verify_chain(h.chain_key) returns nothing for batch:<b>, and verifyAllChains() returns [] (reproduced). A direct verify_chain('batch:<b>') would still report the hash mismatch, but the job never calls it.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Enumerate chains from `select distinct chain_key from kernel.audit_event` (union with audit_chain_head), both in verifyAllChains and in the backup-drill query. In verify_chain, report 'events exist but the chain head is missing' when events are found and no head row exists.

Root cause, confirmed in the code (packages/kernel/sql/0010_audit_trail.sql; no later migration redefines this function):
- packages/kernel/src/audit/verify.ts:18-22: verifyAllChains takes its chain list only from 'select chain_key from kernel.audit_chain_head'.
- kernel.verify_chain, lines 377-380: the head check runs only 'if found', so it never reports that events exist without a head row.
- The backup-drill query (packages/kernel/src/continuity/backup-drill.ts, verifyKernel) has the same flaw: 'from kernel.audit_chain_head h cross join lateral kernel.verify_chain(h.chain_key)'.

With the head row deleted, the whole-database verification skips the tampered chain. The tampering needs no hash recomputation. I found nothing about this in PROGRESS.md's Phase 2 follow-ups, so it is not a known item.

The only file I created is packages/kernel/test/review-tmp/f3.test.ts; git status shows no other changes.
confirmed.skeptic:
I could not refute this. The failure is real, it is reachable with plain DML (no DDL), and I reproduced it.

1. Enumeration from the head table. `verifyAllChains` in packages/kernel/src/audit/verify.ts:18-22 builds its chain list only from `select chain_key from kernel.audit_chain_head`. `verifyKernel` in packages/kernel/src/continuity/backup-drill.ts:480 uses the same list (`audit_chain_head h cross join lateral kernel.verify_chain(h.chain_key)`). Nothing in the repo enumerates from `kernel.audit_event`.

2. `verify_chain` is never redefined. Its only definition is 0010_audit_trail.sql:345-383, and it compares the head only `if found`. `records.verify_chain` (0440:384) just adds tombstone checks and then calls `kernel.verify_chain`. So a chain that has events but no head row is not reported, and it is never visited anyway.

3. Nothing else catches it.
   - `kernel.verify_anchor` (0010:456) and `continuity.external_anchor_problems` (0600:459-494) only compare the stored `audit_event.hash` at the anchored seq. They do not recompute hashes. After a naive payload edit with no hash recomputation, the stored hashes are unchanged, so every anchor check still passes.
   - The finding's line "anchors catch it only if the tampered event is at or before an anchored seq" is therefore too generous to the design. Anchors do not catch this case at all. With the head deleted, a naive edit to any event, however old and however well anchored, passes both the whole-database chain job and every anchor check.
   - Without the head deletion, the same edit is caught by `verify_chain`, as the existing test at audit-trail.test.ts:204 shows. That test covers altering an event, deleting an event and moving the head, but not deleting the head.

4. A chain with events but no head is never legitimate. The retention purge (0440:372-373) deletes the events and the head together. So the suggested check ("events exist but the chain head is missing") has no false-positive case from normal operation.

5. This is in scope. ADR 0007 and ADR 0012 say superuser rewrites must be detected by chain verification. DI-23 is marked IMPLEMENTED with verify.ts as its implementing module, and its behaviour and catalog test are: change an audit row directly in the DB, and the verification job alarms and names the entry. With the head deleted, that job names nothing.

6. It is not a known item. PROGRESS.md:133 only says that `verifyAllChains` must switch to the purge-aware `records.verify_chain`/`verify_anchor`. That is about purge-awareness, not about how chains are enumerated, and following it would not fix this. The Phase 2 follow-ups list at line 210 does not mention it either.

7. Reproduced. packages/kernel/test/review-tmp/f3.test.ts fails at line 67 with: "verifyAllChains reported nothing for batch:... after its head row was deleted". Its precondition assertions pass: with the head row present the alteration is reported, and after the delete the three events remain and a direct `verifyChain` still finds the seq 2 mismatch.

The attack needs database superuser rights, which the design says must be detected rather than prevented, so medium severity fits. A superuser could also redefine the verification functions, but that is DDL and would go to `kernel.ddl_log`; the head-row delete is DML only.

confirmed.title: kernel.ddl_log records no DROP statement, and audit_triggers_ok ignores the insert-only guard triggers
confirmed.description: log_ddl reads only pg_event_trigger_ddl_commands() on ddl_command_end. PostgreSQL collects no commands for DropStmt, so DROP TRIGGER, DROP TABLE, DROP FUNCTION and DROP RULE leave no row, and nothing handles sql_drop. ddl_log is supposed to make a disabled trigger or altered table visible afterwards (0010:70; also 0600:61 and records README). audit_triggers_ok (lines 327-339) checks only the zz_audit_* trigger and not the aa_insert_only_* or aa_no_truncate_* guards, so dropping a guard also leaves GMP writes enabled.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Reproduced as superuser: BEGIN; drop trigger aa_insert_only_testgmp_reading on testgmp.reading; the kernel.ddl_log count is unchanged (1539 before, 1539 after), and kernel.audit_triggers_ok() still returns true. INV-06 now depends only on privileges for that table. The owner, owner-level definer code, or any role granted UPDATE can mutate insert-only rows, and neither the DDL log nor begin_command shows that the guard is gone. By contrast, ALTER TABLE ... DISABLE TRIGGER is logged.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Add a sql_drop event trigger that logs pg_event_trigger_dropped_objects() (object_type, object_identity, session_user). Extend audit_triggers_ok, or add a separate guard check, so it requires the aa_insert_only_* and aa_no_truncate_* triggers of insert-only registered tables to be present and enabled.

confirmed.skeptic:
The facts are right, but the claimed impact does not follow. This is at most a low-severity hardening note, not a medium data-integrity defect.

What is true:
- kernel.log_ddl (packages/kernel/sql/0010_audit_trail.sql:492-503, never redefined later) reads only pg_event_trigger_ddl_commands() on ddl_command_end. PostgreSQL collects no command for a DropStmt, and there is no sql_drop trigger, so DROP TRIGGER leaves no ddl_log row.
- kernel.audit_triggers_ok (0010:327-339) checks only zz_audit_*. It does not check aa_insert_only_* or aa_no_truncate_*.

Why the failure scenario does not hold:
1. Only a superuser can do this. DROP TRIGGER needs ownership of the table. The owner, ebmr_owner, is NOLOGIN (0001_bootstrap.sql), and I found no role granted membership in it. No SECURITY DEFINER function runs a dynamic DROP TRIGGER; the only dynamic trigger DDL is purge's DISABLE/ENABLE at 0440:336-340, which is logged.
2. The other actors the finding names don't exist in production code. No production role has UPDATE or DELETE on any insert-only table. The only UPDATE grants are on stub tables (esig.stub_signable, platform.stub_record, market.stub_*). The UPDATE the reproducer relies on works only because the test fixture packages/kernel/test/support/fixtures.sql:19 grants UPDATE and DELETE on testgmp.reading to ebmr_app. So nothing reachable by the application role or an ordinary user gets through.
3. The mutation is not untraced. With the guard gone, an UPDATE or DELETE still fires zz_audit_* (kernel.audit_row_change, 0010:258-296). That trigger requires a validated begin_command context and a reason_code (EBMR-AUDIT-002), and appends a hash-chained UPDATE or DELETE event with the row hash. The change shows in the audit trail, which is the INV-07/INV-08 guarantee.
4. The design does not rely on ddl_log to detect a superuser, and it can't. ADR-0012 says a superuser is "detected, not prevented". ADR-0007, outline §4.7/§5.3 (lines 269, 328, 529) and architecture.md:935-941 assign that detection to pgaudit (DDL/ROLE/WRITE/MISC classes) writing to an external write-once sink, plus the chain and anchors. The same superuser can switch off ddl_log without any DDL (SET session_replication_role = replica), and can run ALTER EVENT TRIGGER ebmr_log_ddl DISABLE or DELETE FROM kernel.ddl_log. So the missing DROP row gives an attacker nothing they didn't already have. The in-code comments (0010:70, 0600:61, 0440:22) only promise that disabling a trigger or altering a table is visible, and ALTER TABLE ... DISABLE TRIGGER is logged.
5. The DI-23 check is scoped as documented. audit_triggers_ok is described as checking "its audit trigger present and enabled". DI-23's catalog_test (find no disable or purge function; a changed audit row is detected by verification) and its listed tests hold. INV-06 is enforced by privileges plus the guard trigger against every non-superuser role.

Residual item, low hardening, not a finding: add a sql_drop event trigger, and extend a fail-closed check to the insert-only guards, the same way esig.change_triggers_ok (0220:403) and platform.time_model_violations (0500:128) cover their triggers.

The reproduction is accurate, but it does not show a defect at the stated severity. The name part is documented behaviour, nothing is lost or forged, and the display harm needs a viewer that does not exist yet. At most this is low-severity hardening.

1. The code is as described. kernel.begin_command (0010_audit_trail.sql:92-114) only checks that site_zone is non-empty. The live kernel.validate_actor_context (0190_iam_actor_context.sql:23) checks legal_name only when it is present (line 85). kernel.append_audit_event (0010:218, 0010:225) copies both values from the context as given.

2. legal_name being optional is intended and written down: see the 0190 header comment (line 14, "legal_name, when given, is the person's current legal name"), packages/kernel/src/identity/README.md, and ActorContext.legalName?, which is optional in packages/kernel/src/db/command.ts. The printed name at the time is not lost.
   - Every entry carries the validated person_id plus recorded_at, which is the server's clock_timestamp.
   - iam.person_name_event keeps the name history. It is append-only (iam.protect_log blocks update, delete and truncate), and each row is stamped by a server trigger (0110:84-85).
   - iam.person_name_at(person_id, recorded_at) (0110:101) returns exactly the name that applied at the time. The codebase already uses this pattern elsewhere (0120:582, 0170:155).
   - A present but wrong legal_name is rejected (EBMR-IAM-117). So attribution cannot be forged, and "no printed name" in the payload does not break DI-22's requirement of the name at the time.

3. site_zone cannot falsify the time. The audit time is recorded_at = clock_timestamp(), stored as timestamptz and as a UTC 'Z' string inside the hash-chained payload. Neither the app nor a user can change it. The zone is only a rendering hint, and the site's zone can always be recovered, because there is one installation per site (outline L-41) with the site.zone policy.
   - The policy is described as the "IANA zone recorded with actor contexts the identity module creates itself" (0100:166). It is not described as a gate for every command.
   - Kernel migrations 0700 and 0720 deliberately open commands with site_zone 'UTC'. The explicit zone check exists only where the zone becomes part of a legal manifestation, in esig.sign (EBMR-ESIG-035).

4. The harm described has no concrete path in Phase 1. The finding's failure is a view or true copy that renders local time from the entry's zone.
   - No audit viewer exists: packages/ui-kit/src/index.ts is a Phase 0 skeleton.
   - Audit-trail review is Phase 4.
   - Outline 5.x says displays show *site* time, which a viewer can take from the site policy.

5. Only the application server builds the context. An ordinary user cannot choose the zone. Someone holding the app credentials would still be attributed to a validated person, could not move the UTC instant, and would leave the odd zone visible in the hash-chained entry. Nothing is bypassed, deleted or misattributed.

Separate note, outside F5: the same unvalidated context zone also feeds other code, and that is worth checking as its own finding.
   - The platform time-model trigger computes site_utc_offset from it (0530:273-275); assert_time_zone requires only a valid zone name.
   - records.create_schedule uses it when p_site_zone is null (0420:555), and that sets the site day used for purge (0440:96, 0440:275).

confirmed.title: Account lockout counter is reset by ANY successful authentication (including a single-factor badge tap), so lockout can be indefinitely evaded against an actively-working account
confirmed.description: DI-19 requires "lockout after N consecutive failed login or signing attempts" (default 5). authn_finish (line 437-438) locks the account when iam.consecutive_failures(account) >= authn.lockout_threshold. iam.consecutive_failures (0160:181-188) counts FAILURE rows in iam.authn_attempt only where `a.id > coalesce((select max(s.id) ... where outcome='SUCCESS'),0)` AND `attempted_at > last UNLOCKED`. The reset key is 'the most recent SUCCESS of ANY method or purpose'. Every successful authenticate() call inserts a SUCCESS authn_attempt row - including a bare single-factor BADGE_TAP whose purpose is COMMAND (authn_finish success path, lines 461-465; a badge tap needs no secret because v_kind is null for BADGE_TAP, so needs_secret=false and the TS service passes verified=true). So a routine, legitimate badge tap - the normal way an operator attributes each entry on a SHARED/GRADE_A_B terminal (INV-40) - silently resets the failed-password/failed-signature counter to zero. An attacker submitting failed PASSWORD or SIGNATURE guesses against a known login name never reaches the threshold as long as the victim keeps working, so the account never locks. The alerting half of DI-19 still fires (one AUTHENTICATION_FAILED/SIGNING_FAILED alert per attempt), but the automatic-lockout half - explicitly required by EU draft Annex 11 §11 'automatic lock-out after repeated failed log-ins' and supporting 11.300 - is defeated.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Empirically confirmed against a live DB (PoC): seed a SHARED-device operator (badge issued, threshold=5). From any terminal, submit 4 failed PASSWORD logins for that login name, then have the operator do one legitimate BADGE_TAP (COMMAND) - repeat 3x (12 total failed guesses interleaved with 3 taps). Result observed: TOTAL_FAILURES=12, consecutive_failures=0, account_locked=false, LOCK_EVENTS=0 - the account never locks despite 12 failed guesses, because each badge tap inserts a SUCCESS row with a higher id that resets the count clause `a.id > max(SUCCESS id)`. Attempts are serialized on the account row lock (authn_resolve `select ... for update`), so attacker guesses and victim taps simply alternate; the counter is pinned near zero indefinitely. Same effect from any success (login, signature, session unlock) on any device for that account.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Do not let a low-assurance/unrelated success clear the failed-attempt counter used for lockout. Options: (a) count consecutive FAILUREs since the most recent SUCCESS of the SAME purpose class (e.g. only LOGIN/SIGNATURE successes reset login/signing failures; COMMAND badge-tap successes do not), or (b) drive lockout off a persisted consecutive-failure counter on the account that is decremented/reset only by a full-credential success, not by BADGE_TAP COMMAND events. Add a test that interleaves successful badge taps with failed password/signature attempts and asserts the account still locks at the threshold (the current DI-19 catalog test only does N failures with no intervening success, so it passes without covering this path).

The probe tap returned purpose COMMAND with components ['BADGE'] and restricted=false, so it is a single-factor event that proves no secret. All 12 password guesses were rejected as AuthenticationFailedError with reason WRONG_SECRET, and each of the 3 taps succeeded.

Each tap therefore resets the count, and authn_finish's check (`v_failures >= authn.lockout_threshold`) is never met. No later migration redefines consecutive_failures, authn_finish or authn_resolve; a grep over packages/*/sql found only the 0160 definitions.

The loop then stops with lockedAtGuess=5, there is exactly one LOCKED event, and the victim's next tap is refused with reason ACCOUNT_LOCKED. confirmed.skeptic:
I could not refute the core mechanism. It is real, no later migration changes it, nothing documents it as intended, and it contradicts the control's own wording.

Code, all in /home/user/ebmr-review/packages/kernel/sql/0160_iam_authentication_sessions.sql:
1. There is one definition each of iam.consecutive_failures (line 181), iam.authn_resolve (line 247) and iam.authn_finish (line 405). grep finds no redefinition in later kernel or site-services migrations.
2. consecutive_failures counts FAILURE rows only where `a.id > max(id)` of any SUCCESS row for the account. That SUCCESS can be of any method or purpose. It also only counts failures after the last UNLOCKED event.
3. In authn_resolve, BADGE_TAP is allowed only for purpose COMMAND (line ~270). v_kind is null for BADGE_TAP, so no credential is looked up.
4. authn_prepare therefore returns needs_secret=false. packages/kernel/src/identity/authentication.ts:95-99 then passes verified=true to authn_finish.
5. authn_finish takes the success path and inserts an authn_attempt row with outcome 'SUCCESS' (lines ~461-465).
6. The lockout check at lines 437-438 compares consecutive_failures to authn.lockout_threshold. Each badge tap therefore resets the count to zero.

Scenario:
- The attacker needs an enrolled, ACTIVE, non-INSTRUMENT and non-SERVER device, plus the victim's login name. That is realistic for an insider.
- The attacker sends threshold-1 wrong-password LOGIN attempts. These go through authenticate() on the ebmr_authn path, and each records a FAILURE.
- The victim, working on a SHARED or GRADE_A_B terminal, taps their badge for the next GMP command, as INV-40 requires about every 60 s. This records a SUCCESS with a higher id, and the count goes back to 0.
- Repeating this gives the attacker unlimited password or signature guesses, and the account never locks.
- The row lock taken with `for update` in authn_resolve only serialises the attempts. It does not stop them interleaving.

Why this is a defect and not intended behaviour:
- DI-19 says "Lockout after N consecutive failed login or signing attempts".
- The policy row in packages/kernel/sql/0100_iam_foundation.sql:145 says "Consecutive failed login or signing attempts that lock the account".
- A BADGE_TAP COMMAND is neither a login nor a signing attempt. Under the stated requirement, 12 failed logins with no login or signing success between them should have locked the account.
- No ADR, decision, README, test or PROGRESS follow-up says that a badge-tap success should reset the count. It is not a known item.
- DI-19 is a Phase 1 control (target_phase 1, build_status IMPLEMENTED), so this is not work planned for a later phase.
- The catalog test ("[DI-19] five failed signing attempts lock the account...", credentials.test.ts:38) makes only uninterrupted failures, so it never exercises this path.

Limits on the finding:
1. Its claim of the "same effect from any success (login, signature, session unlock)" is standard reset-on-success behaviour and not a defect by itself. The defect is that a single-factor COMMAND badge tap resets the password and signing failure count.
2. Real mitigations reduce the impact:
   - every failure still raises AUTHENTICATION_FAILED or SIGNING_FAILED to the security unit, with acknowledgement and escalation, so the 11.300(d) detection half still works;
   - the attacker needs an enrolled device;
   - the victim must be actively tapping;
   - argon2id verification slows each guess.

Medium severity (a guarantee broken by an edge case) is fair, arguably low-medium. The fix direction in the finding is sound: badge-tap COMMAND successes should not break the run of login and signing failures.

confirmed.title: Independence, INV-03 and involvement rules are checked only when the constrained meaning is signed; signing the other meaning afterwards is never checked
confirmed.description: check_independence (lines 129-177) applies each rule only in one direction. It checks the meaning being signed against signatures that already exist: independent_of, excludes_performers (performers_of = content changers, the provider's entered_by, and signers of PERFORMER-class meanings) and excludes_involved. When the other side is signed later, nothing is checked. PERFORMED has no exclusions. PREPARED is independent of nothing. APPROVED is checked against CHECKED signers only if CHECKED already exists when APPROVED is signed. esig.sign accepts any caller-chosen expected state (line 432), and stub_complete (0250 lines 105-145) and the platform engine do not enforce the order in which signatures are made. esig.invariant_violations() (0240 lines 124-132) only looks backwards (`p.recorded_at < s.recorded_at`, `c.recorded_at <= s.recorded_at`), and it does not check independent_of or involvement at all. So the violation is neither prevented nor detected.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Both scenarios confirmed on a test database. (1) INV-03: A creates a STEP stub. B holds VERIFIER and OPERATOR. B, acting as VERIFIER, signs VERIFIED; performers = {A}, so it is allowed. I could not refute the lifecycle-binding part of F14. I reproduced it. The part about "used by another user" is weaker, and is by design in Phase 1.

**What the code does (last definitions checked; nothing later redefines these)**
- `esig.platform_signature_check` (0230:632-638) only calls `esig.signature_problem`. That checks the signature exists, has the right meaning and aggregate, and that `signature_state` is VALID (sealed, not invalidated, content hash unchanged). `p_actor` is never read.
- `esig.canonical_envelope` (0200:258-262) hashes only aggregate_type, aggregate_id, content_version and content. The provider's `state` is left out. The sample_record provider (0910) puts only title and body in the content.
- `esig.sign` (0230, around lines 423-427) compares the provider state with a `p_expected_state` that the caller chooses. It never relates that state to the meaning or to any transition. The challenge and signature rows do not store the state.
- `platform.transition` (0550:453ff; `verify_signature` in 0500:213) checks the transition permission, the single-use rule (`state_history_signature` unique index and PLAT-075) and the hook. Nothing ties the signature to the from-state, the command, the session or the time of the transition.
- `platform.stub_record_edit_guard` allows content changes only in DRAFT. So a signature made in DRAFT stays VALID through SUBMITTED and CHECKED as long as nobody edits the record.

**Reproduction**
I used a throwaway vitest file in my scratchpad and a fresh template database; no repository files were touched.
1. MBR_AUTHOR creates a sample_record.
2. QA_MBR_APPROVER signs APPROVED with `expectedState` 'DRAFT'. Accepted.
3. The author fires SUBMIT.
4. MBR_CHECKER signs CHECKED and fires CHECK.
5. A different person (QA_REVIEWER) fires APPROVE with the approver's DRAFT-time signature id. Result: `{from: CHECKED, to: APPROVED}`.

Stored timestamps: the APPROVED signature was recorded at 07:52:32.999, the CHECKED signature at 07:52:33.076. `esig.verify_signatures()` and `esig.invariant_violations()` both returned no rows. So a quality-unit approval that was signed before the independent check authorised the CHECKED -> APPROVED transition, and nothing detects it.

**Why this is a defect and not intended behaviour**
- ADR 0012 decision 3 and outline 5.5 step 3 say the signing function runs the record-state guard, inserts the signature and changes state in one transaction. ADR 0012 also says the rules must hold even if the application code has a bug.
- Outline 5.2.1 puts Sig(APPROVED) on the CHECKED -> APPROVED move. The implementation leaves the state guard entirely to the caller, and the engine accepts a signature from any earlier state or command. The database therefore does not enforce the signing order the machine is meant to encode. The same gap also makes the reverse-order independence problem (F13) reachable through the state engine.
- The documented adapter contract (B2 build plan: "valid, not superseded, bound to the record and meaning"; "record state via a caller-supplied expected state") describes what the code does. It does not say that out-of-state signatures are acceptable. The existing platform-hook test only proves that an early signature is refused once the content is edited.
- This is not on the list of known follow-ups. It is Phase 1 scope: "SECURITY DEFINER signing and transitions" and the state-machine engine are Phase 1 deliverables, and the adapter is listed under DI-37.

**Caveats that weaken part of the finding (they do not refute its core)**
- "Used by a person other than the signer" is expected in Phase 1:
  - Migration 0700 gives SAMPLE_RECORD.APPROVE only to QA_REVIEWER.
  - MBR.APPROVE, which is needed to sign APPROVED, belongs only to QA_MBR_APPROVER.
  - `esig.sign` filters authority by the session owner's declared role.
  - The late-entry co-signature (0530 `check_late_entry`) is by design signed by someone other than the actor and goes through the same hook.
  
  So a fix of "signer must equal p_actor" would be wrong. Binding the signature to the same command or session (correlation_id or session_id), or to the from-state, would work.
- "By anyone" is overstated. The signer still needs authority for the meaning and must pass the independence rules at signing time. The person firing the transition needs the transition permission. The signature must still cover the final content, since any DRAFT edit invalidates it. Each signature authorises only one transition.
- Nothing is lost without trace: the out-of-order timestamps are visible in the audit trail. But no guard or integrity job flags them.

Overall severity: medium, as claimed, for the unenforced signing order.

- signature_state recomputes the hash using the alias itself, so the row reports VALID.

What limits the impact, and what I checked that the finding already concedes:
- No gate accepts the alias signature. stub_complete takes p_id uuid and asserts with p_id::text. The approval functions build the id canonically: 0430:272 v.id::text, 0400:337 code:version, 0440, and 0600:727 p_event_id::text. platform.transition passes p_aggregate_id::text from a uuid. signature_problem compares aggregate_id text, so the alias is refused. No GMP action can be completed with it.
- For the real Phase 1 aggregates (di_investigation, restore_event), INV-03 still holds, because performers come from the provider's entered_by, which is computed from the row whatever the spelling. Only the once-per-meaning check (ESIG-042) is bypassed there. The INV-03 bypass is concrete for aggregates whose performers come from content_change or PERFORMER signatures: the esig_stub reference provider today, and Phase 2 signed tables that copy its `p_id::uuid` pattern.
- After a content change the alias signature is not superseded. It then shows CONTENT_MISMATCH, and invariant_violations does report it as INV-09. So that part is detected rather than silent, but it means any application user can generate INV-09 integrity alarms at will. The lock bypass only lets a stale alias signature slip through, and it would also end up as CONTENT_MISMATCH.

Why it is still a defect:
- The database accepts and seals a signing that its own rules forbid: a VERIFIED signature by the performer of that step (INV-03), and a second valid signature of the same meaning by the same person (ESIG-042).
- It stores that signature as VALID in the signature register and evidence package, whose manifestation shows the step as verified by the performer.
- The scheduled detective control (the INV-03 query in invariant_violations) misses it. Signature-to-record linkage is ambiguous: the row's aggregate_ref differs from the record's, although it signs that record's content.
- Nothing in PROGRESS.md follow-ups or the ADRs documents this as intended, and it is not deferred to a later phase.

Severity is arguably low to medium rather than clearly medium, because the rows are inert for every existing gate. The suggested fix is correct: make providers return the canonical id, and have create_challenge refuse or normalise any id that differs from it.

confirmed.description: content_version is 1 + the number of kernel.audit_event UPDATE rows for the record. The audit trigger records every UPDATE, including one that changes nothing. confirmed.title: ALL_APPLY strictness compares criterion ids only, so HARD India acceptance criteria can be replaced with looser content, either as a 'TIGHTER' site value or as an UPDATE while the rule is in force
confirmed.description: For ALL_APPLY, 'a at least as strict as b' is criteria_ids(a) @> criteria_ids(b). The content of each criterion (bands, sampling plan, rounding, stage) is never compared. Every guard relies on this comparator: assess_site_value (0320:61), classify_changes VALUE and HARD_FLOOR aspects (0340:111,116), compute_change_impact (0340:189,191) and the INV-28 second-line check (0300:864). EBMR-MKT-028 enforces identical criterion content only across rows of one document. It says nothing about a site value or about the next table version. A criterion that keeps its id but has weaker content therefore counts as equal or stricter. The TS engine behaves the same way. The INV-28 property tests use isAtLeastAsStrict itself as the oracle, and they generate criteria whose content is a function of the id ({id, plan: id-PLAN}), so this case can never occur in them.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Verified in a scratch DB built with the repo migrations and seed tables. (1) A master-data steward (MARKET.SITE_VALUE_SET, no justification, no approval) runs: select market.set_site_value(<site>, 'tablets.uniformity.acceptanceCriteria', '[{"id":"IP_UNIFORMITY_OF_WEIGHT_BANDS","stage":"IN_PROCESS","pharmacopoeia":"IP","bands":[{"deviationPercent":"50"}]},{"id":"PH_EUR_2_9_40_UNIFORMITY_OF_DOSAGE_UNITS"},{"id":"USP_905_UNIFORMITY_OF_DOSAGE_UNITS"}]', '2026-01-01'). It is accepted with outcome TIGHTER. An OPERATOR then calls evaluate_stub_scope for the site's {IN} tablet batch. The stored evaluation has resolved_value = IP bands 10 / 7.5 / 5 % (HARD, India) and effective_value = the single 50 % band, with site_outcome SITE_TIGHTER. market.batch_flags(batch) returns []. India's HARD value is loosened without a trace, and the record calls it a tightening. (2) The steward publishes tablets v2 as an UPDATE in which only B-14.IN.ipBands changes to the 50 % band (same id, effectiveFrom 2023-12-28). The publish is accepted with loosening = [] and impactCount = 0, so the SOURCE_CORRECTION gate (citation plus two approvers, EBMR-MKT-031) does not apply.
confirmed.suggested_fix: For ALL_APPLY, treat a as at least as strict as b only when every criterion of b appears in a with an identical canonical definition (same id and equal JSON). Make the same change in the SQL and TS comparators. In classify_changes and assess_site_value, treat a known id with changed content as a change that needs the loosening path (SOURCE_CORRECTION, or refusal for HARD). Add tests with same-id, different-content criteria, and give the property tests an oracle that is independent of isAtLeastAsStrict.

confirmed.title: evaluate_stub_scope lets the caller override the site (including JSON null), which drops a site's tighter value or applies another site's approved loosening
confirmed.description: The site whose value is applied is coalesce(p_req -> 'siteId', v_scope -> 'siteId'). A caller-supplied siteId always wins. JSON null wins as well, because p_req -> 'siteId' is jsonb 'null' and not SQL NULL. record_evaluation casts it to NULL, and apply_site_value then returns NO_SITE_VALUE. evaluation.site_id has no FK and no existence check. The TS API (EvaluateStubScopeRequest.siteId) advertises the override. Any role with MARKET.RULE_EVALUATE (OPERATOR, MBR_AUTHOR, BATCH_ISSUER, service accounts) can choose which site's values reach a GMP evaluation.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Verified. The site has tablets.compression.ipcSampleMaxInterval = '15' (TIGHTER than India's 30). An operator runs: select market.evaluate_stub_scope('{"key":"tablets.compression.ipcSampleMaxInterval","scope":{"kind":"PRODUCT","id":"<batch at the site>"},"resolutionPoint":"EXECUTION","asOf":"2026-03-01","siteId":null}'). Without siteId the stored evaluation has effective_value '15' (SITE_TIGHTER). With siteId null, or with a random uuid, it has site_id NULL or foreign, site_outcome NO_SITE_VALUE and effective_value '30'. The site's own stricter limit is bypassed. With siteId = another site that holds an approved LOOSENED value for the key, that site's loosening is applied to this batch.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Derive the site only from the scope (market.scope_markets). Refuse a supplied siteId that differs from the scope's site, including an explicit null. Remove siteId from the TS request type, or document it as assert-only.

Refuted as a high-severity defect. The behaviour is real, but it sits inside the caller-trusted inputs of a Phase 1 stub. It breaks no Phase 1 invariant or control, and it gives the caller nothing they cannot already do through other documented inputs. At most it is low-severity hardening.

What I confirmed:
- 0330_market_evaluations.sql:197 is the live definition. No later migration redefines market.evaluate_stub_scope, market.record_evaluation, market.apply_site_value (0320) or market.scope_markets (0310).
- I ran the finder's reproducer (packages/kernel/test/review-tmp/f21.test.ts) from the repo root:
  - siteId null gives site_id NULL, NO_SITE_VALUE, effective "30".
  - A random siteId gives the same result.
  - siteId = site B gives SITE_LOOSENED, effective "15".
- So the mechanics are as described, including the jsonb 'null' coalesce pitfall.

Why it is not the claimed defect:
1. **It is documented and deliberate.** The p_req contract lists `siteId?` as a caller input (0330 lines 108-109 and 154-155). The coalesce deliberately prefers the request, and the TS EvaluateStubScopeRequest exposes `siteId?`. The function says it derives only "the scope's markets and predicates" and protects only those two: the market set because record_evaluation is owner-only (tested by "[INV-29] ... cannot call the internal writer with a market set of its choosing"), and scope-fixed predicates via EBMR-MKT-055. The site is not in the protected set.
2. **No invariant or control named in the finding is violated.**
   - INV-29: the row stores value, governing markets, predicate branch, table version and inputs. The a_complete trigger recomputes from the stored inputs, site_id is honestly recorded in `inputs` and `inputs_hash`, and the row is audited and attributed to the actor.
   - INV-28 / IN-52: resolved_value (the strictest of India plus the batch's markets) is "30" in every variant, and the market set is derived from the scope and cannot be overridden. IN-52's behaviour text says nothing about site values.
   - ST-01, the control that governs site values and flagging loosening on affected batches, has target_phase 5 (compliance/controls/ST-01.yaml). Even then, in the site-B case the loosening is flagged on the subject through market.batch_flags, and site_id B is visible in the record.
3. **No distinct bypass.** The same outcomes are already reachable through other documented, caller-supplied inputs of this stub:
   - Skipping site A's tighter value: pass an asOf before the site value's effective_from. Nothing binds asOf, and the tablets IPC row has been effective since 2023-12-28, so asOf '2025-12-31' skips a site value effective 2026-01-01.
   - Getting another site's context for a batch: pass scope = a batch at site B with subject = batch A. `subject` is caller-supplied (record_evaluation line 141).

   So the stub already trusts the caller to name scope, subject, asOf, tableVersionId and site. The database guarantees the market set, the India floor, result/input consistency, attribution and audit, and all of those still hold.
4. **Phase scope.** Nothing in Phase 1 reads market.evaluation.effective_value to make a GMP decision (grep finds no consumer outside src/market). Per packages/kernel/src/market/README.md and the 0330 comment at lines 110-111, editions (Phase 2+) record evaluations through record_evaluation from their own SECURITY DEFINER functions that derive inputs from their tables, and the stubs are replaced then.

Residual hardening worth noting, at low severity: treat jsonb 'null' as absent, and make siteId assert-only (refuse a value that differs from scope_markets' siteId when the scope has one).

confirmed.skeptic:
I'm rejecting this as a high-severity finding. The mechanism is real, but it breaks no invariant or control, and nothing in Phase 1 acts on it. What is left is a low hardening item.

**What does happen.** I read `packages/kernel/sql/0330_market_evaluations.sql`. No later migration or site-services SQL redefines `record_evaluation` or `evaluate_stub_scope`. `record_evaluation` (lines 140-141) takes `coalesce(subject, derived-from-scope)`, and `evaluate_stub_scope` (line 195) passes `p_req->'subject'` through unchecked. I ran the reproducer already in the worktree (`packages/kernel/test/review-tmp/f22.test.ts`, run from the repo root). It confirms that a row with scope `PRODUCT:T-IN`, markets `{IN}` and value `"3"` is stored with `subject_id` T-ALL. That row is listed by `listEvaluations(T-ALL)` and lands in audit chain `market_evaluation:T-ALL`. A `SITE_LOOSENED` evaluation of scope I-ALL filed under subject I-IN is missing from `batch_flags(I-ALL)`.

**Why this is not a data-integrity, invariant or control violation.**

1. **The misfiled row is still accurate about itself.** `evaluation_complete` (lines 58-104) recomputes the result from the stored inputs. It also records `scope_kind`, `scope_id` and `market_derivation`. The derivation comes from `scope_markets` (0310 line 200) and names the source batch T-IN with markets `[IN]`, and all of this is covered by `inputs_hash`. Nothing is falsified, altered or deleted. The actor is the operator's own `person_id`, and the audit event records a true insert.
2. **INV-28 holds.** IN is in the set, and the value equals India's value.
3. **INV-29 holds.** Value, governing market, predicate branch, rule-table version and inputs are all stored.
4. **IN-52 is still met.** It requires resolving the strictest value across India and the batch's markets and storing it in the batch record. T-ALL's own evaluation still resolves to 12 over `{EU,IN,US}`, is stored under T-ALL and is flagged correctly. The positive controls in the reproducer pass. The extra row does not change or replace that result.
5. **The loosened flag is not suppressed.** The misfiled I-ALL evaluation is flagged under its subject, I-IN. I-ALL's own evaluation carries its `SITE_LOOSENED` flag.

**The free subject is intended and documented Phase 1 behaviour.** Both function contracts list `subject: {type, id}?` as an optional, unconstrained input (lines 108-109 and 152-155). Its purpose is to file an evaluation of a shared scope under the thing it serves: a LINE, ROOM, EQUIPMENT, SITE or MATERIAL_LOT scope filed under a batch, MBR or step. In Phase 1 there is nothing to check that link against. The stub tables have no batch-to-line, batch-to-MBR or step links. 0310 lines 15-18 say the stubs are replaced, not extended, when the editions arrive. Lines 110-111 say the editions will call `record_evaluation` from their own SECURITY DEFINER functions, which derive context from their own tables. The suggested fix needs exactly that entity model, which the phase plan (outline section 11) places in Phase 2 (MBR), Phase 3 (Tablets lots and lines) and Phase 5 (Injectables).

**No Phase 1 GMP decision reads evaluations by subject.** I searched the whole repo outside tests. The only readers of `market.evaluation` are `listEvaluations` and `batchFlags` in `packages/kernel/src/market/repository.ts` (plain listings), and neither is called outside tests. No release gate, disposition, market-add evaluation or retention logic uses a batch's evaluations yet; those arrive in Phase 4. So there is no concrete route by which the extra row loosens a GMP decision, and a claim that it would is speculation about later phases.

**The test name is accurate.** '[INV-29] the application role cannot call the internal writer with a market set of its choosing' claims only that `ebmr_app` cannot call `market.record_evaluation` directly, and the test proves that (permission denied; grant at line 215). The app also cannot store a market set that disagrees with the stored scope. Whenever the app goes through `evaluate_stub_scope`, `market_set` is the one derived for the recorded `scope_id`.

**What is left.** An app-chosen subject can add a self-described, foreign-scope row to another batch's listing and audit chain, and no test covers this. At most this is a low hardening or test-coverage item: pin the subject for PRODUCT, PACK and MATERIAL_LOT scopes in `evaluate_stub_scope`. It is not a high-severity defect.

confirmed.title: A PACK scope does not force its own destination for PER_DESTINATION keys, so an India-domestic pack can be resolved under US label rules
confirmed.description: The code comment says a PACK scope resolves a PER_DESTINATION key for its own destination. In fact the pack's destination is filled in only when the caller's stated.destination is null. Any destination in the batch's market set that the caller names is accepted. market.resolve skips the INV-28 check for NOT_COMPARABLE keys, and decisionRef is free text. The IN-52 test for this case never tries an override.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Verified. Pack PK-IN has destination IN and belongs to a {IN,US,EU} tablet batch. An operator runs: select market.evaluate_stub_scope('{"key":"kernel.label.manufacturingDate","scope":{"kind":"PACK","id":"<PK-IN>"},"resolutionPoint":"EXECUTION","asOf":"2026-03-01","stated":{"method":"PER_DESTINATION","decisionRef":"x","destination":"US"}}'). The stored evaluation has effective_value 'NOT_REQUIRED' and governing_markets ['US'], while its own market_derivation records destination IN. The India-domestic pack loses the mandatory, uncoded manufacturing date (B-15, Schedule M 17.3.1(d)).
confirmed.suggested_fix: For a PACK scope, set stated.destination to the pack's destination and refuse a different one with a new EBMR-MKT code. Apply the same rule in TS resolveForScope. Add the override attempt to the IN-52 PACK test.

confirmed.skeptic:
The mechanics are as described, but the finding does not show a defect with a concrete GMP failure path in this phase.

1. The mechanics are real. In packages/kernel/sql/0330_market_evaluations.sql:190, market.evaluate_stub_scope fills in stated.destination from the pack only when the caller leaves it null. No later migration redefines this function. market.resolve (0300, NOT_COMPARABLE branch) checks only three things: the destination is in the market set, decisionRef is not blank, and a row exists for that destination. So a PACK evaluation for PK-IN that names US is stored as NOT_REQUIRED, governed by US. The evaluate_stub_scope path is gated by MARKET.RULE_EVALUATE, which OPERATOR holds (0700). The TS resolveForScope in context.ts:90 behaves the same way.

2. The design documents explicitly make PER_DESTINATION a human choice, not a value derived from the pack's destination:
   - ADR 0008 decision 4 says "the author picks the governing source per pack destination; approval needs a regulatory decision reference".
   - Outline 3.3.1 says "the author chooses the governing source for each pack destination and approval is blocked until a regulatory decision reference is attached". ADR 0008's Consequences section adds "non-orderable rules need human decisions (PER_DESTINATION references)".
   - If the governing source always had to equal the pack's destination, there would be nothing for the author to choose.
   - The stated `destination` is therefore the author's chosen governing source, backed by decisionRef. The pack's destination is only the default when nothing is stated.
   - Accepting an explicit choice matches the documented design. The line 189 comment and the IN-52 test "[IN-52] a PACK resolves a per-destination label rule for its own destination" describe that default path, and the test proves it.

3. Nothing is hidden or forged. The stored row keeps stated.destination=US, the decisionRef, and market_derivation {source: PACK, destination: IN}. The trigger (evaluation_complete) recomputes the row, hashes its inputs, audits it and attributes it to the actor. INV-29 holds, and the mismatch is visible in the record.

4. INV-28 is not newly violated. For NOT_COMPARABLE keys, market.resolve deliberately skips the at-least-as-strict check, because ADR 0008 says "stricter" is undefined for label content. The project's own IN-52 test stores NOT_REQUIRED, governed by US, for a pack of an {IN,US,EU} batch. A PRODUCT (batch) scope also lets the caller state any destination in the set, by design. So the PACK path adds no new way to loosen India's value.

5. The claimed harm ("the India-domestic pack loses the mandatory uncoded manufacturing date") has no path in Phase 1:
   - No code reads market.evaluation or kernel.label.* keys to make a decision. A grep finds only 0330 and repository.ts.
   - Labels arrive in later phases: G-21 packaging is Phase 3, and the India-domestic label and IN-31 are Phase 4 (IN-31 target_phase: 4, build_status SPECIFIED).
   - IN-31(b) enforces India-domestic label content separately, through destination-class artwork templates that cannot be approved without an uncoded manufacturing-date field. It does not depend on this evaluation.
   - Validating the decision reference at approval belongs to MBR approval (Phase 2).
   - The stub tables are documented as "replaced, not extended". Editions will call market.record_evaluation from their own SECURITY DEFINER functions, which derive context from their own tables.

At most this is a hardening suggestion: refuse a stated destination that differs from the pack's, the way EBMR-MKT-055 refuses scope predicate overrides. That is not a high-severity invariant or regulatory-logic defect.

confirmed.title: Approvals behind loosening are unverified free UUIDs: source-correction approvers, the site-value QA approval and the policy loosening approval (loosening_requires and level are never enforced)

I read the cited code and it matches the description. The finding still describes a deliberately deferred placeholder that is documented. It is not a new defect, and it is not worse than the known item.

   - `market.set_site_value` (0320:171) checks that `qaApprovalId` is non-null.
   - `market.policy_version_guard` (0350:118) checks that `approval_id` is non-null.
   - The `level` and `loosening_requires` columns are stored and never read.

2. **The placeholder was intended and is documented.**
   - The B3 brief (`docs/build-plan/phase-1/B3-market.md` item 6) says to store the approval ids because "the signing module comes later, so accept an approval-record uuid". It asks for "two approver ids" for source corrections.
   - `PROGRESS.md` lists "approval uuids -> esig" as an open B3 integration item.
   - The market README describes exactly this behaviour: "two distinct approver ids", "a QA approval record" and "an approval record".
   - The finding admits the item is known. Its "worse than described" argument is only that the item was not copied into the Phase 2 follow-up paragraph, and that is a tracking lapse, not code behaviour. The failure scenarios are exactly what "approval uuids -> esig" already implies: the approvals are unverified uuids today. B7's scope was permission checks. The B2 follow-up list named only the records and continuity approvals for e-signature, and those are the ones that were wired. Market was never in that batch.

3. **The requirements belong to later phases, not Phase 1.**
   - E-signature approval of configuration items (policy versions, their approver and change workflow, what a loosening requires) is DI-09, which has `target_phase: 4` and `build_status: SPECIFIED`.
   - Showing a loosened site value on batches is ST-01, which has `target_phase: 5`.
   - DI-35 (phase 1) lists specific signature points. Source correction, site-value loosening and policy loosening are not among them, and the esig catalogue has no meaning types for them.
   - IN-52's behaviour and catalog_test say nothing about source-correction signatures. Its guard text ("two approvers") accurately describes the two approver ids.
   - Enforcing `level` VENDOR vs TENANT needs a vendor-profile path and tenancy that do not exist in Phase 1. PROGRESS says "RLS ... when tenancy lands", no policies are seeded (there is no `compliance/policies/`), and the only role able to define policies is `QA_MBR_APPROVER`.

4. **This is not a privilege-boundary bypass.**
   - Every path is gated by `iam.require_permission`: `MARKET.RULE_TABLE_CORRECT` (regulatory signer only), `MARKET.SITE_VALUE_SET` and `MARKET.POLICY_CHANGE`. Each also calls `assert_not_administrator` and needs a validated `begin_command` context.
   - Every write is attributed to the real actor (`published_by`, `recorded_by`, `author_person_id`) and audited in the hash chain.
   - Site loosening is still refused for HARD and DESIGN values, and it is flagged on every evaluation.
   - A loosening policy version can never reach a batch issued before it took effect (INV-47, enforced by the pin trigger).
   - Nothing is changed without trace, and the app role cannot escalate.

5. **The test is not misleading.** The source-correction test's name claims only "citation and two approvers other than the publisher". It proves refusal with one approver, with the publisher among the approvers, and with a blank citation. It does not claim the approvers are verified signers.

What remains is a tracking and documentation point: "approval uuids -> esig" should be carried into the Phase 2 or Phase 4 follow-up list, and `vendorNoticeRef` should be required when that wiring is done. That is not a high-severity code defect. Because the behaviour is intended, documented and scheduled for a later phase, I rate the finding refuted.

confirmed.title: An approved site loosening is re-applied to any later resolution (tightened table, other predicate branch, other market set) and is left out of the change-impact list
confirmed.description: site_value_in_force selects by (site, key, date) only. It ignores the predicates, market_set, table_version_id and resolution stored with the approval. apply_site_value maps 'LOOSENING against today's resolution, and the value was once LOOSENED' to SITE_LOOSENED and applies it. A QA approval given for one loosening (for example 12 to 18 against India guidance 12) therefore silently covers a different loosening: against a tightened value, against another predicate branch, or against another market's guidance. compute_change_impact deliberately skips approved loosenings (v_hit is false when LOOSENING and approved). The tracked change task that outline 3.3.5 requires for site values when a new table version arrives is never created. set_site_value also accepts a caller-chosen tableVersionId, including an older version, and a back-dated effective_from.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Verified. The steward sets kernel.managementReview.maxIntervalMonths = 18 with justificationRef and qaApprovalId (LOOSENED against India GUIDANCE 12). A kernel v2 UPDATE tightens B-24.IN to '6', and publish returns impactCount 0. evaluate_stub_scope for a batch at the site stores resolved_value '6', effective_value '18' and SITE_LOOSENED. The approval was for 12 to 18; the batch now runs a 6 to 18 loosening that nobody approved, and no impact item exists.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Bind a LOOSENED site value to the resolution it was approved against (resolved value, floor type, predicate branch, market set). Apply it only while the new resolution's value, branch and markets match; otherwise treat it as SITE_VALUE_INADMISSIBLE. Emit a change_impact item for approved loosenings whenever the new version changes the value they loosen. Refuse effective_from dates before today (site calendar).

3. The controls as written are met.
   - ST-01 behaviour and ADR 0008 decision 8 / outline 3.3.2 ask three things: a value looser than HARD is refused; a GUIDANCE loosening needs a CCS reference and QA approval; it is shown on every affected batch. None of them binds an approval to the baseline value, predicate branch or market set.
   - The re-assessment at every use keeps every binding guarantee. A new HARD value, hard floor or DESIGN contribution, from any branch or market, gives REFUSED and so SITE_VALUE_INADMISSIBLE, and the value is not applied. A row stored as TIGHTER or EQUAL that becomes a loosening is never applied (line 117, else branch).
   - The case the finding raises is still flagged on every batch through market.batch_flags. The evaluation shows the new resolved value (6), the effective value (18), the governing markets and the site_value_id, and the site_value row keeps the resolution it was set against. Nothing is hidden or left untraced.
   - IN-52's text says nothing about site values.

4. Other parts are later phases or already known.
   - Turning impact lists into tracked change tasks is marked "later" in the change_impact comment; the change-impact explorer is Phase 6.
   - ST-01's target_phase is 5.
   - In Phase 1, qaApprovalId is an unverified uuid. PROGRESS.md lists B3 "approval uuids -> esig" as an integration item, and B7 wired e-signatures only for record type, disposal, DI-investigation closure and restore. So an approval "for 12 to 18" is not an enforceable, bound record that this path could forge or widen.

5. The side points give no bypass.
   - A caller-chosen older tableVersionId or other predicates only change the stored baseline. apply_site_value re-assesses against the batch's current resolution, so HARD and DESIGN refusal and the need for a LOOSENED row with a justification and approval id still hold.
   - A back-dated effective_from also needs the same justification and approval id. It cannot change stored evaluations (insert-only), and it is not covered by the no-past-effect rule, which the README states for policy versions only.

Whether a QA approval should be re-confirmed when the guidance it departs from changes is a fair design question for the owner. The code implements its documented and approved design, so this is refuted.

confirmed.title: Concurrent apply_policy_tightening can leave a batch on a looser policy position (INV-47 race)
confirmed.description: The TIGHTENING guard reads the batch's newest pin (v_cur) without any lock and compares only against it. Two transactions can both see the issue pin and both insert. The audit chain-head row lock serialises them only in the AFTER trigger, after the check has already passed. market.batch_policy then returns the newest pin by recorded_at, not the strictest. If the looser tightening commits second, the batch drops back from the stricter position.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Verified. The policy has positions [A,B,C] and a batch is pinned at A. V2 = C (TIGHTENING) and V3 = B (direction LOOSENING, relative to C). QA reviewer 1 begins, runs begin_command and select market.apply_policy_tightening(batch, code, V2, 'CC-1'). QA reviewer 2, concurrently, runs apply_policy_tightening(batch, code, V3, 'CC-2'), which blocks in the audit trigger. Reviewer 1 commits, then reviewer 2 commits. market.batch_policy(batch, code) returns position B, direction LOOSENING. The batch went C to B, a loosening that took effect after the batch was issued. Run one after the other, the second call would have been refused with EBMR-MKT-085.
confirmed.suggested_fix: In policy_pin_guard, lock before reading v_cur: pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('market.batch_policy:' || batch_id || ':' || policy_code)), or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the ISSUE pin. Make batch_policy return the pin with the highest position rank.
confirmed.evidence:
Command: cd /home/user/ebmr-review && npx vitest run packages/kernel/test/review-tmp/f26.test.ts

Result: 1 failed. Every setup assertion passed, including the sequential control: applying V3 (B) after V2 (C), one after the other, is refused with EBMR-MKT-085. The failure is at the main safety assertion (line 140):

AssertionError: {"sawLockWait":true,"outcome2":"APPLIED","pins":[{"pin_kind":"ISSUE","position":"A"},{"pin_kind":"TIGHTENING","position":"C"},{"pin_kind":"TIGHTENING","position":"B"}],"applied":{"pinKind":"TIGHTENING","version":3,"position":"B","direction":"LOOSENING",...}}: expected 'B' to be 'C'

There, v_cur was read without a lock and only the uncommitted-invisible ISSUE pin (A) was seen, so rank(B)=2 > rank(A)=1 passed. Reviewer 2 then waited on reviewer 1's audit chain-head FOR UPDATE lock (0010:206) in the AFTER trigger.

The edit added a create-or-replace of market.policy_pin_guard in the per-test database, with the suggested fix: pg_advisory_xact_lock(hashtext('market.batch_policy:' || batch_id || ':' || policy_code)) before the v_cur read. With that, the test passes (1 passed). So the test fails only because of the missing serialisation.

Not in PROGRESS.md "Follow-ups carried into Phase 2" (not a known item). No other repository file was touched; git status shows only the untracked review-tmp directory.

The suggested fix is appropriate: an advisory or row lock per batch and policy before reading v_cur, and/or have batch_policy return the pin with the highest position rank.

confirmed.title: The 'retroactive' test for rule-table loosenings uses a client-supplied time zone, which can shift 'today' back by up to 7 days
confirmed.description: v_today is clock_timestamp() at time zone (actor context site_zone). begin_command and iam's validate_actor_context check only that site_zone is non-empty. Unlike esig (EBMR-ESIG-035), market never compares it with the configured site zone. PostgreSQL accepts POSIX zone strings with offsets up to 167 hours (for example 'X+167'), and 'Etc/GMT+12' also passes IANA validation. A loosening already in force is then classified as future. The UPDATE passes EBMR-MKT-031, and the version's stored loosening list records retroactive:false.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Verified. The steward's command context has site_zone 'X+167', which moves v_today 7 days back. The steward publishes kernel v2 as an UPDATE that closes B-08.IN.selfInspection at today-5 and adds a '36' month row from today-5. The same document under Asia/Kolkata is refused with EBMR-MKT-031. Under X+167 it is accepted with loosening [{...,'retroactive':false}]. Any resolution with an as-of date in the last 5 days now yields 36 months, where India's HARD value is 12.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Compute the publication date from the configured site zone (iam.policy_text('site.zone')) or from the database's UTC date, as esig does. At minimum, refuse a context whose site_zone differs from the configured zone.

Note: f27.test.ts was already in review-tmp (untracked, written 08:26, before this run), probably by an earlier attempt at this same task. I checked every assumption it makes and left it unchanged. No other file was touched.

- kernel.begin_command (0010_audit_trail.sql:92-115) and kernel.validate_actor_context (0190_iam_actor_context.sql:23, the last definition) only require site_zone to be non-empty. I could not refute this. The failure happens as described, and nothing in the code prevents it.

1. **Live code.** `market.publish_rule_table` is defined only in `packages/kernel/sql/0340_market_publish.sql`. No later migration in the kernel or site-services packages redefines it. Line 305 sets `v_today := (clock_timestamp() at time zone coalesce(v_ctx ->> 'site_zone', 'UTC'))::date`. `classify_changes` then marks a loosening as `retroactive` only when `v_from <= p_today`. `EBMR-MKT-031` refuses an UPDATE only when at least one loosening is retroactive.

2. **No check on `site_zone`.**
   - `kernel.begin_command` (0010, around line 100) only checks that `site_zone` is non-empty.
   - The live `kernel.validate_actor_context` (0190) checks the account, person, role, session, device and auth event. It never reads `site_zone`.
   - 0900 and 0910 do not change either function.
   - The only code that compares the context zone with `iam.policy_text('site.zone')` is esig (0230, around line 381, `EBMR-ESIG-035`). So the design already treats the declared zone as untrusted where it matters. The market publish path does not.
   - `platform.assert_time_zone` (0530) is used only by platform time-model inserts, not by the publish path.

3. **PostgreSQL accepts the zone.** On the local PG 16, `clock_timestamp() at time zone 'X+167'` gave 2026-09-21. The Asia/Kolkata date was 2026-09-28, so the date moves back 7 days. 'X-167' moves it forward 7 days.

4. **Reproduced.** I ran the untracked reproducer `packages/kernel/test/review-tmp/f27.test.ts` in `/home/user/ebmr-review`.
   - It uses a real seeded MASTER_DATA_STEWARD with an open session, running as ebmr_app through `begin_command`.
   - Control: under the configured zone, the kernel v2 UPDATE (B-08.IN.selfInspection closed at today-5, a 36-month India row from today-5) is refused with `EBMR-MKT-031`.
   - With `site_zone` 'X+167', the same document is accepted. The stored loosening reads `[{"from":"2026-09-23", "aspects":["VALUE","HARD_FLOOR"], "retroactive":false, ...}]`.
   - `market.resolve` for IN on 2026-09-25 then returns "36", where the HARD value is 12.

5. **Why this is a defect, not intended behaviour.**
   - ADR-0012 says the rules must hold even if the application's database credentials leak. ADR-0016 treats the ebmr_app role as a possible attacker.
   - ebmr_app can `SELECT` `iam.session` (0160:803), so a caller at the application role can build a valid steward context and choose any zone.
   - The trick gets around the SOURCE_CORRECTION route for loosening a value already in force. That route needs a separate permission (`MARKET.RULE_TABLE_CORRECT`), a citation and two approvers other than the publisher.
   - It also writes a false `retroactive:false` into the version record, and it shifts the `due_by` dates in the change-impact list (`compute_change_impact` also uses `v_today`).
   - None of this is documented. `PROGRESS.md`'s "Follow-ups carried into Phase 2" says nothing about the zone. It is not a later-phase item either, because IN-52 targets phase 1 and lists this gate as one of its guards.

6. **Mitigating factors, which justify medium rather than higher.**
   - It needs a live session of someone who holds the steward publish permission.
   - The backdating is limited to about 7 days.
   - The audit event records the odd `site_zone`, so it can be found afterwards.
   - A steward can already publish future loosenings legitimately.
   - The normal product would presumably fill `siteZone` from configuration. No API layer builds contexts yet; `apps/` has no `siteZone` references.

These points lower the severity; they do not make the failure impossible.

confirmed.title: A retention schedule can be put on any aggregate type, so e-signatures (and other records tied to a subject) can be purged while the record they sign is still retained
confirmed.description: create_retention_schedule excludes only the retention machinery ('retention','retention_rule_set','record_hold','tombstone','true_copy'). The record type code is not tied to the aggregate type, and the retention inputs are typed in freely. records.purge then deletes, for the schedule's aggregate type, the rows of every registered table, disabling each table's insert-only guard. As a result a schedule on 'esig_signature:<aggregate_ref>' purges every signature, seal and invalidation of a record while that record stays in retention. This goes against the outline 3.3.6 rule 'Audit trails and signatures follow their record', against DI-47 ('signature records at least as long as their subject record') and against Part 11.70 (signatures cannot be excised). A hold on 'batch:X' does not protect 'esig_signature:batch:X', because holds and blockers are keyed on the exact record key. The known follow-up 'retention of signature rows on purge (Phase 4)' covers the opposite case (signatures left behind after their record is purged); this path is worse. Incident and DI-investigation records are currently protected only by the trigger-name bug reported separately. Once that bug is fixed, a schedule on 'incident:<id>' lets an OPEN CRITICAL incident be purged: this deletes its incident_link rows and lifts the block on every linked batch, because disposal_refusals only looks at blockers attached to 'incident:<id>' itself.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Reproduced in a scratch database built from the repo migrations. The actors are one QA_REVIEWER (holding RECORD.RETENTION_MANAGE and RECORD.DISPOSAL_APPROVE) and the retention job. (1) select records.create_retention_schedule('esig_signature','esig_stub:<id>','BATCH_PROCESSING_RECORD','{"markets":["IN"],"manufactureDate":"2008-01-10","expiryDate":"2010-01-31"}') is accepted, and the effective retention is DATED 2011-01-31. (2) The QA reviewer signs RECORD_DISPOSAL_APPROVED on record_disposal 'esig_signature:esig_stub:<id>@2011-01-31' and calls records.approve_purge. (3) The job runs select records.purge('esig_signature:esig_stub:<id>'). Result: esig.signature rows for aggregate_ref 'esig_stub:<id>' go from 2 to 0, esig.record_signatures('esig_stub',<id>) returns nothing, and the signed stub row still exists. The same steps work on 'esig_signature:record_type_version:<CODE>:<v>': this deletes the approval signature of the register version in force, and records.record_type_approval.approval_signature_id is left pointing at nothing. In Phase 2 they work the same way on 'esig_signature:batch:<id>'.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Store the owning aggregate type on each record type and refuse a schedule whose aggregate type differs from it. Keep an allow-list of purgeable aggregate types. Never schedule records tied to a subject (esig_signature, esig_challenge, state, incident, di_investigation, record_type, iam, market) on their own: derive their retention from the subject automatically (an implicit dependency) and purge them only together with the subject. In purge, also refuse any incident or investigation that is not CLOSED.

I could not refute F29. I reproduced it against the live migrations.

The guard trigger names match here: insert_only_trigger(esig.signature) resolves to aa_insert_only_esig_signature, the name register_audited_table created. The name-mismatch bug affects only tables in the records schema.
- Deletion runs children first: seal and invalidation, then signature. The only foreign keys that point at esig.signature come from those two tables. records.record_type_approval.approval_signature_id and purge_approval have no foreign key, so nothing stops the delete.
- Holds and blockers match the exact record key only (open_blockers: h.record_key = v_key). inv22_violations checks the exact key too.

**Reproduction**
I ran a scratch vitest file from the scratchpad against a template database built from all migrations. No repository files were touched. Actors: QA_REVIEWER (retention manage), a signer QA_REVIEWER (disposal approve) and the SYSTEM retention job.
1. A stub was signed PERFORMED and VERIFIED, then a legal hold was placed on esig_stub:<id>.
2. createRetentionSchedule('esig_signature', 'esig_stub:<id>', 'BATCH_PROCESSING_RECORD', {markets:['IN'], manufactureDate:'2008-01-10', expiryDate:'2010-01-31'}) was accepted.

**Not intended or documented**
- DI-47 (target phase 1, IMPLEMENTED) says audit trails and signature records are kept at least as long as their subject record, and legal holds override disposal.
- Outline 3.3.6 says audit trails and signatures follow their record.
- The PROGRESS follow-up "retention of signature rows on purge (Phase 4)" is about signature rows left behind when their record is purged. Here, signatures are removed while the subject is kept, and even while the subject is under a legal hold. That is not the known item and it is worse.

- The path needs a QA holder of RECORD.RETENTION_MANAGE plus a disposal approver, and it leaves a signed approval and a tombstone, so it is not "without trace".
- The incident part depends on a separate bug being fixed and is speculative.
- The core bypass is still real: a hold or retention period on a subject does not protect its signature records. So this is not refuted, though the severity could reasonably be medium or high.
