confirmed.title: Schedule M 'expiry + 1 year' is skipped when the expiry date is missing, giving a shorter DATED retention instead of OPEN
confirmed.description: IN_SCHEDULE_M_EXPIRY has the predicate {"expiryLabelled": true}, and expiryLabelled is derived from whether an expiryDate is present. An unknown expiry is therefore treated as 'no labelled expiry': the Schedule M rule silently stops applying instead of being MISSING_INPUT:EXPIRY (OPEN). With licenceForm FORM_25 or FORM_28, the manufacture + 5 years rules then produce a DATED result. This contradicts the outline ('Schedule M expiry + 1 y (always)'), the README ('A missing anchor date makes the rule OPEN') and default R3 in the open questions ('stays OPEN when an input date is missing'). The TS and SQL copies share the logic, so the property test cannot catch it.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Verified with the TS mirror, which is proven equal to the SQL copy. Inputs {markets:[IN], licenceForm:FORM_25, manufactureDate:2026-01-10}, where the expiry is not yet entered or is cleared with update_retention_inputs(key,'{"expiryDate":null}',...), give DATED 2031-01-10. The same batch with its real 60-month expiry 2031-01-31 gives 2032-01-31. With FORM_28 and no expiry the result is 2031-01-10 instead of expiry + 2 years. approve_purge and purge accept disposal from 2031-01-11, more than a year before the Schedule M floor.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Remove the expiryLabelled predicate from IN_SCHEDULE_M_EXPIRY so that a missing expiry gives MISSING_INPUT:EXPIRY. Model 'product has no labelled expiry' as an explicit boolean input, separate from 'expiry date unknown', and use it for the Form 28 manufacture branch. Add a test for FORM_25/FORM_28 without an expiry.

Those periods are fixed rule rows in records.retention_rule (RET-2026.1, seeded in the migration), and no app function lowers them. Retention inputs are per-batch facts: market set, expiry date, certification status. The engine is designed to recompute from those facts, and correcting a wrongly entered fact is meant to change the result.

confirmed.title: The offline true-copy verifier accepts a fabricated bundle and an incomplete one, and purge accepts a table-subset copy as the archive
confirmed.description: (a) The verifier only checks that the bundle is consistent with itself. Nothing is secret and nothing is compared with an external reference: not the registered manifest_sha256, not the tombstone's chain_event_hashes or kept_head_hash, not an anchor. A wholly recomputed bundle is therefore reported VERIFIED. The tamper test at true-copy.test.ts:113 covers only an attacker who does not also rewrite the chain. (b) The completeness check loops only over records.tables, so INSERT events for tables left out of records.json are ignored. buildTrueCopyBundle(..., {tables:[subset]}) produces such a bundle; register_true_copy checks only the head; purge's EBMR-REC-038 check compares only head seq and hash. A disposal approval can therefore cite an archive that lacks whole tables, whose insert-only rows exist in the chain only as hashes, and the tombstone still records a verified true copy.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Reproduced with a script that uses no database. (a) Build a bundle for chain batch:1111... holding a row that never existed ('value': 99.999), one INSERT event whose body.row_hash matches it, the event hash, head, part hashes and manifest SHA recomputed. verifyTrueCopyBundleText returns ok:true and the CLI prints VERIFIED. (b) Take the same bundle with records.json tables:[] while audit-chain.json still holds the INSERT event for stub_b4.batch_reading: it returns ok:true, rows:0.
confirmed.suggested_fix: In the verifier, report events for any table not included in the bundle as 'incomplete copy', or require the manifest to list every registered table of the aggregate type. Have the CLI take the expected manifest SHA-256 or head hash (from the register, tombstone or anchor) and print UNANCHORED without it. Pass the manifest's table list to register_true_copy and require, before purge, that the cited copy covers every registered table of the aggregate type.

- Yet the tombstone records the subset bundle's manifest SHA-256 as the true copy of a purge whose purged_tables includes stub_b4.batch_reading (rowCount 2).

- records.approve_purge (line 199) checks only that true_copy.record_key matches.
- records.purge EBMR-REC-038 (line 298) compares only head_seq and head_hash.

- The event hash, head, part hashes and manifest SHA-256 all recomputed.

- The same bundle with records.json tables:[] (the INSERT event still in the chain) also returned ok:true, rows:0.

The verifier has no external input to compare against: no expected manifest SHA-256, head hash, tombstone or anchor. The genesis value is public (sha256('genesis:'+chainKey)).

I checked the code paths the finding cites. The behaviour it describes is real, but none of it is a Phase 1 defect with a concrete path to bypassing a rule.

(a) "A fabricated bundle verifies"

The header of packages/kernel/src/records/true-copy.ts (lines 12-16) and packages/kernel/src/records/verify-true-copy.ts (lines 1-7) both say "needs no database", and exit 0 means "every hash, chain link, checkpoint and row check passed". It never claims the bundle is authentic.
- A verifier that holds no secret cannot tell a wholly recomputed, self-consistent bundle from a real one. Catching that always needs an outside reference, and the design keeps that step separate on purpose:
  - records.true_copy stores manifest_sha256 (0420 lines 346-347: "so an archived bundle can be matched to the record later"). The CLI prints the manifest SHA-256 so it can be compared with that.
  - The disposal-approval signature content (0720 record_disposal_content) signs manifest_sha256, head_seq and head_hash.
  - The tombstone keeps true_copy_manifest_sha256, kept_head_hash and chain_event_hashes, and anchors keep the heads.
- A fabricated row changes the row_hash, which changes the event hash and the head. So a substituted bundle cannot match the register, the tombstone or an anchor. The kernel does not automate that comparison, but that is hardening, not a hole.
- Archive storage, fixity checks and the verifier e-signature on a true copy are DI-46 and DI-41. Both are target_phase 4 and marked build_status SPECIFIED. The records README says Phase 1 is only "groundwork for DI-40, DI-41, DI-46".
- The test at true-copy.test.ts:113 is named "...a recomputed manifest hash by the chain", and that is exactly what it proves. It never claims to cover an attacker who rewrites the chain, so it is not a misleading test.

(b) "Table-subset copy accepted"
- Choosing a subset of tables is documented, deliberate behaviour:
  - buildTrueCopyBundle's doc (lines 113-117): "`tables` narrows the registered tables included".
  - records.json holds rows "in the chosen registered tables" (line 6).
  - The manifest records `tables` and is covered by manifestSha256.
  - A test states the intent: "[INV-08] a bundle can be limited to chosen tables, and completeness is checked for them".
- So the completeness check running only over records.tables is the specified behaviour. A tables:[] bundle reports rows:0, and its manifest says tables:[]. Nothing is hidden, and what the copy covers is bound to the SHA held in the register and the tombstone.
- On purge, a true copy is optional: approve_purge takes p_true_copy_id default null, and records.purge accepts an approval with no copy. DI-47's behaviour and catalog_test, and INV-22 (outline §5.3: nothing purged before retain-until or on hold; purge only through the retention function, with tombstone and checkpoint), require no archive before disposal, let alone a complete one.
- Purging with a subset copy therefore allows nothing that purging with no copy does not already allow. Retention has ended, a QA person signs a disposal approval that names the exact copy (manifest SHA and head), and a tombstone is written. No GMP rule, privilege boundary or invariant is bypassed, and no attribution is lost.
- EBMR-REC-038 guarantees what it says: the cited copy covers exactly the current head (0440 lines 292-302). The tombstone records the copy's id and manifest SHA, not any "verified complete" claim.
- Requiring a complete archive before disposal belongs to the Phase 4 archival work (DI-46, and ADR 0007 point 7's "verified true-copy packages").

The finding's fixes (printing UNANCHORED without an expected SHA, and requiring a copy to cover every registered table before purge) are reasonable Phase 4 hardening. What it describes now is intended, documented Phase 1 behaviour or an inherent limit of an offline check, with no exploitable path. Refuted.

confirmed.title: An implicit DI-investigation blocker (activity after opening) appears without moving the blocker epoch
confirmed.description: The blocker-epoch contract (0400:99-103) is that the release module evaluates open_blockers, then locks the epoch inside the disposition transaction and checks it has not moved. open_blockers also blocks a record when the investigated person wrote to it inside the window after the investigation was opened (the audit_event branch). That write happens through the normal audit trigger and never calls bump_blocker_epoch; it is linked, and the epoch bumped, only at the next refresh or at closure. The epoch check therefore passes although a new disposition blocker has appeared.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Reproduced. Open an investigation on subject S with window [now, now+1h). open_blockers('batch',B) returns an empty list and lock_blocker_epoch('batch',B) returns 0. S then inserts a stub_b4.batch_entry for B. open_blockers('batch',B) now returns [DI_INVESTIGATION, blocks_disposition=true], but lock_blocker_epoch('batch',B) still returns 0. A disposition screen evaluated before the write, and signed after it, would release B.
confirmed.suggested_fix: When the actor of an audited write is the subject of an OPEN investigation whose window covers the write, bump the record's blocker epoch in the same transaction. This can be done in kernel.audit_row_change through a records hook, or by linking and holding the record at write time. Alternatively, make re-evaluating open_blockers under the epoch lock a documented requirement of the contract.

The mechanics are correct, but the failure the finding describes ("would release B") has no concrete path, either in Phase 1 or in the release design it relies on.

What is true: records.open_blockers (0440:47-54) has an implicit branch. It fires on an INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE audit event by the subject on the record's own chain inside the window. That write goes through kernel.audit_row_change (0010), and nothing in 0010 or any later migration calls records.bump_blocker_epoch. The only bump sites are 0410, 0420 (holds) and 0430 add_investigation_link, so the epoch stays the same until refresh or closure links the record.

Why this is not a defect with a failure path:

1. The epoch's documented scope is narrower than the finding assumes. 0400:99-100 says it is bumped "in the same transaction as any change to the incidents, DI investigations or holds linked to that record". The implicit branch is by definition an unlinked record, and what it reacts to is a write to the record itself, not a change to any incident, investigation or hold. The blocker epoch was never the token for changes to the record's own content.

2. No Phase 1 consumer relies on the epoch alone. Its only Phase 1 users re-run the blocker check after taking the lock:
   - records.approve_purge (0440:194-195) locks the schedule and runs disposal_refusals (which calls open_blockers) in the same transaction.
   - records.purge (0440:266-272) locks the schedules and blocker epochs, then runs disposal_refusals under the lock.
   So no Phase 1 path acts on a stale open_blockers result.

3. The release module that would compare epochs is Phase 4 (outline 11: "G-REL with evidence epochs"; ADR 0013 item 9). By design it cannot pass on the blocker epoch alone:
   - Outline 5.7 (L-45): each lot and batch has an evidence_version, incremented in the same transaction by "any write that can affect release (... correction, audit event in review scope)". The disposition transaction locks and checks these epoch rows. The subject's stub_b4.batch_entry insert is an audit event on batch:B's own chain (the implicit branch requires e.chain_key = v_key). That is exactly such a write, so the evidence epoch moves and the confirmation inside the signing transaction refuses.
   - G-REL item 1 (outline 5.2.7) also requires the records to stay QA_REVIEWED with unchanged reviewed-content hashes, and the batch audit-trail review's high-water mark to cover every in-scope audit event. A new entry after evaluation breaks both.
   - Release signatures are bound to a content hash (esig.content_hash_of in 0230/0220, with SUPERSEDED_BY_CHANGE invalidation), which also detects a change to the signed content.
   Because the implicit blocker can only appear through a write to the very record being dispositioned, the designed evidence-epoch, review high-water-mark and content-hash checks all catch it. The blocker epoch covers the other case: changes to incidents, investigations and holds that do not touch the record's own chain.

At most, the TS docstring on lockBlockerEpoch (retention-store.ts) and the records README ("compare with the epoch seen when evaluating") could note that the blocker epoch alone does not cover implicit DI blockers. That is a documentation note for the Phase 4 implementer, not a medium-severity concurrency defect: the stated failure needs a later-phase module built against its own specification.

confirmed.title: State engine accepts a signature applied before the transition's from-state, and by someone other than the actor, so one person can both check and approve (INV-04)
confirmed.description: For a transition that needs a signature, platform.transition checks only four things: the signature id is well formed, it has not been used by an earlier transition, and the SIGNATURE hook says it is a valid, unsuperseded signature with that meaning on that aggregate. It does not require the signature to have been applied after the aggregate entered the from-state, so it is not bound to the aggregate version or state. It also does not require the signer to be the actor: the hook receives p_actor, and esig.platform_signature_check ignores it. The signed content hash leaves out the state (esig.canonical_envelope hashes only content_version and content). esig.sign lets the caller pass any p_expected_state, so an APPROVED signature can be applied while the record is still DRAFT. esig independence rules look only at earlier signers: APPROVED excludes earlier PREPARED/CHECKED signers, and CHECKED excludes only PREPARED signers. Signing in reverse order therefore defeats them, and the engine then accepts the early signature. Nothing in iam statically separates MBR_CHECKER from QA_MBR_APPROVER.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Person P holds MBR_CHECKER and QA_MBR_APPROVER. (1) The author inserts platform.stub_record R and creates its state (DRAFT, content_version 1). (2) P, in a command with role QA_MBR_APPROVER, calls esig.create_challenge('sample_record', R, 1, 'APPROVED', <hash>) and then esig.sign(<challenge>, <auth event>, 'DRAFT'). This gives a valid APPROVED signature S_A, because no CHECKED signer exists yet. (3) The author calls platform.transition('sample_record','sample_record',R,'SUBMIT',1,'{}'). (4) P, with role MBR_CHECKER, signs CHECKED (independent_of = PREPARED only, so it passes) as S_C and fires CHECK with S_C. (5) Any SAMPLE_RECORD.APPROVE holder calls platform.transition(...,'APPROVE',3,'{"signature_id":"S_A"}'). verify_signature passes (right meaning and aggregate, content unchanged, never used), and R becomes APPROVED with checker = approver and an approval signature dated before the check. The same gap lets a signature taken before a RETURN to DRAFT be used after resubmission, as long as the content did not change.
confirmed.suggested_fix: In platform.transition, require the signature's recorded_at to be later than the aggregate's latest state_history.recorded_at. Better: store the aggregate version or from-state in the challenge and signature and require it to equal v_state.version/v_state.state. Require signer = actor unless the transition declares a co-signature, which means passing the actor through the SIGNATURE hook and checking it there. Make esig independence symmetric by also excluding persons who hold later-applied meanings listed as incompatible (CHECKED vs APPROVED). Add a bypass test with real esig signatures signed in reverse order.

2. platform.verify_signature (0500:213) passes v_ctx to the SIGNATURE hook. The registered hook, esig.platform_signature_check (0230:632, registered in 0910), ignores p_actor and returns esig.signature_problem. That function checks only that the signature exists, has the right meaning, belongs to the right aggregate, and is VALID (sealed, not invalidated, content hash unchanged).

3. esig.canonical_envelope (0200) hashes only aggregate_type, aggregate_id, content_version and content. The provider's 'state' is left out, so a state change never makes a signature CONTENT_MISMATCH. Signatures are invalidated only by content changes (the only insert is at 0220:312).

4. esig.sign (0230:432) compares the provider state only with p_expected_state, which the caller supplies ("the record state the caller saw", signing.ts:107). It is a check against a stale screen, not a rule about which state each meaning may be signed in. That falls short of ADR-0012 decision 3, which lists "record state" among the signing guards and says the rules must hold even when the application has a bug.

5. esig.check_independence (0230:129) excludes only earlier signers of the meanings in independent_of. So the reverse order passes both checks.

6. iam has no static role-incompatibility rule; evaluate_segregation is purely dynamic.

This breaks INV-04 ("author, checker and approver are distinct persons (checker = approver only if S4 allows)"; S4 defaults to no). It also breaks DI-17 (target_phase 1, IMPLEMENTED: "the MBR author, checker and QU approver are three different users"). What checks out: in 0530_platform_time_model.sql, occurred_trust is in the ebmr_app column INSERT grant on platform.stub_step_entry (line 323). platform.time_basis picks occurred_at only for DEVICE_SYNCED. platform.is_late_entry counts only USER_CLAIMED and PAPER as late. No later migration redefines stub_step_entry_time_model or these helpers. So the sample insert would be accepted with is_late=false and time_basis='OCCURRED_AT'.

Why it is still not a finding:

1. It is documented, intended behaviour. packages/kernel/src/time/README.md, in the "Two times per event" table, lists occurred_at + occurred_trust as "Set by: caller, optional". Open question T2 in docs/decisions/phase-1-open-questions.md records the owner's default: only person-claimed times are late, and device-buffered times are not. The only related PROGRESS item (which trusts count as late) is already on the owner-question list.

2. The table is a demonstration with no consumers. The file calls platform.stub_step / stub_step_entry "Demonstration tables". A grep finds nothing outside 0530 and the tests that reads stub_step_entry or its time_basis, and no hold-time or other time constraint exists in Phase 1. The claimed harm (late-entry controls skipped, hold times evaluated at a claimed time) has no GMP record or constraint to act on in this phase.

3. The proposed fix needs things from later phases. Deriving trust from a reading, a device and that device's sync state requires:
   - data points with channel, reading, entry mode and device (outline section 5 data model);
   - the site gateway that "buffers with source timestamps and stamps device IDs from each device's enrolled identity" (outline 4.6);
   - instrument integration controls DI-20 and DI-32.
   The site-gateway core and data-point blocks are Phase 2 (outline section 11), and full instrument adapters are Phase 6. In Phase 1, INSTRUMENT devices cannot even open a session (0160 line 289), so there is no reading or instrument identity to derive trust from. The late-entry control itself, DI-28, has target_phase 4.

4. No Phase 1 control is concretely violated. DI-27 requires that the time of an action comes from the server clock and that user-entered event times are kept separate and flagged. INV-16 requires that recorded_at comes from the database clock and that any claimed time is stored separately with a trust level. Both still hold: recorded_at is forced by enforce_db_time and cannot be granted to the app, and occurred_at is a separate column.

5. The "ordinary operator" framing is overstated. An operator does not run SQL; the application chooses the trust. Exploiting this needs an application bug or stolen application credentials. With those, the caller could equally leave out occurred_at to avoid late-entry handling, or send any measured value, because nothing in Phase 1 lets the database check where a value came from.

For Phase 2: when real data-point tables are built on this pattern, trust should be derived from the reading and device record rather than accepted from the caller.

confirmed.title: Time-fault review windows are bounded by the faulty clock, so entries recorded across a clock step are never flagged
confirmed.description: window_start is the recorded_at of the last within-threshold sample, window_end is the clearance's recorded_at, and entries are selected by kernel.audit_event.recorded_at between the two. All three values come from the same database clock whose fault is being reviewed. A large offset usually appears or is corrected by a step: VM snapshot revert or hypervisor sync, a manual date change, failover to a node that is behind, or an NTP step correction. After such a step the entries' recorded_at fall outside [window_start, window_end] and are left out of the DI-27 review list. The TIME_FAULT_WINDOW row flag (0530 line 305) only covers entries inserted after the alarm commits, so entries between the step and the alarm are missed by both mechanisms. Only the per-aggregate CLOCK_REGRESSION flag can catch them, and only when that aggregate had a later event.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Backward step: (1) A check at node time 10:00:00 is healthy (last good sample 10:00:00). (2) At true 10:00:20 the node clock steps back 1 h. (3) Operators record entries whose audit_event.recorded_at is 09:00:20-09:00:59. (4) The check at node 09:01:00 sees offset -3600 s and raises DRIFT_EXCEEDED with window_start 10:00:00, which is later than the alarm's own recorded_at. (5) Entries continue from 09:01 to 09:30, the clock is corrected, and a check at node 10:31 clears the alarm. (6) select * from platform.entries_in_time_fault_windows() lists none of the entries from 09:00:20 to 09:30, because all are earlier than window_start. Forward case: the node is 5 s ahead, NTP steps it back at T and the clearing check runs at T+1 s. window_end is T+1, and entries from the last 4 s before the step (recorded_at in (T+1, T+5]) are omitted. The DI-27 window test covers only REFERENCE_LOST with a correct clock.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Bound windows by a position that does not depend on the clock. Store the kernel.audit_event id high-water mark (or pg_current_xact_id/WAL LSN) with each drift sample, alarm and clearance, and select entries by id range. Also report entries whose recorded_at is below the last good sample's recorded_at but whose id is above it. Add a test that simulates backward and forward steps by inserting samples and entries with shifted times through a superuser set-up.
confirmed.evidence:
I ran `cd /home/user/ebmr-review && npx vitest run packages/kernel/test/review-tmp/f43.test.ts`. The test fails, and only at the final safe-behaviour assertion (line 193). The positive controls at lines 166 and 180 pass. They show that, before the step's recorded_at values are rewritten, the same entries are listed for the open alarm. So the alarm, the window and the entry filter are set up correctly, and the entries disappear only because of the clock-stamped times.

Output:
AssertionError: DI-27 review list per alarm; windows and entry times: {"backward":{"window":{"window_start":"2026-09-28 09:05:06.427619+00","window_end":"2026-09-28 09:05:06.512253+00"},"entries":{"682d8966-...":"2026-09-28 08:05:06.452553+00","62cdc4d6-...":"2026-09-28 08:05:06.499094+00"},"e1Flags":[],"e2Flags":["TIME_FAULT_WINDOW"]},"forward":{"window":{"window_start":"2026-09-28 09:05:06.520055+00","window_end":"2026-09-28 09:05:06.578428+00"},"entries":{"cf1f177e-...":"2026-09-28 09:05:36.563337+00"},"e3Flags":["TIME_FAULT_WINDOW"]}}: expected { backward: [], forward: [] } to deeply equal { backward: [ …(2) ], …(1) }
  - backward: [62cdc4d6-..., 682d8966-...]  - forward: [cf1f177e-...]
  + backward: []                            + forward: []
Tests 1 failed (1)

What this shows:
- Backward step: the DRIFT_EXCEEDED window runs from 09:05:06.43 (the last good sample, from the true clock) to 09:05:06.51 (the clearance). Both entries carry audit recorded_at 08:05:06, because the clock had stepped back 1 h. platform.entries_in_time_fault_windows() (0520:328-339) returns nothing for that alarm.
- E1 was recorded after the step but before the alarm. Its review_flags are [] (no TIME_FAULT_WINDOW), so both mechanisms miss it, as the finding says.
- Forward case: window_end is 09:05:06.578 (the clearance, after the NTP step). The entry was stamped 09:05:36.56 while the node ran 30 s ahead, so it is left out even though its row has TIME_FAULT_WINDOW.

Then a superuser set-up, using the existing helper withTriggersDisabled (session_replication_role = replica for that one transaction), shifts recorded_at on the rows written after the step and before the correction. The rows are in kernel.audit_event, platform.drift_sample and platform.alarm. The last good sample and the clearance keep their true times, which is exactly what a stepped node clock would produce.

A fix that bounds windows by clock-independent positions (such as audit_event id high-water marks) would list E1, E2 and E3 and pass. The same holds for a fix that widens windows by the measured offset. PROGRESS.md's Phase 2 follow-ups do not mention this, so it is not a known item.
confirmed.skeptic:
I could not refute this finding. The defect is real, although I think "medium" fits better than "high".

What I checked in /home/user/ebmr-review (Phase 1 merge ff630ae):

1. **These functions are still live.** No later migration redefines time_fault_windows, entries_in_time_fault_windows, time_window_start or raise_alarm. 0900_integration_wiring.sql redefines only raise_time_incident, and that version still calls raise_alarm, so window_start still comes from time_window_start. Nothing in packages/site-services/sql touches them.

2. **All three bounds come from the clock under review.** In 0520 lines 77-84, time_window_start takes max(drift_sample.recorded_at) over the node's within-threshold samples. drift_sample.recorded_at, alarm_clearance.recorded_at and kernel.audit_event.recorded_at all come from clock_timestamp(): enforce_db_time forces the first two, and kernel.append_audit_event in 0010 lines 195 and 232 sets the third. Nothing makes audit_event.recorded_at monotonic.
   - time_fault_windows (0520:310-317) returns window_end = c.recorded_at.
   - entries_in_time_fault_windows (0520:328-339) selects entries with `e.recorded_at >= w.window_start and (w.window_end is null or e.recorded_at <= w.window_end)`. It never uses audit_event.id or any other ordering that is independent of the clock.
   - The monitor (drift-monitor.ts lines 10-13) measures the offset against the database's own clock_timestamp(), so a 1 h step back shows as a -3600 s offset and raises DRIFT_EXCEEDED.

3. **The backward-step trace holds.**
   - The healthy check at node time 10:00:00 leaves a within-threshold sample at 10:00:00.
   - After the clock steps back 1 h, the check at 09:01 raises DRIFT_EXCEEDED. time_window_start(node, current check) returns 10:00:00, which is later than the alarm's own recorded_at of 09:01.
   - Entries at 09:00:20-09:30 fail `e.recorded_at >= window_start` and are left out of the DI-27 review list.
   - The TIME_FAULT_WINDOW row flag (0530:305) is set only in the stub_step_entry trigger and only once the alarm has committed.
   - next_aggregate_seq is called only from 0530:297 (stub_step_entry) and 0550:359 (state engine). It flags only aggregates that already had a later recorded_at, so a new batch or any other audited table gets no flag at all.
   - The incident text built in 0900 ("Entries recorded from <window_start> ... are flagged") also points QA at the wrong interval.

4. **The ahead-then-corrected case is the stronger scenario.** A node that is ahead and then corrected by a step makes window_end (the clearance time on the corrected clock) earlier than the recorded_at of entries made just before the correction.
   - Example: a node 10 min ahead is fixed and the next check, 1 min later, clears the alarm.
   - The review list then omits every entry made during the fault whose recorded_at falls in (T+1 min, T+10 min].
   - ntpd steps any offset above 128 ms by default, so this is a normal way for a positive DRIFT_EXCEEDED fault to end, not an exotic one.

5. **Documentation does not cover it.**
   - docs/decisions/phase-1-open-questions.md T5 makes a step back that stays within threshold a documented choice ("flagged and ordered by counter, no incident"). That part of the finding is by design.
   - T5 does not cover a step large enough to raise DRIFT_EXCEEDED. For that case DI-27's behaviour applies: "entries made during the fault are flagged for review". The one generic mechanism for doing that leaves out exactly the entries that carry the faulty time.
   - The ha-and-restore.md runbook check (clock_timestamp() later than the newest audit recorded_at before writes resume on a new primary) covers failover only. It does not cover a manual date change, a hypervisor step or an NTP step on a running primary.
   - This is not a PROGRESS.md Phase 2 follow-up, and DI-27 is target_phase 1 with status IMPLEMENTED.

6. **The test does not exercise a clock step.** The DI-27 test "entries recorded in a fault window are flagged for review" covers only REFERENCE_LOST with a correct clock.

On severity: the failure needs an infrastructure clock step, and neither the application role nor an ordinary user can cause one. An incident is still raised and the stub rows made after the alarm still carry TIME_FAULT_WINDOW. So medium fits better than high, but the finding stands as a defect.

confirmed.title: Edit guard and SUBMIT guard read each other's rows without locking: content can change after submission and the has_body guard can be bypassed
confirmed.description: The edit trigger allows an update when a plain SELECT of platform.aggregate_state shows DRAFT, with no lock. platform.transition locks only the aggregate_state row, and the has_body guard reads stub_record with a plain MVCC read. The two transactions therefore never conflict (write skew). Outline 5.2 requires guards to run 'with the relevant rows locked'. The sample record is the stand-in for MBR versions, policies and rule tables, so this edit/guard pattern will be copied. Signatures are not affected, because esig.content_changed and esig.sign serialise on esig.aggregate_lock, but SUBMIT carries no signature.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Session A: begin; select kernel.begin_command(<author>); update platform.stub_record set body = '' where id = R. The trigger sees DRAFT and passes, and the transaction stays open. Session B: begin; select kernel.begin_command(<author>); select platform.transition('sample_record','sample_record',R,'SUBMIT',1,'{}'). has_body reads the committed non-empty body and passes; commit. Session A: commit. R is now SUBMITTED with an empty body, and its content changed after the submission committed. Neither EBMR-PLAT-074 nor EBMR-PLAT-068 fired.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Make the edit trigger take a lock that conflicts with the transition's FOR UPDATE: select state ... from platform.aggregate_state ... for share. Alternatively, have platform.transition (or each content guard) lock the domain row with select ... for update before evaluating guards. Document this as a rule for every guard/edit pair and add a two-session race test.
confirmed.evidence:
Command: cd /home/user/ebmr-review && npx vitest run packages/kernel/test/review-tmp/f44.test.ts

Result: 1 test, 1 failed. It fails on the final safe-behaviour assertion. The sequential positive controls all passed first:
- SUBMIT of an empty body is refused with EBMR-PLAT-068.
- An edit after SUBMIT is refused with EBMR-PLAT-074.
- The actors can edit a DRAFT and submit it.

So the setup is correct, and only the interleaving changes the outcome.

Failure output (evidence JSON):
{"scenario1":{"editA":{"ok":true},"submitB_before_commitA":{"status":"blocked","waitingOn":"transactionid:ShareLock"},"commitA":null,"submitB":{"ok":true},"commitB":null,"final":{"state":"SUBMITTED","version":"2","body":""}},

AssertionError: expected [ …(2) ] to deeply equal []
+ "scenario 1: record SUBMITTED with an empty body (sample_record.has_body bypassed, EBMR-PLAT-068 never fired)"
+ "scenario 2: record SUBMITTED but its content changed after submission to \"changed after submission\" (EBMR-PLAT-074 never fired)"

What happens in each scenario:
- Scenario 1 (the finding's order):
  1. A updates the body to '' in an open command. The edit guard sees DRAFT and passes.
  2. B calls platform.transition SUBMIT. The has_body guard reads the committed, non-empty body and passes.
  3. Only after the guard has passed does B wait (transactionid ShareLock). The wait is on the audit chain-head row for 'sample_record:R' (kernel.audit_chain_head FOR UPDATE, 0010), which A holds.
  4. A commits, then B completes and commits. R ends up SUBMITTED with an empty body.
- Scenario 2 (reverse order):
  1. B's SUBMIT runs and stays open.
  2. A's update runs. The edit guard reads DRAFT from a plain SELECT and passes.
  3. A then waits on the same chain-head lock. B commits, A resumes and commits.
  4. The SUBMITTED record's body is changed after submission.

Neither guard takes a lock the other side conflicts with before it runs:
- The edit guard (0551:21) does a plain SELECT on aggregate_state.
- has_body (0551:36-40) does a plain SELECT on stub_record.
- platform.transition (0550:473-474) locks only the aggregate_state row.

The only blocking comes from the audit chain head, which is taken after the guards have already been evaluated.

Nuance: the finding says <author> for both sessions, but the two commands need different iam.session rows. kernel.validate_actor_context (0190:91) runs `select ... from iam.session ... for update`, so two commands in the same session are serialised as a whole. The test therefore uses two MBR_AUTHOR actors, which models two authors or one person on two workstations.

Expected behaviour after a fix (reasoned, not run, because repo SQL must not be edited):
- If the edit guard takes FOR SHARE on aggregate_state, or the transition takes FOR UPDATE on stub_record before running guards, the loser waits and then re-reads committed data.
- Scenario 1 would then refuse with EBMR-PLAT-068 and scenario 2 with EBMR-PLAT-074, and the test would pass.
confirmed.skeptic:
I could not refute F44. I confirmed it by reading the code and by running a reproducer.

Code (these are the live definitions; no later migration redefines them):
- packages/kernel/sql/0551_platform_sample_record.sql:16-27. platform.stub_record_edit_guard is a BEFORE UPDATE trigger. It checks the state with a plain `select state ... from platform.aggregate_state` and takes no lock.
- 0551:33-41. platform.guard_sample_record_has_body is a STABLE SQL function that reads stub_record with a plain MVCC read.
- packages/kernel/sql/0550_platform_state_engine.sql:453-537. platform.transition is the only definition. It locks only the aggregate_state row (`for update`, line 474), then runs the guards (line 512).

Other locks on the path, and why none of them closes the race:
- iam.platform_authority (0710) runs before the guards and takes no lock that the edit also takes.
- The AFTER-row audit trigger locks the chain head of 'sample_record:R' (kernel.append_audit_event, 0010:206). Both sides append to that chain, so it serialises the two commits. It is taken only after the edit guard (BEFORE trigger) and after has_body have already passed, and nothing re-runs a guard after the wait.
- esig.aggregate_lock (0220:279) is taken by esig.content_changed on the edit side, but transition takes it only through verify_signature. SUBMIT carries no signature.
- The database runs READ COMMITTED with explicit locks (architecture 5.5), so serializable snapshot isolation does not catch the write skew.

Reproducer: the untracked file packages/kernel/test/review-tmp/f44.test.ts. I ran `npx vitest run packages/kernel/test/review-tmp/f44.test.ts`. The sequential positive controls passed: an empty SUBMIT is refused with EBMR-PLAT-068, and an edit after SUBMIT is refused with EBMR-PLAT-074. Both concurrent scenarios then broke the rule.
1. A: `update body=''`, left open. B: SUBMIT blocks on a transactionid ShareLock (A's chain-head row lock), after has_body has already passed. A commits, B's SUBMIT completes and B commits. Final state: SUBMITTED, version 2, body ''.
2. Reverse order. B: SUBMIT, left open. A: edit (the edit guard sees DRAFT and passes), then blocks. B commits, A completes and commits. Final state: SUBMITTED, body 'changed after submission'.

No EBMR-PLAT-068 or EBMR-PLAT-074 fired in either scenario. This breaks outline 5.2 ("guards run ... with the relevant rows locked") and the documented DRAFT-only edit rule. The issue is not in the PROGRESS.md Phase 2 follow-ups, and it is not deferred to a later phase: the table and its triggers ship in the kernel migrations, and ebmr_app has insert and update on it.

The finding's step list needs two corrections:
- B cannot commit before A. B waits on the audit chain head until A commits, so in the finding's order the empty body commits just before SUBMITTED. The "content changes after submission committed" variant needs the reverse order (scenario 2).
- The two commands must use different iam sessions (two authors, or one person on two workstations). kernel.begin_command locks the actor's iam.session row FOR UPDATE (0190:91), so two commands from the same session are fully serialised.

Neither correction changes the defect. Medium severity is fair: the sample record is state-engine scaffolding, but it is the reference pattern later phases will copy for MBR versions, policies and rule tables.

confirmed.title: create_aggregate_state has no permission or administrator check and lets any caller pin a new aggregate to a superseded machine version
confirmed.description: The function is granted to ebmr_app and checks only that some validated actor exists. It does not call iam.assert_not_administrator (DI-18) and has no creation permission, and B7's regression test cannot see the gap because it only inspects functions whose source contains a GMP permission literal. It writes a state_history row attributed to the caller, a BUSINESS audit entry on the GMP aggregate's chain and a reserved-topic 'state.created' message. p_machine_version lets any caller choose any published version, including one superseded because it lacked a guard or signature, with no permission, reason or record that an old version was chosen deliberately. That defeats the rule that a tightening ships as a new version for newly created records (ADR-0010 upgrade policy). state-machine.test.ts line 411 relies on this.
confirmed.failure_scenario: (a) A SYSTEM_ADMINISTRATOR command runs select platform.create_aggregate_state('sample_record','sample_record','<uuid>'). It succeeds and writes GMP state, history and an audit entry attributed to an administrator. (b) After a migration publishes sample_record v2 that adds, say, a signature on SUBMIT, an author runs select platform.create_aggregate_state('sample_record','sample_record',<new id>,1). The new record follows v1 for its whole life and can be submitted without the signature v2 requires.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Call iam.assert_not_administrator() and a per-machine creation permission. Allow p_machine_version other than the newest only through a privileged, reasoned path, or derive it from the parent record's pinned configuration (e.g. the MBR version). Store the reason in the history row. Add platform functions to the authorization regression test.

confirmed.title: Site time zone and offset stored with GMP entries come from the client-supplied actor context
confirmed.description: The trigger stores new.site_zone := v_ctx ->> 'site_zone' and derives site_utc_offset from it after checking only that it is a valid IANA name. kernel.begin_command/validate_actor_context check only that site_zone is present (0010 line 100). esig.sign compares the context zone with iam.policy_text('site.zone'), but the time model does not. The zone that determines the stored offset, the displayed local time and the site-local calendar day (manufacturing dates, daily rules, shifts) is therefore chosen by the caller. The DI-27 test '[DI-27] entries store the UTC instant with the site time zone ...' records two entries in the same step with Asia/Kolkata and Europe/Berlin and treats both as correct.
confirmed.failure_scenario: At an Asia/Kolkata site, an operator's command context carries site_zone 'America/Los_Angeles'. An insert into platform.stub_step_entry at 2026-09-28 01:00 IST (2026-09-27 19:30 UTC) stores site_zone America/Los_Angeles with offset -07:00. platform.site_calendar_day(recorded_at, site_zone) returns 2026-09-27 instead of 2026-09-28, so any daily rule or manufacturing date computed from the stored zone is wrong. Nothing refuses the command.

confirmed.title: Drift decision ignores measurement uncertainty: a sample with uncertainty above the threshold clears alarms and becomes the 'last good sample'
confirmed.description: within_threshold is abs(offset) <= threshold, and uncertainty_s is stored but never used. The monitor estimates the offset as the midpoint of two node-clock reads around the reference read, and its uncertainty is half the bracket. The default read timeout is 5 s, so the uncertainty can reach 2.5 s against a 1 s default threshold. Such a sample proves nothing about the offset, yet it counts as healthy. It clears DRIFT_EXCEEDED (line 274), which ends the fault window, and time_window_start (line 80) uses it as the last good sample for later windows. The midpoint estimator is also biased when the reference returns its time at resolution rather than at the midpoint.
confirmed.failure_scenario: The node is truly 1.8 s ahead and a DRIFT_EXCEEDED alarm is open. A slow reference read with a 3 s round trip, where the reference timestamp is taken near the end of the bracket, reports offset_s '0.400000' with uncertainty_s '1.500000' for both sources. record_drift_check marks both within_threshold, clears the alarm and closes the fault window. Entries recorded afterwards are neither flagged nor listed, although the clock is still 1.8 s off.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Treat a sample as within threshold only when abs(offset_s) + uncertainty_s <= threshold. Treat uncertainty_s > threshold as indeterminate: it neither raises nor clears, and for REFERENCE_LOST/DEGRADED it counts as unreachable. Size the reader timeout from the threshold, and add tests with large uncertainty.

- Expected / + Received:

  uncertainSamplesWithinThreshold: expected [false,false], received [true,true]

  entryAfterwardFlagged: expected true, received false

The cause is in packages/kernel/sql/0520_platform_time_sources.sql:237: within_threshold is set to v_reachable and abs(v_offset) <= v_threshold, and the table's CHECK constraint at line 43 enforces the same rule. Because those samples counted as within threshold, the clear rule at line 274 closed DRIFT_EXCEEDED and ended the fault window. time_window_start (line 80) now takes that check as the node's last good sample.

An operator entry recorded right afterwards, while the node was still 1.8 s off, got no TIME_FAULT_WINDOW flag. entries_in_time_fault_windows() does not list it for the alarm either. confirmed.skeptic:
I checked the cited code. packages/kernel/sql/0520_platform_time_sources.sql:237 and :242 do test only abs(offset) <= threshold, uncertainty_s is stored but never read, and no later migration redefines record_drift_check. The 0900 migration redefines only raise_time_incident, and it still calls raise_alarm and time_window_start unchanged. The mechanics the finding describes are accurate. What it claims is a defect is not.

1. The code does what the spec says. docs/build-plan/phase-1/B5-platform.md says to raise an alarm "when |offset| > threshold". The module README's alarm table says DRIFT_EXCEEDED fires when "a reachable source's absolute offset is above time.drift_alarm_threshold_s". DI-27's type_detail says "No rule sets a clock tolerance" and calls the 1 s threshold a design choice. No regulation or listed invariant asks for an uncertainty guard band. Adding one would improve the measurement, but the current code does not compute a regulatory rule wrongly.

2. The failure scenario depends on a reader that does not exist yet. Phase 1 has no production TimeReference or NTP reader, and nothing schedules the monitor. The only readers are the injected ones in the tests, and drift-monitor.ts says "Production wiring supplies readers". To produce the reported 0.4 s against a true 1.8 s, BOTH independent references must take about 3 s per read, fully one-sided, with the reference timestamp taken at the end of the bracket. A plain SNTP reader returns the server's transmit timestamp, which on symmetric paths falls at the midpoint of the bracket, so the midpoint estimator is not biased there. Whether any bias exists depends on how the future reader is written. That makes the path speculative for Phase 1.

3. The stated impact is overstated. The finding says entries recorded afterwards are "neither flagged nor listed". In fact, the next ordinary check that still sees the 1.8 s offset raises DRIFT_EXCEEDED again through raise_alarm. Its window_start comes from time_window_start(node, new_check), which is the latest within_threshold sample, i.e. the uncertain check itself. So the new fault window starts where the cleared one ended. Every audit event recorded after the uncertain check falls inside it, and platform.entries_in_time_fault_windows() lists it for review, which is the DI-27 flag-for-review mechanism. A new incident is also requested. What is actually lost is small: entries written between the uncertain check and the next check do not get the TIME_FAULT_WINDOW review_flags value set at insert time (0530:305 uses time_fault_open()), and one alarm is cleared and raised again. That lasts only as long as the two-source, 3-second asymmetric latency keeps up on every check.

At most this is low-severity hardening: use abs(offset)+uncertainty, or treat a large-uncertainty sample as indeterminate. It is not a medium defect that breaks a guarantee. The reproducer at packages/kernel/test/review-tmp/f47.test.ts asserts behaviour the spec does not require, and it checks the review listing right after the uncertain check, before any later check has run. The sample being marked "within_threshold" and the stored cleared alarm are the documented behaviour.

confirmed.title: record_drift_check aborts instead of alarming for extreme offsets and for thresholds with more than 3 decimals; nothing detects a monitor that cannot record
confirmed.description: offset_s is numeric(14,6), which holds absolute values below 1e8 s (about 3.2 years), but the input regex accepts any length. threshold_s is numeric(6,3), while v_threshold, used to compute within_threshold, is unrounded. The check constraint within_threshold = (reachable and abs(offset_s) <= threshold_s) is evaluated on the rounded stored values, so it can disagree with the computed flag. In both cases the INSERT fails and the whole check rolls back: no sample, no alarm and no incident. runDriftCheck just throws, and no heartbeat or staleness alarm exists. The largest faults are the ones that go unreported. Confirmed with psql: '-1790000000.123456'::numeric(14,6) raises 'numeric field overflow'.
confirmed.failure_scenario: (a) The RTC resets the node clock to 1970, or a reference returns an NTP era-rollover time. The monitor submits offset_s '-1790000000.000000', the regex accepts it, the insert into drift_sample overflows, and the call aborts with no DRIFT_EXCEEDED, no incident and no TIME_FAULT_WINDOW flags while entries are stamped 1970. (b) A PROCESS_OWNER sets time.drift_alarm_threshold_s to '0.1235', which is a valid DECIMAL within 0.1-5. threshold_s stores 0.124. A reading of 0.123800 is computed as exceeded (0.1238 > 0.1235), but the check constraint computes within (0.1238 <= 0.124), so every check in that band aborts and the exceedance is never alarmed. Offsets sent with more than 6 decimals close to the threshold fail the same way.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Store offsets without a precision limit, or clamp them and record an OUT_OF_RANGE sample that counts as exceeded. Compute within_threshold from the same rounded values the constraint uses, or drop the scale on threshold_s, and limit the setting to 3 decimals. Validate input lengths up front with a coded error that still raises an alarm. Add a liveness alarm when a node has no recorded check for N intervals.

- The drift_sample table is defined at lines 30-44:
  - offset_s is numeric(14,6), so it overflows at |value| >= 1e8 s (about 3.17 years).
  - threshold_s is numeric(6,3).
  - The check constraint at line 43 is within_threshold = (reachable and abs(offset_s) <= threshold_s), evaluated on the stored, rounded values.

- No guard catches either failure first:
  - No per-sample exception handler.
  - No sanity check in drift-monitor.ts measureReference/runDriftCheck. It always produces 6-decimal strings of arbitrary magnitude via microsToSeconds.
  - No audit-chain time-monotonic guard that would block or alarm.

- (a) A reference offset of -1.79e9 s (node clock at 1970, or equally one faulty reference, as in the 2012 USNO NTP incident that served year 2000) makes runDriftCheck throw 'numeric field overflow'. The positive control at 1e7 s does raise DRIFT_EXCEEDED. The whole transaction rolls back: no sample, no DRIFT_EXCEEDED alarm, no incident.requested. The valid reading from the second reference is lost too, and open alarms are neither raised nor cleared.
- (b) With time.drift_alarm_threshold_s set to '0.1235', an offset of 0.123800 fails with 'violates check constraint drift_sample_check1'. The function computes the sample as exceeded (0.1238 > 0.1235), while the constraint sees 0.1238 <= 0.124. The positive control at 0.125 alarms.
- (c) The >6-decimal case fails the same way. However, the real monitor always sends exactly 6 decimals, so (c) is reachable only by a direct SYSTEM caller and is weak on its own.

Why it is a defect and not later-phase or documented behaviour:
- DI-27 is target_phase 1 and build_status IMPLEMENTED. Its behaviour line reads "Beyond the threshold, an alarm and an incident are raised".
- An offset far beyond the threshold, the case the monitor exists for, produces neither.
- No document caps the offset range or the threshold precision.
- PROGRESS.md "Follow-ups carried into Phase 2" does not mention it.

- The finding says "no TIME_FAULT_WINDOW flags". That is right, but for a backward jump, entries on existing aggregates can still get CLOCK_REGRESSION flags via platform.next_aggregate_seq. This is partial detection only, with no alarm or incident, and nothing for a forward jump or a bad reference.
- The "no liveness/heartbeat alarm" part is closer to a missing feature: Phase 1 has no scheduler that calls runDriftCheck. It is not needed for the finding to stand.
- (b) needs an unusual 4-decimal threshold and an offset inside a band of at most 0.5 ms, so it is a true edge case.

Overall, medium severity is justified mainly by (a).

confirmed.title: 'Validated' time sources are not verified: one administrator can swap the references and neutralise drift monitoring
confirmed.description: The outline and DI-27 call the time source a validated configuration item (R-33). validated_by, however, is an arbitrary uuid with no FK to a person, signature or validation record, and validation_ref is free text. PLATFORM.TIME_SOURCE_MANAGE is held by SYSTEM_ADMINISTRATOR alone (0700 line 112) with no QA approval, signature or second person. The same administrator can therefore register a source of their choosing and deactivate the traceable ones. The DI-27 test named '[DI-27] a time source is a validated configuration item ...' registers sources with randomUUID() as the validator and only checks that the text was stored.
confirmed.failure_scenario: A SYSTEM_ADMINISTRATOR runs select platform.register_time_source('Local', 'NTP', '10.0.0.9', 'anything', gen_random_uuid(), 'n/a'), then platform.set_time_source_active(<NPL id>, false) and platform.set_time_source_active(<NIC id>, false), with a reason. The monitor now measures only against 10.0.0.9. If that server follows the database host's clock, DRIFT_EXCEEDED never fires, and only a MINOR REFERENCE_DEGRADED alarm with no incident is raised. DI-27 monitoring is disabled by one person, with no approval or verifiable validation evidence.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Require validated_by to reference a QA/CSV e-signature (a meaning such as TIME_SOURCE_VALIDATED) by a person other than the registrant, checked in register_time_source and when a source is activated. Require a second person to deactivate a source that would leave fewer than time.min_references validated sources. Make the test assert that an unvalidated source is refused.

The code does what the finding says, but what it describes is the documented Phase 1 design, not a defect. No control or invariant requires what the finding asks for.

1. **Assigning time sources to the system administrator is deliberate and tested.**
   - packages/kernel/sql/0700_authorization_catalogue.sql:111-112 grants PLATFORM.TIME_SOURCE_MANAGE to SYSTEM_ADMINISTRATOR under the comment "K23 system administrator: IT functions only (restore operation, kiosk hardening, time sources, IT alarms)".
   - The role design (docs/design/features-ux-roles-configuration.md:90) gives K23 "deploy configuration under change control; backups, time sync, monitoring". Change control is a procedural (PQS) activity outside the system in Phase 1.
   - The B7 brief (docs/build-plan/phase-1/B7-authorization.md:52) allows "drift/time-source administration" to be classed as IT.
   - test/integration/authorization.test.ts:86, 142 and 486-498 assert that the system administrator, and only that role, registers time sources.

2. **No requirement asks for approval, an e-signature or a second person.**
   - DI-27 behaviour and catalog_test only cover server time, UTC storage, drift monitoring, alarm plus incident, flagging of affected entries and the no-blocking rule.
   - R-33 (critique-regulatory.md, rated minor and marked "verify, not in inputs") asks only that the reference be a validated configuration item recorded with the drift samples. drift_sample.source_id does that.
   - The "author, approver" rule in outline 3.5 applies to policy switches. Even those have no in-system approver in Phase 1: platform.set_setting (0500:319) lets one PROCESS_OWNER change a setting with a reason.
   - The validation pack and CSV evidence are Phase 7. The threat model (docs/security/threat-model.md:19) lists "the site's time source is validated" as an assumption, i.e. a procedural control.

3. **Nothing happens without trace.**
   - platform.time_source is an audited table (0520:345). kernel.audit_row_change (0010:279) refuses any UPDATE without a reason_code.
   - So each deactivation is a hash-chained audit event with the administrator's identity and reason. registered_by records who registered the source.
   - With fewer reachable references than time.min_references, a REFERENCE_DEGRADED alarm is raised; with none active, a NO_TIME_SOURCE incident is raised. The change is visible.

4. **The attack does not depend on this database function.**
   - In Phase 1 the monitor's readers are injected (drift-monitor.ts: "Production wiring supplies readers"). The endpoint column is not what gets queried.
   - An administrator who controls the NTP server, the reader wiring or the host's time sync can defeat monitoring without touching platform.time_source. A second-person check inside register_time_source would not close that path.

5. **The test is not mis-named.** '[DI-27] a time source is a validated configuration item, registered with its reference and validation' checks exactly that: reference and validation_ref are stored, the INSERT is audited, and an operator is refused. It does not claim that an unvalidated source is refused.

What remains is at most low-severity hardening, not a medium regulatory-logic defect: validated_by is a free uuid with no foreign key.

confirmed.title: Incarnation guard misses physical restores that finish with crash recovery; counters reissue values from the restored block
confirmed.description: current_incarnation() is system_identifier:WAL timeline:database OID:counter table OID. A physical restore carries the source cluster's system identifier and every OID. The timeline only changes after archive recovery (recovery.signal) or a promotion. Two common restores leave all four parts unchanged: a pg_basebackup -X stream copy started without recovery.signal, and a storage or VM snapshot rollback. - continuity.next_counter_value() (0600:318) refuses only when ceiling_incarnation differs from that value.

What a physical copy keeps:
- A physical copy keeps pg_control, so it keeps the system identifier, every OID and the counter table OID.
- The WAL timeline changes only when archive recovery is requested (recovery.signal or standby.signal) or on a promotion.
- A pg_basebackup -X stream copy started with only backup_label does crash recovery on the same timeline. A storage or VM snapshot rollback does the same.

Test result:
- incarnationBeforeBackup = ceilingIncarnation = incarnationAfterRestore = '7623409829129200177:00000001:12001353:12000904'.
- Server log: 'starting backup recovery ... on timeline ID 1'.
- checkAgainstLedger returned ok=true with no findings.
- The restored database issued 11 again, although the original had already issued 11..30 after the backup. INV-27 is violated.
- The unique index cannot catch this, because rows 11..30 do not exist in the restored database.

Why this is a defect and not documented behaviour:
- The 0600:220-222 comment says the incarnation changes on "a restore into a new database or cluster". So do the continuity README (line 21: "a restored, copied or failed-over database issues nothing"), the DI-45 guard text ("next_counter_value refuses after a restore, copy or failover") and ha-and-restore.md 5.1 ("A restore into a new cluster ... change[s] it"). All four are false for a physical restore that ends with crash recovery.
- The only known residual (PROGRESS.md:164 and ha-and-restore 5.1) is "data-only reload keeps DB incarnation". Physical copies and snapshot rollbacks are not mentioned, so this is broader than the known item.
- It is not a later-phase item: DI-45 and INV-27 are target_phase 1 and marked IMPLEMENTED.

Mitigating factors (these bear on severity, not validity):
1. A restore done by the SOP always runs record_restore_event and after_restore (steps 6-8). That retires the block whatever the incarnation, so the failure needs a restore nobody recorded. That is exactly the case the guard exists to catch ("A restore is never silent").
2. checkAgainstLedger (restore.ts:166) would flag the restore if any anchor was exported after the restore point. Every anchor exports high-water marks that include its own anchor id, which gives SEQUENCE_BEHIND_LEDGER, and the changed chain heads show as an anchor PROBLEM. So with the check running, the gap is limited to a lost interval shorter than one anchor period (minutes). However, checkAgainstLedger has no caller outside tests in Phase 1. The database guard is the enforcement point per ADR 0012/0016, and it fails for every such restore or copy regardless of timing.
3. In the HA topology, a snapshot rollback of the primary would probably cause a failover or degraded mode. A single-node restore, a standalone base-backup restore or a physical clone would not.

Minor inaccuracies in the finding:
- Once the block runs out, reserve_counter_ceiling will usually not raise LEDGER_AHEAD. The ledger floor (50) equals the restored ceiling (50), so the reuse stays completely silent. That is worse than the finding describes, not better.
- The point that checkAgainstLedger ignores lastValue adds little. Any anchor exported after the restore point already produces an ERROR through the sequence high-water marks.

Verdict: a real, reproducible INV-27 / DI-45 guard violation. The severity could arguably be medium rather than high, given the anchor-window condition.

Every audited write before that step draws ids from the restored sequence, i.e. ids already issued in the lost window. These writes include: record_restore_event (restore_event INSERT plus business entry), the e-signature challenge and signature, approve_restore_event, and after_restore's own first sequence_bump rows (keys sorted before 'kernel.audit_event.id'). An incident raised before completion also reuses an incident_no. Nothing detects the reuse afterwards. I could not refute this finding. The mechanism is real, I reproduced it, and the relevant parts are in Phase 1.

**Code**
- No later migration redefines continuity.record_restore_event, approve_restore_event or after_restore. The live definitions are in packages/kernel/sql/0600_continuity_core.sql at lines 601, 694 and 742.
- kernel.audit_event.id is `generated always as identity` (0010_audit_trail.sql:32).
- records.incident.incident_no is also an identity column (0410:35). 0900_integration_wiring.sql:12 registers it as a protected PG_SEQUENCE and describes it as "quoted in CAPA, CERT-In reports".
- PG_SEQUENCE sources have no issue guard. Only COUNTERs have one: the incarnation check in next_counter_value, which returns EBMR-CONT-012.
- The only setval on protected sequences is inside after_restore (0600:805). It is the last step of the runbook (ha-and-restore.md 5.2 step 8) and of the TS procedure (restore.ts: record, approve, completeRestore).
- Every audited write before that step takes an id from the sequence value restored by pg_restore. That value is the backup's, so the new ids are ones the source already issued after the backup. Those writes are:
  - record_restore_event: its INSERT plus audit_business_event.
  - The esig challenge and the signature.
  - approve_restore_event.
  - after_restore's own sequence_bump rows for 'kernel.audit_anchor.id' and 'kernel.audit_checkpoint.id'. That table is audited (0600:192), and these keys sort before 'kernel.audit_event.id', so their rows are written before that sequence is moved.
- Nothing detects the reuse afterwards. checkAgainstLedger only compares the sequence's last_value with the ledger mark (SEQUENCE_BEHIND_LEDGER).

**Incident path**
Runbook step 4 runs the clock offset check before the restore event exists. A failing check (NO_TIME_SOURCE, REFERENCE_LOST or DRIFT_EXCEEDED) goes through platform.record_drift_check, then platform.raise_time_incident (redefined in 0900), then records.raise_incident. That incident gets its number from the unbumped sequence. This is plausible after a restore onto new hardware.

**Reproduction**
The finder left a reproducer at packages/kernel/test/review-tmp/f56.test.ts. It is untracked in the review worktree, and I did not modify it. I ran it with `npx vitest run` against the local server. Both INV-27 assertions failed:
- Audit event ids 173–176 were issued again in the restored database. They went to the restored incident, the restore_event INSERT and BUSINESS entries, and esig_challenge:restore_event. The source had used those ids for batch:<id> and incident events after the backup.
- The incident opened in the restored database before completion got INC-000002. The source had already issued that number to a lost-window incident.

**Test weakness**
restore.test.ts '[INV-27] no number, audit event id or anchor id issued before the restore is ever issued again' only asserts max(id) > sourceMaxEventId and a greater anchor id. In its own flow, record, sign and approve run before completeRestore, so reused ids are present and the test still passes. Its name claims more than it proves.

**Why this is not intended, documented or later-phase**
- The docs say the opposite. The README says protected sequences move past the ledger after a restore. ADR 0007 says a restore "can never silently reuse" numbers. registered restore_margin exists precisely to cover values issued after the last exported mark.
- INV-27 and DI-45 are Phase 1 items. The incident register and the incident_no registration (0900) are also in Phase 1.
- PROGRESS.md follow-ups mention only a "restore runbook signing step", which is unrelated.

**Limits on impact**
- Audit event id reuse happens on every restore. Its external harm is limited in Phase 1, because exports and review high-water marks referencing ids come later.
- Incident number reuse is conditional, since an incident must be raised before completion. When it happens it is concrete: two different incidents share a reference that may already be quoted outside the system.

Medium severity is appropriate.

The code behaves as the finding says, but the failure depends on an actor the design deliberately leaves to detection rather than database enforcement. The fix it proposes also would not stop that actor.

Nothing later redefines any of these functions.

The application role cannot do either: 0010_audit_trail.sql:480-482 revokes all and grants only SELECT on audit_event and audit_anchor. No SECURITY DEFINER function deletes anchors; records.purge only deletes audit_event rows and leaves a tombstone. Without a superuser, an absent anchor can only come from a real restore or failover. A standby holds only a prefix of the primary's WAL, so in that case the chain lacks the anchored seq. That is exactly what DISCARDABLE is meant to cover.

3. The design places superuser tampering under "detected, not prevented": ADR 0012 context and consequences, and decision 7 (break-glass is two-person, time-boxed and logged by pgaudit to a sink administrators cannot write). ADR 0007 says detection comes from chains, anchors and the external pgaudit log. ha-and-restore.md 5.1 repeats that superuser sessions are logged by pgaudit. In the finding's scenario the external ledger still holds A2 with the original seq-3 hash, and pgaudit records the superuser's UPDATE and DELETE. The tampering remains evident outside the database. The restore event only labels the mismatch in the database's own view, and it names A2 and the chain.

4. The fix would not close the path for that actor. restore_event_is_approved (0600:571-582, the only definition) checks only the content hash and that approval rows exist. It checks neither signature_id nor the external ledger's RESTORE_EVENT entry. A superuser who can delete anchor rows can just as easily insert a continuity.restore_event row (content_hash = sha256 of continuity.restore_event_content) and matching restore_event_approval rows, with triggers off. verify_external_anchors then reports COVERED with no SYSTEM_ADMINISTRATOR or QA involved. Checks inside compare_external_anchors or record_restore_event give no protection against this actor. The attacker simply skips them.

5. The rest of the path is a human two-person control working as designed: a SYSTEM_ADMINISTRATOR records a FAILOVER that never happened, and a QA approver signs it. The signed content (restore_event_content, which 0720 feeds into the RESTORE_APPROVED signature) shows event_kind FAILOVER with no backup, discarded anchor A2, affected_chains restored_seq 3 = external_seq 3, and a problem text saying the chain "differs" at seq 3. Runbook 5.3 says a failover with no lost history shows only MATCH. So an approver who signs this is colluding or negligent, which is a procedural failure, not a database defect.

Because the precondition is superuser tampering that the design scopes to external detection, and the superuser already has a simpler direct path that the proposed checks would not affect, this is not a concrete bypass by the application role or an ordinary user.

confirmed.title: Counter reservation writes the ceiling to the external ledger before the actor and permission are checked: product-limited issuers burn serial blocks and trigger CRITICAL LEDGER_AHEAD alarms
confirmed.description: reserveCounterBlock appends the CEILING entry to the ledger (line 77) before it opens the transaction, calls kernel.begin_command and calls continuity.reserve_counter_ceiling, which checks DI-18 and CONTINUITY.COUNTER_RESERVE at the actor's location. Any attempt that fails those checks leaves a ceiling in the ledger that the database never acknowledged. Examples: a product-limited BATCH_ISSUER (the README says these cannot reserve), an expired session, a DI-18 refusal. The next authorised reservation sees the ledger ahead, skips the whole range and raises a CRITICAL LEDGER_AHEAD alarm. That alarm is the only database signal of an unrecorded restore, and here it fires in routine operation. It also burns serial space: with {SEQ:4} and block 50, about 200 failed attempts exhaust a rule (EBMR-SITE-012).
confirmed.failure_scenario: Scratch probe: rule PX-TAB with block 50. An unrestricted issuer allocates PX0001 (ledger ceiling 50), and a product-limited issuer allocates up to PX0050. That issuer then makes 4 more attempts. Each fails with EBMR-IAM-040, but the ledger ceiling grows 100 -> 150 -> 200 -> 250. The next unrestricted allocation returns PX0251, and continuity.open_alarm holds {severity: CRITICAL, alarm_code: LEDGER_AHEAD, external_floor: 250, database_ceiling: 50}. Serials 51-250 were never issued but are now recorded as possibly issued elsewhere.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Authorise before writing outside the database. Inside the transaction, call begin_command and a prepare step that runs assert_not_administrator and require_permission and locks the counter row. Only then append to the ledger, then acknowledge (a two-phase reserve). Alternatively, have withProtectedNumbers skip the reservation for actors without CONTINUITY.COUNTER_RESERVE and surface EBMR-CONT-011 instead.
