It records a LEDGER_AHEAD sequence_bump from 5 to 25, raises a CRITICAL LEDGER_AHEAD alarm in normal operation, and issues PX0026. Serials 6-25 are skipped and never issued.

This is the scenario from the finding, with block size 5 instead of 50 so the test runs fast. It needs only ordinary users: a BATCH_ISSUER with a grant limited to one product, which the README says cannot reserve. The issue is not in the PROGRESS.md Phase 2 follow-ups.

Note: the test calls site.define_batch_number_rule and site.allocate_batch_number through raw SQL. It does not import the site-services TypeScript, because .dependency-cruiser.cjs (kernel-is-self-contained) forbids packages/kernel from importing it.
confirmed.skeptic:
I could not refute F58. The code does what the finding says, the effect reproduces, and nothing I found documents it as intended.

1. Code order (packages/kernel/src/continuity/numbers.ts, reserveCounterBlock). Line 77 calls ledger.append({type:'CEILING', ...}) before the transaction starts. The transaction (line 78, 'begin'), kernel.begin_command (line 80) and continuity.reserve_counter_ceiling (line 81) all come after it. The authorisation checks run only inside continuity.reserve_counter_ceiling: iam.assert_not_administrator(), then iam.require_permission('CONTINUITY.COUNTER_RESERVE', iam.actor_location_scope()). That function is in packages/kernel/sql/0600_continuity_core.sql:345, and it is the only definition; no later migration redefines it. When the check fails, the catch block rolls back the database transaction. The ledger entry is not undone and cannot be, because the ledger is write-once.

2. The unauthorised caller is a supported, realistic actor. packages/kernel/src/continuity/README.md says: "a grant limited to one product does not cover it (the counter has no product), so product-limited issuers rely on ceilings reserved by an unrestricted issuer or a service account". site.allocate_batch_number checks BATCH_NUMBER.ALLOCATE, which the product-limited issuer holds. So once the block is used up, the database raises EBMR-CONT-011 and withProtectedNumbers (line 119) calls reserveCounterBlock. That call appends a ceiling to the ledger and then fails with EBMR-IAM-040. Every further attempt does the same, because the database ceiling never moves. The next ceiling is computed from the ledger floor (lines 71-76), so each attempt raises the ledger ceiling by one more block.

3. Reproduced. I ran the existing probe packages/kernel/test/review-tmp/f58.test.ts (block 5; the steps match the finding's scenario). The product-limited issuer made 4 attempts after the block ran out; each failed with IAM-040. The ledger ceiling then read 25 while the database still had reserved_ceiling 5. The next unrestricted allocation returned PX0026, not PX0006. continuity.open_alarm held {severity: CRITICAL, external_floor: 25, database_ceiling: 5}, and continuity.sequence_bump recorded 5 -> 25 with reason LEDGER_AHEAD. Serials 6-25 were never issued and are lost.

4. Not intended or documented. The SQL comment at 0600:340-344 and the test packages/kernel/test/continuity/numbers.test.ts:54 describe LEDGER_AHEAD as a crash or lost-acknowledgement case ("values up to 10 may be in use"), or as an unrecorded restore, and treat it as CRITICAL. No document says that a refused authorisation writes to the ledger or raises this alarm in routine use. The site-services authorization test avoids the case altogether ("the write-ahead block the unrestricted issuer reserved above is used, so no ceiling reservation is needed here").

5. Not a known item. It is not among the "Follow-ups carried into Phase 2" in PROGRESS.md. Continuity and INV-27 are Phase 1 work.

Mitigating points:
- INV-27 uniqueness still holds; skipping forward is safe.
- Alarms do not block operations.
- Administrators fail at allocate before EBMR-CONT-011 is raised, so they never reach the ledger write.
- An expired session only reaches it in a narrow race.

So the realistic trigger is the product-limited issuer. Even so, a user without CONTINUITY.COUNTER_RESERVE can cause a change outside the database that later moves a protected counter. That change is recorded under the correlation id of the next authorised reserver, not the user who caused it. It also produces false CRITICAL LEDGER_AHEAD alarms, which weaken the signal meant for snapshot or unrecorded restores. Repeated attempts burn serial space, which can end in EBMR-SITE-012 exhaustion of a rule, possibly a site-wide rule other products use. Medium severity is appropriate.

confirmed.title: User IDs (login names) issued in a restore's lost window are unprotected and can be issued to another person after the restore
confirmed.description: INV-27 lists user IDs as never reused 'including after a restore', and PROGRESS reports INV-27 as proven. The continuity mechanism protects only numeric PG sequences and counters. Login names are chosen strings held only in iam.issued_identifier / iam.account inside the database. They are not written to the external ledger, not in the anchor high-water marks, and there is no recovery path like site.recover_batch_number. After a restore, a login name created in the lost window is simply unknown to the restored database.
confirmed.failure_scenario: (1) At 10:05 an administrator creates account 'asharma' for person A, who signs paper-transcribed or printed records. Exports and ERP entries carry 'asharma'. (2) The site database is restored to 10:00 and the restore procedure completes. (3) Before lost-window re-entry, the administrator creates 'asharma' for a different person B. iam.create_account accepts it because iam.issued_identifier in the restored database never saw the name. The same user ID now identifies two people across records. lostWindow() lists only chain keys (account uuids), not the names.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Write each issued login name (normalised) to the external ledger before or with account creation. On a restore, re-register the ledger's names in iam.issued_identifier (as reserved or unknown-owner) before the restore can be completed, or refuse create_account for names found in the ledger. Cover this in the restore test.
confirmed.evidence:
Command: cd /home/user/ebmr-review && npx vitest run packages/kernel/test/review-tmp/f59.test.ts

Result: 3 tests, 2 passed, 1 failed.
- The precondition test passed. In the source database 'asharma' belongs to person A. The restore event status is COMPLETED after record, signed approval and completeRestore. lostWindow() lists only `account:<uuid>` and not the login name.
- The control test passed. The seeded administrator can create an account in the restored database for a third person under a fresh name. Person B has no account in the restored database, so INV-11 (EBMR-IAM-024) cannot be the reason for a refusal.
- The INV-27 test FAILED because of the defect:

  FAIL > [INV-27][DI-15] a login name issued before the restore (in the lost window) is never issued again, to anyone
  AssertionError: user ID 'asharma' (issued to person 353f1b69-0f5f-475d-8f8d-55d40df5dbda before the restore) was issued again to person a2f14c72-e88a-4b3c-8bd8-1b551bc3ef5d after the restore: expected 'a2f14c72-e88a-4b3c-8bd8-1b551bc3ef5d' to be undefined

Why it happens:
- iam.create_account (packages/kernel/sql/0110_iam_persons_accounts.sql:340) checks the name only against iam.issued_identifier in the restored database.
- continuity.after_restore (packages/kernel/sql/0600_continuity_core.sql:742) moves only protected sequences and counters past the ledger's high-water marks.
- No login name is written to the external ledger or re-registered during the restore.

So after the full, approved restore procedure, the user ID 'asharma' that belonged to person A was accepted for person B. No later migration redefines create_account or after_restore. This is not listed in the PROGRESS.md Phase 2 follow-ups.
confirmed.skeptic:
I could not refute F59. The cited code is correct, nothing guards the path, and the gap is not listed as a known item.

1. Scope and requirement. Outline line 499 defines INV-27 as "Batch numbers, contingency-form numbers, user IDs and signature IDs are never reused, including after a restore". INV-27 is a Phase 1 exit criterion (outline 11, Phase 1 exit list includes 26-29). The login name is the "user ID": esig manifestation writes 'user_id' = login_name (0230_esig_sign.sql:305). PROGRESS lines 155 and 166 say "INV-27 proven" and "the login-name part of INV-27 proven". The Phase 2 follow-up list (PROGRESS 210-218) does not mention login names or restore. The only restore residual risk it names is the data-only reload, which is a different issue. So the gap is not a known item.

2. The login-name protection lives only inside the database. iam.issued_identifier (0110:160) and iam.create_account (0110:340) are never redefined later; there is no `create or replace` in any later migration. create_account refuses a name only if `exists (select 1 from iam.issued_identifier where identifier = v_login)`. That table is rolled back by a restore, like every other table.

3. The continuity mechanism does not cover login names:
   - continuity.after_restore (0600:742) loops only over continuity.protected_sequence, which holds PG sequences and COUNTERs, plus unregistered ebmr_owner sequences.
   - The identifier_kind 'USER_ID' exists in the CHECK constraint (0600:39), but nothing registers it. The only registrations are the kernel audit, anchor, checkpoint and DDL-log sequences in 0600, and incident, investigation, outbox and state_history in 0900.
   - exportAnchor (src/continuity/anchors.ts) writes to the ledger only the anchor (chain_key/seq/hash heads, merkle root) and readHighWater. No login name ever reaches the external ledger.
   - continuity.lost_window (0600:844) returns only chain keys such as 'account:<uuid>', not names.
   - ha-and-restore.md 5.2 step 10 provides evidence-based recovery only for batch numbers (site.recover_batch_number). There is no step for login names.
   - The incarnation guard applies only to next_counter_value. create_account uses no counter, so a restored database accepts it even before after_restore runs. The only block is the application-level start-up check.

4. Concrete path:
   - 10:05: an administrator with IAM.ACCOUNT_MANAGE runs iam.create_account(A, 'asharma', 'HUMAN'). issued_identifier and account rows are committed, and an anchor carrying the head of 'account:<uuid>' is exported.
   - The database is restored point-in-time to 10:00. Then record, approve and after_restore run; all succeed, and none looks at login names.
   - iam.create_account(B, 'asharma', 'HUMAN') succeeds. The `exists` check finds nothing and no trigger checks anything external (account_guard only checks that the name is in the local register for this account).
   - Paper, printed or ERP records from the lost window that show user ID 'asharma' for A now match a different person, B. Even without an immediate collision, the name stays free indefinitely because no source of truth outside the database records it.

5. The tests do not prove this part. restore.test.ts's INV-27 test claims only "no number, audit event id or anchor id issued before the restore is ever issued again". The DI-15/INV-27 identity test covers a deactivated account's ID in normal operation, not after a restore. So PROGRESS's "INV-27 proven" overstates what the tests show for user IDs.

Medium severity fits: it needs a restore with a lost window in which accounts were created, followed by a reissue of the same name.

confirmed.title: Co-signer actor context stays validated for the rest of the transaction; the application role can re-install it and act as the co-signer
confirmed.description: For a co-signature, esig.sign installs the co-signer's context with iam.set_internal_actor (0230:483), which writes a kernel.command_marker row (0010:138) and an iam.command_log row (0100:327) keyed only by (xact_id, backend_pid, ctx_hash). It then switches back to the terminal owner's context (0230:506) but never removes those two rows. kernel.actor_context_validated (0010:155) and iam.actor_is_validated (0100:285) accept ANY context whose hash still has a marker in the current transaction, and the actual context is read from the transaction-local GUC ebmr.ctx, which any role may set with set_config. So after a legitimate co-signature, the application role can set ebmr.ctx to the co-signer's exact context (it knows the base context it sent to begin_command and can read person_id/account_id/role_code/auth_event_id/legal_name from the just-written esig.signature row) and every downstream guard treats the command as the co-signer. This defeats the authorization boundary: iam.platform_authority (0710:52), iam.require_permission, iam.assert_not_administrator and the hash-chained audit writer all trust iam.actor_is_validated / kernel.current_actor.
confirmed.failure_scenario: PoC (proven): performer P (OPERATOR) and verifier V (VERIFIER) at a shared terminal. The app runs the normal co-signature: challenge for VERIFIED with signerAccountId=V, V authenticates, esig.sign commits the co-signature. Still inside the same DB transaction the app runs: select set_config('ebmr.ctx', (current_setting('ebmr.ctx')::jsonb || (person_id,account_id,role_code,auth_event_id,legal_name of V from esig.signature))::text, true). iam.actor_is_validated() now returns true with person=V, and records.raise_incident(...) inserts an incident with raised_by_person=V and an audit event whose actor.person_id=V. Observed: raised_by_person and the audit actor were V, not P. The same trick lets the app act as V for any GMP write or authority check in that transaction, forging attribution and impersonating a second person.
confirmed.suggested_fix: When esig.sign restores the terminal owner's context, delete the co-signer's marker and iam.command_log row for this transaction (or scope validation so only the single most-recently-installed context of the transaction is valid). More generally, kernel.set_actor_context should invalidate the previous context's marker on every switch within a transaction, so a context is validated only while it is the current one.
confirmed.evidence:
Reproduced: the test fails because of the defect, not because of a mistake in the test.

Command: cd /home/user/ebmr-review && npx vitest run packages/kernel/test/review-tmp/f68.test.ts

Result: 1 test, 1 failed. Every precondition assertion passed before the final assertion:
- the challenge is a co-signature;
- esig.sign committed the co-signature;
- after esig.sign, assert_validated_actor returns the performer again;
- the control incident is attributed to the performer;
- the esig.signature row names the verifier as signer (ebmr_app can read it).
Only the final assertion failed:

AssertionError: expected { actorIsValidated: true, ...(2) } to deeply equal { actorIsValidated: false, ...(2) }
  {
-   "actorIsValidated": false,
-   "currentActorPerson": null,
-   "forgedIncident": StringMatching /^EBMR-(IAM|AUDIT)-\d+$/,
+   "actorIsValidated": true,
+   "currentActorPerson": "98fc4ff2-c8c9-41bc-8f6b-c3858ead1d7f",
+   "forgedIncident": {
+     "accepted": true,
+     "auditActorIsVerifier": true,
+     "auditInPerformersSession": true,
+     "auditReusesConsumedSignatureEvent": true,
+     "raisedByVerifier": true,
+   },
  }

What happens: after a real co-signature (VERIFIED by a VERIFIER at the OPERATOR's SHARED terminal), the application role (ebmr_app) runs one statement in the same transaction: select set_config('ebmr.ctx', (current_setting('ebmr.ctx')::jsonb || <signer_person, signer_account, signer_role_code, auth_event_id, signer_legal_name from esig.signature>)::text, true).
- iam.actor_is_validated() then returns true, and kernel.current_actor() returns the verifier.
- records.raise_incident is accepted. The incident's raised_by_person is the verifier, and its hash-chained audit event names the verifier as actor. That event also reuses the verifier's already-consumed signature auth event (INV-40) and sits in the performer's session, a pairing that begin_command refuses directly with EBMR-IAM-111.

Why: esig.sign (packages/kernel/sql/0230_esig_sign.sql, around line 483) installs the co-signer context with iam.set_internal_actor. That writes a kernel.command_marker row (0010) and an iam.command_log row (0100). esig.sign later restores the performer's context with kernel.set_actor_context (around line 506) but never removes those two rows. kernel.actor_context_validated and iam.actor_is_validated accept any context whose hash has a marker in the current transaction, and none of these functions is redefined in a later migration.

Note: the earlier reproducer packages/kernel/test/review-tmp/f1.test.ts (F1) covers the same root cause through an esig.stub_signable insert. F68 is effectively a duplicate of F1, shown here through the INCIDENT.RAISE authority check and incident attribution.
confirmed.skeptic:
I could not refute F68. I read the code and ran the reproducer, and the defect is real.

Code path (the last definitions are the live ones; nothing later redefines these functions):
- `kernel.set_actor_context` (packages/kernel/sql/0010_audit_trail.sql:138) inserts a `kernel.command_marker` row (xact_id, backend_pid, ctx_hash). It only prunes markers from other, finished transactions and never removes markers of the current one.
- `iam.set_internal_actor` (0100_iam_foundation.sql:327) also inserts an `iam.command_log` row with the same key.
- `kernel.actor_context_validated` (0010:155) and `iam.actor_is_validated` (0100:286) accept whatever is in the GUC `ebmr.ctx`, as long as its sha256 has a marker (and a command_log row) in the current transaction. Any role can set that GUC with `set_config`.
- In the co-signature branch of `esig.sign` (0230_esig_sign.sql:482-485), `iam.set_internal_actor(v_actor || {person_id, account_id, role_code, auth_event_id, legal_name of the co-signer})` is called. At 0230:505-507 `kernel.set_actor_context(v_actor)` restores the performer's context, but the co-signer's marker and command_log rows are never deleted.
- The application can rebuild the co-signer's context exactly:
  - The jsonb text form is canonical.
  - `ebmr.ctx` after the sign is `v_actor::text`.
  - The five added values are all readable: ebmr_app has SELECT on `esig.signature` (0220:484), which holds `signer_person`, `signer_account`, `signer_role_code`, `auth_event_id` and `signer_legal_name`.
  - So `set_config('ebmr.ctx', (current_setting('ebmr.ctx')::jsonb || <those fields>)::text, true)` produces the same hash as the marked context.

Downstream guards add no protection:
- `iam.require_permission`, `iam.assert_not_administrator` and `records.actor_person` all trust `iam.assert_validated_actor()` or `kernel.current_actor()`.
- The audit writer (0010 `append_audit_event`) trusts `kernel.current_actor()`.
- No deferred check or `esig.signing_challenge` guard prevents it.
- One partial limit: `iam.actor_location_scope` returns '{}' because the co-signer does not own the session. Location-scoped checks therefore need an unrestricted grant. The attribution and authority bypass still works wherever the scope comes from the aggregate (for example the platform authority hook) and wherever the grant is unrestricted.

Empirical confirmation: I ran the existing untracked reproducer `packages/kernel/test/review-tmp/f68.test.ts` against the live test Postgres. After a legitimate co-signature and the `set_config`, it observed:
- `iam.actor_is_validated() = true`
- `kernel.current_actor()->>'person_id'` is the verifier
- `records.raise_incident` was accepted, with `raised_by_person` set to the verifier
- the audit event's `actor.person_id` is the verifier, reusing the verifier's already-consumed signature auth event, in the performer's session

Why it is not intended, known or out of phase:
- ADR-0016 ("Consequences / Positive") explicitly promises that "a validated command [cannot] swap in another person's context mid-transaction".
- ADR-0012 assumes the application credentials may leak.
- PROGRESS.md follow-ups do not mention this. The only related entry is the original set_config gap, which is described as fixed.
- It is Phase 1 kernel scope.

Preconditions and severity: a real co-signature must happen in the same transaction, and the application role must be malicious or compromised. Given that, a validated command can attribute further GMP writes and authority checks to a second person who authenticated only for one signature. That is a forged-attribution / Part 11 breach, so critical or high is justified.

The fix suggested in the finding is sound: delete the co-signer's marker and command_log row on restore, or more generally invalidate the previous context's marker on every switch.

confirmed.title: platform.raise_time_incident is app-callable with no authority or source check, so any user can forge and, worse, suppress data-integrity time-fault incidents
confirmed.function: platform.raise_time_incident (redefined here; granted to ebmr_app in 0520:351-356)
confirmed.description: platform.raise_time_incident raises a platform.alarm and a DATA_INTEGRITY/TIME_SYNC incident, calling platform.raise_alarm and records.raise_incident as owner. It is granted EXECUTE to ebmr_app and performs NO source='SYSTEM' check and NO permission check of its own (unlike platform.record_drift_check, which refuses any actor whose source is not SYSTEM at 0520:204-206). The 0520 comment states the design intent that 'raise_alarm ... stay private: alarms without an incident come only from the monitor', but raise_time_incident hands the application exactly that ability. Any actor holding INCIDENT.RAISE (every shop-floor GMP role) can call it directly.
confirmed.failure_scenario: PoC (proven): (a) an OPERATOR calls select platform.raise_time_incident('DRIFT_EXCEEDED','ghost-node','MINOR','{}') and a MINOR data-integrity incident + alarm attributed to the operator is created and platform.time_fault_open() becomes true, flagging every concurrent GMP entry with TIME_FAULT_WINDOW. (b) Suppression of a real fault: an OPERATOR pre-raises a MINOR DRIFT_EXCEEDED alarm for the real db node; when a genuine 3.5 s clock drift is later measured, platform.record_drift_check raises nothing (its 'raise once per open condition' guard, open_alarm_id, sees the operator's open alarm) and no MAJOR alarm or automatic DI incident is created. Observed: the monitor's raised[] was empty and only the operator's MINOR USER incident existed, so DI-27's 'a genuine time fault raises an alarm and an incident' was defeated.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Revoke EXECUTE on platform.raise_time_incident from ebmr_app (make it owner-only, called only from record_drift_check), or gate it exactly like record_drift_check: require source='SYSTEM' and platform.authorize('platform.time_check.record', ...). Ensure user-raised time incidents cannot pre-empt the monitor's condition tracking.
confirmed.evidence:
Reproduced. The test fails because of the defect, not because of a mistake in the test.

Command: cd /home/user/ebmr-review && npx vitest run packages/kernel/test/review-tmp/f69.test.ts

Result: 1 failed. The control assertions passed first: on an untouched node ('db-f69-control'), the SYSTEM monitor's 3.5 s drift check raised DRIFT_EXCEEDED and a MAJOR incident (DATA_INTEGRITY, source TIME_SYNC, detected_by SYSTEM). That shows the test's readings do trigger the monitor. The final assertion then failed with this diff:
  - "ghostRaise": StringMatching /^(PERMISSION_DENIED|EBMR-...)$/   + "ghostRaise": "ACCEPTED"
  - "ghostNodeAlarms": 0                                            + "ghostNodeAlarms": 1
  - "timeSyncIncidentsRaisedByOperator": 0                          + 1
  - "timeFaultOpenAfterOperator": false                             + true
  - "preemptRaise": StringMatching ...                              + "preemptRaise": "ACCEPTED"
  - "monitorRaisedOnRealNode": ["DRIFT_EXCEEDED"]                   + []
  - "monitorIncidentOnRealNode": [{TIME_SYNC, DATA_INTEGRITY, MAJOR, SYSTEM}]  + []
  - "openAlarmsOnRealNode": [{DRIFT_EXCEEDED, MAJOR, MONITOR}]      + [{DRIFT_EXCEEDED, MINOR, OPERATOR}]

What this shows:
(a) An ordinary OPERATOR, a seeded real identity on a PERSONAL device with source UI, calls select platform.raise_time_incident('DRIFT_EXCEEDED','ghost-node','MINOR','{}') inside kernel.begin_command. The call succeeds. It creates a platform.alarm and a TIME_SYNC incident attributed to the operator, and platform.time_fault_open() becomes true.
(b) The operator pre-raises a MINOR DRIFT_EXCEEDED alarm for 'db-f69-real'. The SYSTEM monitor then calls platform.record_drift_check on that node with a genuine 3.5 s offset, and raised[] comes back empty. The "raise once per open condition" guard (platform.open_alarm_id(p_node,'DRIFT_EXCEEDED') at 0520_platform_time_sources.sql:258) sees the operator's alarm. So no MAJOR alarm and no automatic SYSTEM data-integrity incident is created. The only open alarm is the operator's MINOR one, which defeats DI-27.

Root cause: the live platform.raise_time_incident (packages/kernel/sql/0900_integration_wiring.sql:50) runs SECURITY DEFINER with no source='SYSTEM' check and no platform.authorize('platform.time_check.record', ...). EXECUTE on it is granted to ebmr_app at 0520:351-356. The only gate is records.raise_incident's INCIDENT.RAISE, which every shop-floor role holds (0700:100-104).

Fix check: I temporarily added "revoke execute on function platform.raise_time_incident(text,text,text,jsonb,uuid) from ebmr_app, public" to the test's beforeAll and re-ran. The result was 1 passed. So the test passes once the defect is fixed. I then restored the file to the version above (confirmed by grep and a re-run, which failed again the same way). No other repository file was changed.
confirmed.skeptic:
The grant is intended, it is gated, and the claimed "suppression" does not hide the fault.

1. The grant and the lack of a SYSTEM check are intended and documented.
- platform.raise_time_incident is the incident hook for any component that detects a time fault, not only the drift monitor.
- The test at packages/kernel/test/platform/drift-monitor.test.ts:340 calls it as ebmr_app with CLOCK_REGRESSION, a kind the monitor never raises.
- platform.clear_alarm exists for alarms "raised by another component" (0520 comment above clear_alarm).
- B7-authorization.md:37 requires that raising an incident be possible for SYSTEM accounts and for shop-floor roles.
- The finding misreads the 0520 grant comment. It says "raise_alarm and time_window_start stay private: alarms without an incident come only from the monitor". raise_time_incident always creates an incident (0900:50-88 calls records.raise_incident), so it is consistent with that comment.

2. It is not ungated. The live definition (0900:50) calls records.raise_incident (0410:169-215) as the caller, and that function runs:
- iam.assert_not_administrator() (DI-18);
- iam.require_permission('INCIDENT.RAISE', iam.actor_location_scope()) (DI-17).
Any role holding INCIDENT.RAISE can already raise a DATA_INTEGRITY / TIME_SYNC incident directly.

3. Scenario (a) is not forgery.
- The alarm stores raised_by_person from the validated context. The incident stores detected_by='USER' plus the operator's person and account. Both tables are audited.
- A false time-fault alarm only makes flagging more conservative: entries get TIME_FAULT_WINDOW and are listed for review.
- No record is altered, hidden or misattributed, and no GMP rule is bypassed. An alarm on a node the monitor never checks stays open until someone clears it with platform.alarm.clear. That is a review nuisance, not an integrity breach.

4. Scenario (b) does not suppress the fault. If the operator's DRIFT_EXCEEDED alarm is open on the real node when a genuine drift is measured, every DI-27 outcome still holds:
- a DRIFT_EXCEEDED alarm is open on that node, and it is a time-fault kind (is_time_fault);
- an open DATA_INTEGRITY/TIME_SYNC incident is linked to that alarm;
- time_fault_open() is true;
- the fault window starts at the last good sample, the same start the monitor would compute, and stays open until record_drift_check sees the condition resolved;
- entries are flagged and returned by entries_in_time_fault_windows();
- the out-of-threshold drift_sample rows are stored and audited.
The only differences are that the severity is MINOR instead of MAJOR and detected_by is USER instead of SYSTEM. INCIDENT.INVESTIGATE can reclassify the severity (records.reclassify_incident).

5. The timing is not realistic. The operator's alarm has check_id NULL. The next healthy monitor check clears it, because DRIFT_EXCEEDED is resolved when v_ok_refs>0 and v_exceeded=0, and NULL is distinct from the new check id (0520:268-282). The only guard (role_permission_guard, 0120:423) blocks mixing ADMINISTRATION and GMP permissions in one role, but a single administrator can still add GMP-WRITE/GOVERNANCE permissions to any GMP role, and GOVERNANCE permissions to their own admin role. confirmed.title: reserve_counter_ceiling is authorized at the actor's location, letting an issuer tamper with another site's protected number counter
confirmed.description: reserve_counter_ceiling checks CONTINUITY.COUNTER_RESERVE in the actor's location scope (session site/room) rather than the scope of the counter being reserved. The counter identifies a specific site's batch-number rule (key 'site.batch_number:<rule_code>'). A batch issuer whose grant covers their own site therefore passes the check for a counter that belongs to a different site's rule. The 0710 scope-derivation choice (point-of-work actions checked at the actor's location) is wrong for this resource, which is scoped to a named site.
confirmed.failure_scenario: PoC (proven): a steward defines a PROCESSING rule for SITE-2 (creating counter 'site.batch_number:<rule>'). A BATCH_ISSUER whose grant is limited to SITE-1, with a session at SITE-1, calls continuity.reserve_counter_ceiling('site.batch_number:<rule>', 9999, 10000, 'forged receipt') and it succeeds (returns 10000, counter row updated), writing a ceiling reservation with a fabricated external-ledger floor and receipt into SITE-2's number-protection records. A foreign-site user can thus desynchronise another site's write-ahead ledger relationship (INV-27 machinery) and interfere with its number issuance, with no grant covering SITE-2.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Authorize CONTINUITY.COUNTER_RESERVE (and the counter's owning module actions) in the scope of the counter/rule's site (look up the protected_sequence's owning site), not at the actor's session location.

   - The DI-17 control guard text says the same ("at the actor's location ... for point-of-work actions"), and so does the site-services batch-numbers README ("needs CONTINUITY.COUNTER_RESERVE at the issuer's location").
   - The kernel object also has no site. continuity.protected_sequence and continuity.counter have no site column. The key is free text defined by the owning module, and the kernel cannot resolve 'site.batch_number:<rule>' to a site.

2. **An ordinary user cannot reach it through the application.**
   - The application calls reserve_counter_ceiling only from reserveCounterBlock / withProtectedNumbers (packages/kernel/src/continuity/numbers.ts). The key comes from the EBMR-CONT-011 detail of a command the user was just running.
   - allocate_batch_number checks BATCH_NUMBER.ALLOCATE in the rule's site and product scope (site-services 0600, line 247) before next_counter_value can raise CONT-011. So a SITE-1 issuer never triggers a reservation of SITE-2's counter.
   - The PoC therefore needs raw SQL from the application role, run with a SITE-1 issuer's session.

3. **The harm described does not depend on the site check.**
   - The damage comes from a fabricated external floor and ledger receipt. The database cannot verify either one, by design: the application writes the ledger first and the database records the acknowledgement.
   - The same fabricated call is open to any SITE-2 batch issuer, or to a SERVICE_ACCOUNT holding COUNTER_RESERVE, whenever the application role supplies such a context. Scoping the check to the counter's site would not close this.
   - A legitimate cross-site reservation, with the ledger written first, only acknowledges a write-ahead block. It issues, alters or deletes no batch number record.

4. **Nothing is lost or reused.**
   - Counters only move forward: reserved_ceiling >= last_value, guard_registry forbids decreases, and a LEDGER_AHEAD move raises a CRITICAL alarm. So INV-27 (numbers never reused) holds.
   - continuity.ceiling_reservation and continuity.sequence_bump are audited, hash-chained tables (0600, lines 191-192). The row carries the command's correlation_id, so the actor is attributed.
   - If the ledger has no CEILING entry for the forged ceiling, the next genuine reservation is refused with EBMR-CONT-013 ("write-ahead record is missing"). The retry, whose ledger entry is now written, bumps the counter forward with an alarm, so the tampering shows up.

What remains is at most a hardening suggestion: add a per-counter owning scope. It is not a defect that violates DI-17 or INV-27 as the code is designed and documented.

confirmed.title: Denied platform permissions (EBMR-PLAT-006) leave no stored evaluation; the failed check is not logged
confirmed.description: iam.platform_authority stores every evaluation via iam.evaluate_authority (INV-26), but on denial the surrounding command raises EBMR-PLAT-006 and rolls back, discarding the stored row. Unlike iam.require_permission denials (EBMR-IAM-040), which withGuardedCommand re-logs outside the rolled-back transaction, EBMR-PLAT-006 is not re-logged (authority.ts only handles EBMR-IAM-040/041). APPROVED excludes PREPARED and CHECKED signers; CHECKED excludes PREPARED signers. Signing the later-stage meaning first (before the earlier one exists) evades the mutual exclusion, and the state engine accepts a signature captured while the aggregate was in an earlier state as long as its content hash is unchanged. The ordered, independent two-person review that INV-04/DI-17 intend is thus not enforced by the mechanism; it depends on signing order.
confirmed.failure_scenario: PoC (proven): (G) an APPROVED signature is created while the sample record is in DRAFT (before SUBMIT); after SUBMIT and a separate CHECKED, the APPROVE transition accepts that pre-made APPROVED signature. The exclusion is one-way: APPROVED is independent of PREPARED and CHECKED, but CHECKED is independent only of PREPARED (0210 seed).
- esig.sign (0230:335-503) compares the provider state only with the caller's p_expected_state. Nothing ties a meaning to the lifecycle states it may be signed in.
- platform.transition (0550:501-511) accepts any VALID signature of the right meaning and aggregate that no other transition has used.
- sample_record_content (0910) keeps state out of the hash (esig.canonical_envelope, 0200:260). So an APPROVED signature captured in DRAFT stays VALID through SUBMIT and CHECK if the content does not change.
- Scenarios G and J therefore run on the sample_record machine.

Why it is not a Phase 1 defect:

1. **Documented, intended semantics.**
   - The DI-35 control describes the rule as "which earlier signers on the same object it must differ from".
   - The 0210 catalogue header says independent_of means "meanings whose earlier signers on the same record this signer must differ from".
   - The provider contract (0200:198-199) documents state as "checked against the caller's expected state at signing".
   - platform-hook.test.ts deliberately signs CHECKED with expectedState 'DRAFT'. It expects a refusal only because the content was then edited, so signing in an earlier state is an anticipated path, not an oversight.
   - The kernel provides an order-based primitive. Ordering belongs to the domain lifecycle that uses it.

2. **No Phase 1 GMP record is exposed.**
   - Only two aggregate types can carry CHECKED or APPROVED signatures today: platform.stub_record/sample_record and esig_stub. The first is state-engine scaffolding ("stands in for the controlled records later phases build"); the second is esig test scaffolding.
   - Every real Phase 1 approval uses a meaning with an empty independent_of: RECORD_TYPE_APPROVED (0400:337), DI_INVESTIGATION_CLOSED (0430:272), RECORD_DISPOSAL_APPROVED (0440:205) and RESTORE_APPROVED (0600:727). They are checked through esig.assert_signature.
   - Market policies and rule tables (0340, 0350) use no signatures. So no Phase 1 path lets an application role or an ordinary user bypass a GMP rule this way.

3. **INV-04 belongs to Phase 2.**
   - Outline section 11 lists INV-04 and the MBR life cycle as Phase 2 exit items; the Phase 1 exit list has no INV-04.
   - INV-04 lets the checker also approve when S4 is on, and S4 is configurable (outline 3.5 and 7.2). The kernel's unconditional "APPROVED independent of CHECKED" rule therefore cannot be the final INV-04 enforcement. Phase 2's MBR module has to implement checker ≠ approver (subject to S4) and the MBR state sequence itself, with the bypass tests INV-04 requires.
   - The finding itself frames the impact as what "the Phase-2 master-record approvals ... inherit". That is a later-phase concern.

4. **DI-17 does not change this.**
   - Its Phase 1 implemented_by list and tests do not claim the MBR author/checker/approver triad.
   - Its type_detail claims "author-not-checker". The editor of the content is excluded from CHECKED and APPROVED through esig.content_change in performers_of, whatever the signing order.
   - No Phase 1 test name claims order-independent checker ≠ approver. The DI-35 test "the preparer ... never checks or approves it" proves what it says, because the preparer is also the content enterer.

Worth recording as a Phase 2 design input, not as a Phase 1 finding: the MBR (and later batch QA_REVIEWED, MANUFACTURER_RELEASE, QC) lifecycles must not rely on signing order. They should bind approval signatures to the lifecycle state or version, or enforce symmetric exclusion in a transition guard. The same one-way pattern appears in QA_REVIEWED/PRODUCTION_APPROVED and MANUFACTURER_RELEASE/PRODUCTION_APPROVED, which are Phase 3-4 records.

confirmed.title: Co-signature leaves the co-signer's validated actor context installable by the application for the rest of the transaction (attribution forgery)
confirmed.description: For a co-signature, esig.sign calls iam.set_internal_actor(v_actor || {person_id: signer, account_id: signer_account, role_code: v_role.code, auth_event_id: p_auth_event, legal_name}) (lines 482-486). That writes a kernel.command_marker row (0010 kernel.set_actor_context, line 145-149) and an iam.command_log row (0100 line 330) for the co-signer context. Line 506 only restores ebmr.ctx with kernel.set_actor_context(v_actor); nothing removes the co-signer marker. kernel.actor_context_validated() and iam.actor_is_validated() accept any context whose hash has a marker in this transaction, so the application can re-install the co-signer context with set_config for every later statement of the transaction. Every value in that context is known or readable by ebmr_app (its own context, the signer's person/account, signer_role_code from esig.signature, p_auth_event, legal_name from iam.person). The marker design ("set_config alone can never attribute a write to anyone") is defeated, and INV-40 is bypassed because the forged context never passes kernel.validate_actor_context (no fresh tap of the co-signer is consumed for these writes). Verified end to end.
confirmed.failure_scenario: Operator on a SHARED kiosk; a VERIFIER co-signs VERIFIED at that kiosk. In the operator's command transaction (ebmr_app): begin; select kernel.begin_command(<operator ctx with reason_code>); select esig.sign(<challenge>, <verifier SIGNATURE event>, 'OPEN', null, false); select esig.seal_signature(...); select set_config('ebmr.ctx', (current_setting('ebmr.ctx')::jsonb || jsonb_build_object('person_id', <verifier person>, 'account_id', <verifier account>, 'role_code', 'VERIFIER', 'auth_event_id', <event>, 'legal_name', <verifier legal name>))::text, true); -- kernel.current_actor() now returns the verifier and iam.actor_is_validated() = true; update esig.stub_signable set value='13.000' where id=<entry>; select records.raise_incident('OTHER','FORGED','MINOR','x','', '[]'); commit. PoC result: the UPDATE audit event carries actor person_id = verifier, role VERIFIER; records.incident.raised_by_person = verifier; esig.content_change now lists the verifier as a person who changed the record (so the verifier's own signature is superseded and they become an INV-03 'performer'). Any permission-gated function works with the co-signer's grants (require_permission evaluates the forged person/account/role).
confirmed.suggested_fix: Never leave a second validated identity in the transaction: have set_actor_context keep exactly one marker per (xact, backend) (replace, not add) or delete the internal context's marker/command_log row when esig.sign restores the command context; better, stop switching the actor for the co-signature and pass the signer identity explicitly to the audit writer for the esig.signature insert. Add an INV-40/INV-07 bypass test that re-installs a co-signer context after esig.sign and expects EBMR-AUDIT-009 / EBMR-IAM-002.

I could not refute F74. I confirmed it by reading the code and by running the reproducer against the live database as ebmr_app.

Code path (none of these functions is redefined by a later migration; I grepped all kernel and site-services SQL):
- packages/kernel/sql/0230_esig_sign.sql:482-486. In the co-signature branch, esig.sign calls iam.set_internal_actor(v_actor || {person_id: signer, account_id: signer_account, role_code: v_role.code, auth_event_id: p_auth_event, legal_name}).
- iam.set_internal_actor (0100_iam_foundation.sql:327) inserts an iam.command_log row for that context's hash. It then calls kernel.set_actor_context (0010_audit_trail.sql:138), which inserts a kernel.command_marker row (xact, backend, hash). set_actor_context only prunes markers of other, finished transactions, so a marker stays until the transaction ends.
- 0230:506 restores the operator with kernel.set_actor_context(v_actor). That adds or keeps the operator's marker but never removes the co-signer's marker or command_log row.
- kernel.actor_context_validated (0010:161) and iam.actor_is_validated (0100:286) only check that the hash of the current ebmr.ctx has a marker (and a command_log row) in this xact and backend. The app can therefore set_config the co-signer context back in and it counts as validated.
- jsonb::text is canonical, so the app's own `(current_setting('ebmr.ctx')::jsonb || overlay)::text` hashes to the same value.
- The app can get every overlay value from the esig.signature row it just wrote (signer_person, signer_account, signer_role_code, auth_event_id, signer_legal_name) or from its own inputs.

Guards checked, and none of them block this:
- No per-statement check ties ebmr.ctx to the session owner.
- No later migration replaces set_actor_context, current_actor, actor_context_validated, set_internal_actor or esig.sign.
- PROGRESS.md "Follow-ups carried into Phase 2" does not list this.
- ADR-0016 explicitly claims the opposite: "nor can a validated command swap in another person's context mid-transaction". The attribution.test.ts bypass test only covers a person who never had a marker.

Reproducer run: packages/kernel/test/review-tmp/f74.test.ts, using db.app, which is the ebmr_app pool per test/support/db.ts:42. As a control, the same overlay applied before esig.sign is correctly not validated. After esig.sign plus seal, applying the same overlay gave:
- actorIsValidated = true, and kernel.current_actor() returned the verifier.
- The UPDATE of esig.stub_signable was accepted. It committed with an audit event whose actor is the verifier, one esig.content_change row names the verifier, and the value is now 13.000.
- records.raise_incident was accepted under the verifier's grants (iam.require_permission INCIDENT.RAISE evaluated for the forged actor), and records.incident.raised_by_person is the verifier.

So the marker design's guarantee ("set_config alone can never attribute a write to anyone") is broken for any person who co-signed earlier in the transaction. INV-40, INV-07 and DI-22 attribution are bypassed for those writes, and the verifier becomes a recorded changer of the record they signed (INV-03). The impersonation is limited to the co-signer of that transaction, but it is a real attribution forgery that the application role can exploit.

confirmed.title: Retention purge accepts any aggregate type with invented retention dates: a QA reviewer plus the retention job erase the batch-number register and a batch number is issued again
confirmed.description: records.create_retention_schedule (0420 line 549) accepts any aggregate type except five retention-machinery types (line 569) and any approved record type; nothing binds a record type to the aggregate types it governs. Retention inputs (dates, market set, licence form) are unverified caller claims, may be set by the same QA reviewer (or the SERVICE_ACCOUNT, which holds RECORD.RETENTION_MANAGE), and the disposal-approval signature content (0720 records.record_disposal_content) shows neither the inputs nor who set them and has no entered_by, so the same QA reviewer who wrote the inputs signs RECORD_DISPOSAL_APPROVED. records.purge then deletes, from every audited table registered with that aggregate type in any schema (lines 305-347, disabling insert-only guards), all rows whose aggregate column equals the id, plus the chain. Kernel control records therefore become purgeable: site.batch_number_* (aggregate batch_number_register:<site>), iam.policy_value (iam_policy), esig.policy_value, platform time alarms/drift samples (time_node), continuity reservations/bumps (number_sequence), signatures (esig_signature). Records-schema aggregates (incident, di_investigation) are only saved by an unrelated bug: records.insert_only_trigger (line 219) renders p_table::text under a search_path that contains records, so it looks for 'aa_insert_only_incident' instead of 'aa_insert_only_records_incident' and the delete is refused. Verified end to end for the batch-number register.

confirmed.suggested_fix: Declare in the record-type register which aggregate type(s) a record type governs and refuse schedules for other aggregate types; keep an explicit allow-list of purgeable aggregate types (never registers, policy histories, signatures, alarms, continuity or iam records). Fix records.insert_only_trigger to build the name with the schema-qualified name (nspname || '.' || relname) and add bypass tests for non-batch aggregate types.

confirmed.skeptic:
I could not refute this. I reproduced it end to end at ff630ae. The only thing I wrote was a vitest file in my scratchpad, run against a throwaway test database built from every kernel and site-services migration. Nothing in the repository was changed.

**Code checked (the definitions at these lines are the live ones)**
- **Schedule creation (0420_records_retention.sql:549-583):** `records.create_retention_schedule` checks three things: RECORD.RETENTION_MANAGE, that the record type has an approved version, and that the aggregate type is not one of five retention-machinery types (line 569, mirrored by the table CHECK). Nothing ties the record type to an aggregate type. The inputs are only normalised and checked for shape, and `retention_key` is copied from the record type.
- **Grants (0700):** QA_REVIEWER holds RETENTION_MANAGE and DISPOSAL_APPROVE. SERVICE_ACCOUNT holds RETENTION_MANAGE and PURGE.
- **Disposal signature content (0720:120, `records.record_disposal_content`):** it shows record_key, retain_until, record type and zone. It does not show the inputs or who entered them, and it has no `entered_by`. So `esig.performers_of` (0230:98) does not exclude the person who wrote the inputs from signing.
- **Approval (0440:176, `records.approve_purge`):** it only requires that the approver is the one who signed.
- **Purge (0440:225, `records.purge`):** it loops over every row of `kernel.audited_table` with that aggregate type, in any schema. For each table it calls `records.insert_only_trigger`, disables the guard trigger it finds, and deletes the rows where the aggregate column equals the id. Then it deletes the chain.
- **Batch-number register (site-services 0600:99-102):** its four tables are registered as `batch_number_register` keyed on `site_code`. Schema `site` is on neither search_path, so the trigger names match and the guards are disabled.
- **Uniqueness check:** `site.register_external_batch_number` looks only at `batch_number_allocation` and its unique index. It does not look at tombstones.

**Reproduction**
The test used one QA_REVIEWER (signerActor), a BATCH_ISSUER, and a SYSTEM service actor as the retention job. Record type F75_RT had retention key BATCH_RECORD.
1. Registering PLANT1-0001 succeeded. A second registration was refused with EBMR-SITE-013.
2. The QA reviewer created a schedule on (`batch_number_register`, `PLANT1`) with inputs `{markets:[IN], licenceForm:FORM_25, manufactureDate:2000-01-01}`. It was accepted, with retain-until 2005-01-01.
3. The same QA reviewer signed RECORD_DISPOSAL_APPROVED and called `approve_purge`. Both were accepted.
4. The service actor ran `records.purge('batch_number_register:PLANT1')` with reason RETENTION_ENDED. It returned a tombstone listing `site.batch_number_allocation` (1 row). The approver in the tombstone is the same person who created the schedule and entered the inputs.
5. The site's register export then had 0 rows, and registering PLANT1-0001 again was accepted. That breaks INV-27 (numbers are never reused).
6. After the fact, `site.batch_number_invariant_violations()` returned nothing. Only `records.inv22_violations` flagged it, as WRITE_AFTER_PURGE and ROWS_REMAIN_AFTER_PURGE.

**The side bug is also real.** `kernel.register_audited_table` renders the table name under search_path `pg_catalog, kernel`, so the trigger is named `aa_insert_only_records_<table>`. `records.insert_only_trigger` renders it under a search_path that includes `records`, so it looks for `aa_insert_only_<table>` and finds nothing. The delete then hits `kernel.reject_mutation`, and that error is not caught by the `foreign_key_violation` handler. So insert-only records-schema aggregates cannot be purged, even legitimately.

**Why this is not intended, documented or deferred**
- INV-22, INV-27 and DI-47 are Phase 1 exit criteria (outline §11). DI-47 says no user can delete a record during retention. The batch-number register has no legitimate retention end.
- The schema already excludes some aggregate types ("records of the retention machinery itself are never subject to purge"). That shows an exclusion list was intended, and it misses the kernel and site registers.
- PROGRESS follow-ups cover splitting SERVICE_ACCOUNT, replacing the ALTER TABLE trigger disable, and "retention of signature rows on purge (Phase 4)". None of them covers binding a record type to an aggregate type, or purging registers or policy histories.

**Mitigating points, which bear on severity but are not a refutation**
- The attack needs a QA_REVIEWER acting in bad faith with their own signing credentials, plus the retention job. The application role cannot do it alone.
- Every step stays attributed: the retention chain keeps the schedule, the inputs with `entered_by_person`, and the purge approval, and the tombstone keeps the approver and executor. The claim is permanent loss of the register and reuse of a batch number, not an untraceable deletion.
- Letting QA type in retention inputs by hand is the Phase 1 design. The defect is that such a schedule can be attached to any aggregate.
- Finding F29 covers the same missing aggregate-type restriction with `esig_signature`. F75 is a separate, confirmed consequence of it.

High severity is defensible for the source-correction path.

confirmed.title: Audit trigger records a change of a row's aggregate column only in the new aggregate's chain; the old aggregate's trail never shows the row leaving
confirmed.description: v_key is computed from the NEW row (DELETE excepted), so an UPDATE that moves a row from aggregate A to aggregate B appends one UPDATE event to chain B only. Chain A keeps the INSERT and nothing else, so an audit-trail review of A (outline 5.4 reviews per-aggregate chains) still shows the row as belonging to A and misses the change. esig.on_signed_content_change handles old and new aggregates; the audit writer does not. Currently reachable on app-writable audited tables whose aggregate column is updatable (market.stub_pack.batch_id, stub_product_qualification.product_id, stub_person_qualification.person_id, stub_mbr_limit.mbr_code) and on every future edition table registered the same way. Verified.
confirmed.failure_scenario: MASTER_DATA_STEWARD: insert market.stub_pack (code 'PK1', batch_id B1); later, with a reason: update market.stub_pack set batch_id = B2 where id = PK1. kernel.audit_event: chain market_stub_batch:B1 has only the INSERT of PK1; the UPDATE (old batch_id B1 -> new B2) is only in chain market_stub_batch:B2. Reviewing B1's trail shows pack PK1 as still part of B1.
confirmed.suggested_fix: In kernel.audit_row_change, when TG_OP = 'UPDATE' and the old aggregate value differs from the new one, append an event to both chains (or refuse updates of the aggregate column for registered tables).

I could not refute F77. The mechanism is real, reachable today and not documented as intended. It also breaks a Phase 1 feature that assumes each aggregate's chain holds that aggregate's complete history.

1. **The code does what the finding says.** kernel.audit_row_change is defined only once, in packages/kernel/sql/0010_audit_trail.sql at lines 258-306; no later migration redefines it. For an UPDATE it sets v_row := to_jsonb(new) and v_key := aggregate_type || ':' || (v_row ->> aggregate_column). It then makes a single call to append_audit_event(v_key, ...). Nothing in it compares the old and new aggregate values.

2. **The application role can reach it.** In 0310_market_scopes.sql:
   - line 287 registers market.stub_pack with aggregate market_stub_batch and aggregate column batch_id, not insert-only;
   - line 318 grants plain UPDATE on the table to ebmr_app, with no column restriction;
   - the only guards are a0_authorize (MASTERDATA.CHANGE) and check_markets (the destination must be in the new batch's markets). Neither stops a change of batch_id.

   The same applies to stub_product_qualification.product_id, stub_person_qualification.person_id and stub_mbr_limit.mbr_code.

3. **I ran the reproducer and it fails as described.** I ran packages/kernel/test/review-tmp/f77.test.ts against the live database.
   - A MASTER_DATA_STEWARD inserts pack PK1 on batch B1, then updates it to batch B2 with a reason.
   - Chain market_stub_batch:B1 holds only the INSERT of PK1.
   - The UPDATE (batch_id B1 -> B2) is only in chain market_stub_batch:B2.

4. **This is not intended behaviour, and the codebase shows it.**
   - esig.on_signed_content_change (0220_esig_signatures.sql:344-363) explicitly notifies both the old and the new aggregate when the aggregate column changes. Moving a row between aggregates is an anticipated case.
   - Outline 5.4 defines tamper evidence as per-aggregate hash chains, and DI-22 requires the audit trail to "travel with" its record.
   - PROGRESS.md does not list this among the follow-ups carried into Phase 2.

5. **It breaks something in Phase 1, not only the Phase 4 review.** The DI-25 batch review itself is Phase 4. But the true copy (packages/kernel/src/records/true-copy.ts) is built and checked per chain:
   - verifyRecordsPart (lines 455-462) requires every row inserted in the chain and never deleted to be in the bundle. B1's true copy therefore reports "market.stub_pack row PK1: in the audit trail but missing from the bundle (incomplete copy)".
   - Around line 440 it requires an INSERT for every present row. B2's true copy therefore reports "no INSERT event in the chain".
   - After such a move, neither aggregate can produce a true copy that verifies cleanly.
   - Inferred from the code, not run: records.purge (0440_records_blockers_and_purge.sql, around line 372) deletes the whole B1 chain. That would remove PK1's creation event while PK1 still exists under B2.

**Mitigations.**
- No event is lost outright: the UPDATE body keeps the old and new batch_id, so a search by table and record would find it. This is why I don't rate it higher than medium.
- The only tables where the app can reach this today are the market stub tables, which are Phase 1 placeholders ("replaced, not extended"). The claim about future edition tables is speculative.

Even so, the per-aggregate completeness that Phase 1 relies on (true copy, purge, chain design) is violated in a concrete, reproducible scenario, so the finding stands.

I checked each claim against the live code. Some are wrong, and the rest are either intended Phase 1 scaffolding, hypothetical, or already covered by a known follow-up.

1. raise_time_incident is gated, so this claim is wrong. The live definition is the one in packages/kernel/sql/0900_integration_wiring.sql:50, which replaced the 0520 version. It calls records.raise_incident unconditionally. That function (0410_records_incidents.sql:169, never redefined) starts with iam.assert_not_administrator() (EBMR-IAM-042) and then iam.require_permission('INCIDENT.RAISE', iam.actor_location_scope()). The alarm insert happens first, but in the same transaction, so a refusal rolls it back. Both checks read the validated actor. So a CONTRACT_GIVER_REVIEWER (RECORD.READ only) or a SYSTEM_ADMINISTRATOR is refused, which contradicts the finding's scenario. The inputs are also constrained: the alarm kind by a CHECK on platform.alarm, severity by records.raise_incident (MINOR/MAJOR/CRITICAL). A holder of INCIDENT.RAISE can already raise a TIME_SYNC incident directly. The extra fault window for an invented node only flags more entries for review, which is the safe direction. It bypasses nothing. The monitor clears alarms on real nodes by itself (record_drift_check).

2. platform.transition is not ungated in any real case. Every published transition (only sample_record v1 in 0552) has a permission_code, and it goes through the AUTHORITY hook (iam.platform_authority in 0710). Publishing is owner-only, from migrations. The DI-18 concern does not apply because of static segregation: INV-11 / iam.check_static_segregation stop an administrator role from holding SAMPLE_RECORD.* (GMP), so an administrator is refused with EBMR-PLAT-006. "A transition published without a permission_code" does not exist and could only come from a future migration.

3. create_aggregate_state has no permission check, but in Phase 1 this only touches intended, documented scaffolding. The only machine is sample_record, which 0551 describes as a stand-in for later-phase records. Its content table platform.stub_record is directly insertable by ebmr_app with no gate. The catalogue (0700:66-69) deliberately defines only SUBMIT/CHECK/APPROVE/RETIRE, labelled "Phase 1 scaffolding", with no create permission. The documented flow (engine.ts createAggregateState, state README, and the authorization.test.ts:503 sample test) has the application insert stub_record and call create_aggregate_state in the same command. So a read-only user creating a DRAFT sample aggregate is the same ungated scaffolding creation the finding itself calls scaffolding.
   - Attribution is truthful: it is the validated actor's own person, account and role in state_history and in the audit event.
   - Nothing existing is altered or deleted.
   - The orphan aggregate cannot move: every transition needs a permission, and SUBMIT's has_body guard also needs the record to exist.
   - The "pin an older version" scenario needs a machine v2, which does not exist; versioned pinning is a documented parameter (README "[, version]", ADR 0010).
   - The "pre-empt a module's creation" scenario needs someone to predict a random UUID before the module creates it. In the sample flow, record and state are created in one transaction, so there is no window. That is speculation, not a concrete path.
   - Gating creation of real GMP aggregates is a matter for the later-phase modules that define those machines.
   - The audit side (any validated actor adds a BUSINESS entry, attributed to itself, to any chain) is the known PROGRESS follow-up: "revoke kernel.audit_business_event ... today any validated actor may add a business entry to any chain, attributed to itself". This is not worse than described there.

4. The regression-test claim is not a false-proof test. Both the test's title and DI-17's guard text say the scope is exactly "every function of market, records and continuity (and site services)". appWritableFunctions (authorization.test.ts:106) checks exactly those schemas, so the test proves what its name claims. The platform writers with permissions (set_setting, the time-source functions, record_drift_check, clear_alarm, transition) are gated through the AUTHORITY hook and each has its own test.

5. The scaffolding tables (esig.stub_signable, platform.stub_record, platform.stub_step/_entry) are documented stand-ins for later-phase records, and they accept writes on purpose.

What remains is at most a hardening suggestion: revoke create_aggregate_state from ebmr_app before real machines arrive. That is a later-phase design decision, not a demonstrable Phase 1 bypass.

confirmed.title: Site/area/product-scoped qualification requirements are skipped whenever the authority request has no scope in that dimension (training gate fails open)
confirmed.description: A requirement is applied only if iam.scope_covers(requirement scope, request scope); scope_covers returns false when the requirement names a site and the request does not. Grants fail closed in that case, requirements fail open. Every installation-wide check evaluates in '{}' (records incidents investigate/close, retention, holds, purge approval, record-type approval, DI investigations, market publish/policies) and esig.sign evaluates in the provider's scope, which is empty for every Phase 1 provider (esig_stub without site, sample_record, record_type_version, di_investigation, record_disposal, restore_event). So a training requirement limited to a site never applies to these actions or signatures, contrary to INV-26 (IN-04 says the training gate is a hard block). Verified.
confirmed.failure_scenario: TRAINING_COORDINATOR: select iam.create_qualification_type('SOP-VERIFY-1',...); select iam.add_qualification_requirement('SOP-VERIFY-1', null, 'STEP.VERIFY', '{"site":"SITE-1"}', 'site SOP'). A VERIFIER without that qualification (unscoped grant): iam.evaluate_authority(p, a, 'STEP.VERIFY', '{}', null, 'VERIFIER') -> allowed = true; with '{"site":"SITE-1"}' -> allowed = false, MISSING_QUALIFICATION. esig.sign of a VERIFIED signature on a stub entry whose provider returns no site therefore succeeds for the unqualified verifier.
confirmed.suggested_fix: Evaluate requirements whose scope is not covered by the request as applicable (fail closed) unless the request scope is known to exclude them, or require every authority request for site-bound work to carry the object's (or the session's) site; make providers return scope and refuse signing without it.

confirmed.skeptic:
The code does what the finding says. packages/kernel/sql/0130_iam_qualifications_authority.sql:238 applies a requirement only when iam.scope_covers(requirement scope, request scope) is true, and no later migration redefines evaluate_authority or scope_covers. But this is the documented scope model, and no Phase 1 path evaluates site-bound work without its site.

1. **The requirement scope is designed as "applies to work in this scope".** The DI-21/INV-26 test (packages/kernel/test/identity/authority.test.ts, first test) creates a site-limited requirement. It then asserts: "Elsewhere (no requirement at that site) the same person may still act". A SITE-1 requirement governs SITE-1 work and nothing else. A TRAINING_COORDINATOR who wants training enforced everywhere, including installation-wide actions, adds the requirement with an empty scope. scope_covers(null, null, null, any) is true, so it then applies to every request, '{}' included. Fail-closed coverage is always available through configuration.

2. **Installation-wide checks in '{}' are documented design.** The header of 0710_authorization_scope_and_platform.sql and packages/kernel/src/identity/README.md ("Scope of a check") both say this. Rule tables, policies, the record register, retention, incident handling, DI investigations, restores and attestations are installation-wide objects. Only a grant not limited to a site covers them. These objects have no site column, so they are not "work at SITE-1", and a SITE-1 SOP requirement does not govern them.

3. **Site-bound work carries its site.**
   - Site values and batch numbers are checked in the object's scope.
   - Point-of-work actions and every platform permission use iam.actor_location_scope(). It takes the site from the session, and iam.session.site_code and iam.device.site_code are both NOT NULL.
   - esig.sign uses the provider's scope. esig.stub_content returns the entry's own site, area and product.
   - The record_type_version, di_investigation, record_disposal, restore_event and sample_record aggregates are installation-wide and have no site.

4. **The failure scenario does not show a bypass.** It needs a stub entry whose site is NULL. That entry is not SITE-1 work, so a SITE-1 requirement correctly does not apply. The entry cannot become SITE-1 work while keeping the signature. Changing site is a signed-content change (esig.register_signed_table lists site), which supersedes the signature and reopens the entry.

5. **Scope and phase.** IN-04 has target_phase 4 and build_status SPECIFIED. Real step records with their own site arrive in later phases. PROGRESS.md already lists "per-aggregate scope lookup ... when editions arrive" as a known follow-up.

No Phase 1 path lets an unqualified person perform site-bound work without the site's training requirement being applied. What remains is a documented design choice about requirement scope, not a defect.

plausible.title: Merkle root order depends on the database collation, so anchors stop verifying after a locale or collation change
plausible.description: Leaves are ordered with `order by h ->> 'chain_key'` under the database default collation. Real chain keys sort differently under C and linguistic collations. For example, under C 'batch:<uuid>' sorts before 'batch_number_register:SITE-1' and 'retention:<k>' before 'retention_rule_set:<v>'; under en-US ICU the order is reversed (checked on this server). The root of the same heads therefore depends on the locale of the database doing the computation. verify_anchor and continuity.external_anchor_problems recompute it in the current database.
plausible.failure_scenario: Anchors are created on a production database with collation C.UTF-8. The database is later restored with pg_dump into a cluster initialised with en_US.UTF-8, or verified after a glibc collation change. kernel.merkle_root(heads) then differs for every anchor that contains such a key pair. verify_anchor reports 'anchor root does not match its heads', and external_anchor_problems returns an anchor-level problem, so compare_external_anchors classifies the anchor as UNEXPLAINED, which a restore event can never cover. Intact data is reported as tampered and restore acceptance is blocked.
plausible.suggested_fix: Sort with an explicit byte order: `order by (h ->> 'chain_key') collate "C"` in merkle_root, and in create_anchor's jsonb_agg for consistency. This matches what 0430 already does for its extract.
plausible.skeptic:
I could not refute F7. The defect is real, and low severity is right.

1. Only one definition of kernel.merkle_root exists: packages/kernel/sql/0010_audit_trail.sql:408-436, and no later migration redefines it. It orders leaves with `order by h ->> 'chain_key'` and no explicit collation, so it uses the database default collation. It is also declared IMMUTABLE. Its callers all recompute the root in whatever database they run in: kernel.verify_anchor (0010:465), records.verify_anchor (0440:417) and continuity.external_anchor_problems (0600_continuity_core.sql:478). kernel.create_anchor (0010:445) also sorts its jsonb_agg by the default collation.

2. Real chain keys sort differently under different collations. The registrations include 'backup'/'backup_job' (0610:76-77) and 'esig_signature' (0220), and there is an 'esig:' business chain. I ran a read-only query on the local server. Under C: backup:b1 < backup_job:nightly and esig:x < esig_signature:y. Under en-US-x-icu both pairs are reversed. The Merkle step hashes sha256(level[i] || level[i+1]), which depends on order, so the same heads give a different root.

3. The failure does not depend on anyone misconfiguring anything.
   - The databases differ already: CI uses the postgres:16 image (en_US.utf8, glibc), while the local server's databases are C.UTF-8.
   - A logical restore follows the collation of the target database. `createRestoreDatabase` (packages/kernel/src/continuity/backup-drill.ts:347-360) copies the locale only if a database with the source's name exists on the admin server. The documented drill usage puts --admin-url on a different host ("drill-host"), where that lookup finds nothing, so the restore uses that host's default locale.
   - A glibc or ICU upgrade can change the order under the same locale name (for example glibc 2.28). Locale matching cannot prevent that.
   - Retention-grade logical backups are kept for 15 years or more (ha-and-restore.md:49), so a restore under different collation rules is likely at some point.

4. The result contradicts documented behaviour; it is not intended. ha-and-restore.md section 5.3 (line 99) says a move to a new cluster (pg_upgrade, new hardware) is recorded as a CLUSTER_MIGRATION restore event and "the anchor comparison shows only MATCH". ADR 0007 says the hash functions must stay reproducible for decades and that archived records can be verified without the application. With a different collation:
   - external_anchor_problems returns an anchor-level problem (chain_key null).
   - compare_external_anchors (0600:528-531) therefore classifies the anchor as UNEXPLAINED, even one that would otherwise be DISCARDABLE.
   - verify_external_anchors then reports PROBLEM.
   - kernel.verify_anchor / records.verify_anchor report 'anchor root does not match its heads'.
   The net effect is that intact data raises tamper alarms, and a restore or migration cannot be closed cleanly.

5. This is not a known item and not planned for a later phase. PROGRESS.md mentions no collation or locale issue for anchors, and anchors are Phase 1 work. Elsewhere the codebase consistently uses `collate "C"` for deterministic ordering (0430:88, 0420, 0300, 0200 canonical JSON, 0550), so the omission in merkle_root and create_anchor is an inconsistency, not a design choice.

Severity stays low. The failure makes intact data look tampered; it does not let tampering go undetected, and nothing can be bypassed. The suggested fix is correct: use `order by (h ->> 'chain_key') collate "C"` in kernel.merkle_root, and the same ordering in create_anchor's jsonb_agg. Existing anchors made on C / C.UTF-8 databases keep verifying after the fix. Anchors made on en_US databases (as in CI) would need a versioned verifier.

plausible.title: A co-signature leaves the co-signer's identity validated for the rest of the transaction, so the application can act as the verifier
plausible.description: For a co-signature, esig.sign calls iam.set_internal_actor(v_actor || {person_id: signer, account_id, role_code, auth_event_id, legal_name}) at lines 482-486. That writes a kernel.command_marker row (through kernel.set_actor_context) and an iam.command_log row for the hash of that context. At line 506 the function switches back with kernel.set_actor_context(v_actor), but it never removes the co-signer's marker or log row. kernel.current_actor(), iam.actor_is_validated() and iam.assert_validated_actor() only check that a marker and a log row exist for sha256(ebmr.ctx) in the current transaction and backend. After esig.sign returns, ebmr_app can therefore set_config the exact co-signer context. The context is deterministic jsonb, and every value in it can be read from esig.signature. From then on, every write and permission check in the transaction runs as the co-signer, inside the performer's session. ADR 0016 promises that 'a validated command cannot swap in another person's context mid-transaction'; this path breaks that promise.
plausible.failure_scenario: Confirmed on a test database built from this worktree. Performer P and verifier V are both on a SHARED kiosk. P's command creates a challenge for V's account, and V authenticates (badge + PIN) for it. In P's command: `select esig.sign(ch, ev, 'OPEN')`, then seal it. Then, as ebmr_app: `select set_config('ebmr.ctx', (current_setting('ebmr.ctx')::jsonb || jsonb_build_object('person_id', s.signer_person, 'account_id', s.signer_account, 'role_code', s.signer_role_code, 'auth_event_id', s.auth_event_id, 'legal_name', s.signer_legal_name))::text, true) from esig.signature s where s.id = '<sig>'`. After that, `iam.assert_validated_actor()` returns V's person_id and `iam.require_permission('STEP.VERIFY')` passes as V. `insert into esig.stub_signable ...` writes an audit INSERT event whose actor is V, carrying V's signature auth_event_id, and an esig.content_change row with person_id = V. The application, or whoever holds its credentials, can create or change GMP data and use V's permissions (for example QA functions when V is QA) under V's name, with no further authentication by V.
plausible.suggested_fix: Do not install the co-signer as the transaction's actor. One option: attribute the esig.signature insert through a one-shot, owner-only channel that the audit trigger consumes for exactly that row, like esig.signing_challenge. Another: delete the co-signer's kernel.command_marker row right after the insert. kernel.current_actor requires the marker, so removing it invalidates the context, and the marker table is owner-writable. Alternatively, add a random nonce to the co-signer context that is never stored anywhere readable, so its hash cannot be rebuilt. Add a bypass test to test/identity/attribution.test.ts for the co-signature path.

So the application role can attribute arbitrary GMP writes to the co-signer. It does this inside P's session, with no command authentication by V; this bypasses validate_actor_context's session-account check (IAM-111) and the INV-40 per-command event.

This is not intended behaviour. ADR-0016 (Consequences, Positive) says a validated command cannot swap in another person's context mid-transaction. The PROGRESS.md Phase 2 follow-ups do not mention it; the nearest item is the audit_business_event gating, which is unrelated. No deferred or commit-time check catches it; the only deferred triggers are the seal check and idempotency.

One detail I did not verify: iam.require_permission is not granted to ebmr_app, so I could not call it directly. The mechanism (assert_validated_actor, which needs the marker and the log row, both present) implies that permission-gated app functions would pass as V.

Scope of the attack: it needs V to authenticate for a real co-signature in a transaction the application drives. This is the leaked-credentials or compromised-app threat that ADR-0012/0016 explicitly cover. It turns V's authentication, which should be bound to one challenge, into general-purpose impersonation of V for the rest of that transaction. The finding stands.

My files are only in the scratchpad (/tmp/claude-0/-home-user/0f393df3-64ef-5de6-9328-48ce9ce2b1a5/scratchpad/f12/). I changed nothing in the repository. The untracked packages/kernel/test/review-tmp/ was already there before I started.

plausible.title: The seal payload leaves out auth_method and session_person, and the integrity job does not cross-check them
plausible.description: The 0240 header states that any change to a signature row changes the sealed payload. seal_payload covers most columns directly or through manifestation_sha256, but not auth_method or session_person. esig.signature_problems does not compare auth_method with iam.auth_event.method, or session_person with esig.challenge.session_person or iam.session.person_id. The audit row_hash would differ, but nothing verifies it.
plausible.failure_scenario: A database superuser disables triggers (session_replication_role = replica) and changes a co-signature's session_person to another person, or changes auth_method from BADGE_PIN to PASSWORD. esig.verify_signatures() and the TypeScript seal check still report nothing, so the evidence package misstates in whose terminal session, and by which method, the signer authenticated.
plausible.suggested_fix: Add both fields to a v2 seal payload, cross-check them in signature_problems against the auth event and the challenge, and correct the 0240 comment.
plausible.skeptic:
Not refuted. The core claim holds, and low severity fits.

What I confirmed:
- No later migration redefines esig.seal_payload, so the version at packages/kernel/sql/0230_esig_sign.sql:223 is the live one. esig.signature_problems, verify_signatures and evidence_package are defined only in 0240.
- The seal payload covers every esig.signature column except auth_method and session_person. Each other column is covered in one of three ways:
  - directly;
  - through manifestation_sha256, with build_manifestation compared in signature_problems (legal name, login, role name, meaning title and text, cosignature);
  - through a separate check (manifestation_text, and aggregate_ref via the CHECK constraint and the seal's aggregate_ref).
- esig.signature_problems (0240:14-80) compares the challenge only on aggregate_ref, content_hash, content_version, meaning_code, signer_account, signer_person, session_id and device_id. It never compares session_person. It compares the auth event only on person_id, account_id, challenge_id, purpose and device_id. It never compares method with s.auth_method. Nothing checks session_person against iam.session.person_id.
- The TypeScript integrity check (packages/kernel/src/esig/integrity.ts:29-58) verifies only the seal over esig.seal_payload. No SQL or TS code checks either column (grep finds them only in the DDL, in esig.sign, and in two tests).
- The attack is within the project's own detection scope. The test manifestation.test.ts:125-146 ("[DI-36] ... a change made by a superuser is detected") uses exactly `set session_replication_role = replica` plus an UPDATE on esig.signature, and expects the integrity job to catch it. The 0240 header also says any change to the row changes the payload. That promise is false for these two columns.

Concrete path:
1. As superuser, run `set session_replication_role = replica`.
2. For a co-signature S (cosignature = true), run `update esig.signature set session_person = '<third person uuid>', auth_method = 'PASSWORD' where id = S`, and optionally the same session_person change on esig.challenge.
