The same role can claim the head message and mark it delivered. Nothing is lost or altered without trace: platform.outbox and outbox_attempt are insert-only, and the PENDING state, attempts and last_error stay readable by ebmr_app for monitoring.

4. Later-phase scope. The Phase 1 outbox brief (docs/build-plan/phase-1/B5-platform.md item 5) requires only: enqueue in the business transaction, a SKIP LOCKED relay, attempts recorded, delivery at least once, consumer-side deduplication, and tests that a rollback leaves no row and that two relays never deliver the same row. All of these are met. Dead-letter handling, fault injection and "no silent loss under fault injection" belong to Phase 6 (build-outline section 11). No Phase 1 control, DI-27 included, requires an outbox lag or parking alarm. DI-27's behaviour and catalog_test concern trusted time, and the drift or reference-loss alarm and incident are raised synchronously.

At most this is a hardening suggestion for when a real relay and consumers exist. It is not a defect with a concrete path to breaking a guarantee in this code.

rejected.title: Guard implementations can be re-registered, changing published and pinned machine versions without changing their hash
rejected.why:
The code is as described. platform.register_guard (0550_platform_state_engine.sql:35-46) upserts on code, and machine_canonical_text/machine_definition_hash hash only the guard codes. This is still not a defect in the Phase 1 threat model.

1. Only the owner can reach it. register_guard is not granted to ebmr_app (0550:601; test state-machine.test.ts:250 proves the app role is refused), and ebmr_app has only SELECT on platform.state_guard. The only path is an owner-run migration, which is a software release. That is the change-controlled channel, not a bypass by the application role or an ordinary user. The finding itself concedes this.

2. The upsert is not a distinct weakness. The same owner migration can simply `create or replace function platform.guard_sample_record_has_body(...)` with a different body. That changes what SUBMIT enforces, keeps the definition hash the same and reports no integrity violation, without touching state_guard at all. Making state_guard insert-only would close nothing. Guard implementations are code, like platform.transition itself, which a migration can also redefine.

3. The design is intended and documented. machine_integrity_violations() is documented (0550:584, src/state/README.md) as detecting a superuser rewrite of the sealed definition rows (states and transitions with their guard codes). It does not claim to fingerprint executable code. ADR 0010 point 6 deliberately governs behaviour changes in code at the release level: a semantic-change report, a pre-upgrade check against open batches, and a QA impact decision for fixes that change the semantics of code in use. Behaviour for in-flight work is pinned by recording the software release per batch, not by hashing function bodies.

4. The cited controls belong to a later phase. DI-09 (change and configuration management, drift from the validated baseline) and DI-10 (version-in-force stamping, including the software release) both have target_phase: 4, with implemented_by empty and build_status SPECIFIED.

At most this is an optional hardening idea: hashing guard prosrc into the canonical text. It is not a concrete failure path in Phase 1.

rejected.title: Late-entry co-signature is verified against the batch, not the entry it approves
rejected.why:
F54 describes a failure that cannot happen in the Phase 1 code. It depends on a later phase, and the finding says so itself ("Once a batch content provider exists").

1. The only caller is a demonstration table. platform.check_late_entry(..., 'batch', batch_id) is called only from platform.stub_step_entry_time_model (0530:290), the trigger on platform.stub_step_entry. The B5 brief (docs/build-plan/phase-1/B5-platform.md item 1) and packages/kernel/src/time/README.md both call it a demo table showing the pattern. Real step and entry tables arrive in Phase 2 with the engine-level generic blocks and the generic shop-floor step screen (outline section 11). Nothing checks, compares or chains that aggregate type. The literal string 'batch' is simply passed on to verify_signature.

2. In Phase 1 the path fails closed. The SIGNATURE hook is esig.platform_signature_check (0910), which calls esig.signature_problem (0230). That requires a real esig.signature row with meaning_code LATE_ENTRY_APPROVED and aggregate batch:<id>. esig.create_challenge raises EBMR-ESIG-011 when the aggregate has no content provider. The only providers registered are sample_record (0910), record_type_version, di_investigation, record_disposal, restore_event (0720) and esig_stub (0250). None is 'batch', and register_content_provider is owner-only. So nobody (app role, supervisor or operator) can create a signature that check_late_entry would accept. The misattribution in the scenario (Y approved by a signature meant for X) cannot occur today.

3. The tests are not misleading. The test "[INV-16] within the window a reason suffices; beyond it a valid supervisor co-signature is required" proves what its name says: refusal without a signature, with a random id, and with the wrong meaning; acceptance with a valid LATE_ENTRY_APPROVED; and one signature per entry (EBMR-PLAT-076). A separate test proves fail-closed when no verifier is registered. None of them claims the signature covers the entry's value or time.

4. Part of the scenario is also weaker than stated. Once a batch provider exists, signature validity requires the batch content hash at use time to equal the hash at signing (esig.signature_state reports CONTENT_MISMATCH or SUPERSEDED_BY_CHANGE otherwise). Any other write to the batch between signing and use would therefore invalidate the co-signature.

What remains is a fair design recommendation for Phase 2, when the real block tables and the batch aggregate are built: co-sign the pending entry's own content. It is not a Phase 1 defect with a concrete failure path, so under the rules (belongs to a later phase, not currently exploitable) it is refuted. It is not in the PROGRESS.md "Follow-ups carried into Phase 2" list, so it would be worth noting there as a design input.

rejected.title: reserve_counter_ceiling trusts the caller's external floor and ledger receipt; a COUNTER_RESERVE holder can extend ceilings without writing the ledger
rejected.why:
The facts in the finding are accurate. I still refute it as a defect: it describes a trust boundary the design depends on, the harm needs an event the attacker cannot cause, and the only fix is new infrastructure outside Phase 1.

What is accurate:
- continuity.reserve_counter_ceiling (packages/kernel/sql/0600_continuity_core.sql:345) is the only definition; no later migration replaces it.
- It is granted to ebmr_app (line 913). BATCH_ISSUER and SERVICE_ACCOUNT hold CONTINUITY.COUNTER_RESERVE (0700_authorization_catalogue.sql:96 and 108).
- It only checks that p_ledger_receipt is non-blank and that p_external_floor >= c.reserved_ceiling. A caller who holds the app's database credentials can pass floor = the current ceiling and receipt = 'x'. The database accepts the new ceiling with no ledger entry.

Why this is not a defect in this function:
1. **The database cannot see the external ledger, by design.** The application is the only ledger client (ExternalLedger in src/continuity/ledger.ts). The ledger is write-once object storage (S3 Object Lock, WORM), which does not sign anything. Every continuity function that uses ledger data receives it as a parameter from the application:
   - record_restore_event(p_event, p_external_anchors), line 601
   - compare_external_anchors(p_anchors), line 502
   - verify_external_anchors(p_anchors), line 857
   - after_restore(p_restore_event_id, p_external_high_water, ...), line 742
   
   reserve_counter_ceiling is one more case of the same rule. Its header comment says it records a ceiling "that has already been written to the external ledger", so it records the caller's claim. EBMR-CONT-013 is a consistency check against honest callers (a lost acknowledgement, or a restore the database did not record). It was never meant to authenticate the ledger.
2. **The ledger protects against a different threat.** In the threat model (DB-6, section 7, and the assumption that DB superuser and storage root are different teams) and in ha-and-restore.md 4.3, the ledger stops database administrators from undoing history through a restore. The application writes it. No code, design document or ADR claims that ebmr_app cannot misreport ledger state, and no signing ledger service exists in the architecture or the Phase 1 plan. The proposed fix (signed receipts, with a key ring like the esig seals) adds a new component; it does not correct a coding mistake.
3. **The attacker cannot bring about the harm.** Numbers get reused only if a restore by database administrators happens after the unrecorded reservation and before the next anchor export. The anchor job runs every few minutes and copies each counter's reservedCeiling and lastValue to the ledger. ledgerHighWater() includes those marks and completeRestore passes them to after_restore, which sets the counter to the greatest of its restored value, its restored ceiling and the ledger mark.
   - A synchronous-standby failover keeps the reservation row, so it does not trigger reuse.
   - With ebmr_app alone the attacker cannot start a restore, since restores need database-administrator action or RESTORE_OPERATE plus an approved restore event.
4. **Detection covers every other case.** checkAgainstLedger reports LEDGER_BEHIND_COUNTER as an ERROR at start-up. The next honest reservation fails with EBMR-CONT-013. This matches the "detected" category the outline allows in 9.1 and ADR 0012 decision 8.

A narrower point in the finding's favour: the bypass test in numbers.test.ts:76 is named "...cannot ... forge a reservation record", but it only proves that a direct INSERT is refused. That is at most a naming weakness in a test. It does not make this design choice a defect.

Weighing an inherent, documented-by-architecture trust in the application as ledger client, harm that depends on a coincidental administrator restore within one anchor interval, and a fix that is a new component: I treat this as a known architectural limitation (hardening for a later phase), not a defect.

rejected.title: register_external_batch_number takes the site time zone from the caller, so the register's allocation date can be wrong
rejected.why:
I read the code and it does what the finding says. site.register_external_batch_number (packages/site-services/sql/0600_batch_number_register.sql:300-345) only checks that p->>'site_zone' exists in pg_timezone_names (line 317). It then stores that value in batch_number_allocation.site_zone, and the view site.batch_number_register (line 449) computes allocation_date as (recorded_at at time zone a.site_zone)::date. No later migration redefines either object. Even so, I do not think this is a defect in Phase 1, for these reasons:

1. **The zone is an input by design, and the rest of Phase 1 works the same way.** The function header (line 298) and the README (packages/site-services/src/batch-numbers/README.md) list site_zone as a caller input. Other modules also take the zone from the caller and only check that it is a valid zone:
   - the two-timestamp time model uses the actor context's site_zone (0530_platform_time_model.sql:273-275);
   - the retention schedule uses p_site_zone or the actor's zone (0420:555-567);
   - market publish uses the actor's zone (0340:305);
   - define_batch_number_rule (line 189), which supplies the zone for GENERATED numbers, checks it the same way.

   The only place that compares a declared zone with a site zone is esig signing (0230:381, EBMR-ESIG-035). That check uses the global iam policy 'site.zone', which is described as the zone for "actor contexts the identity module creates itself". There is no per-site zone record that site services could check against.

2. **The master data the fix needs belongs to later phases.** The outline's data model lists "organisation units with time zone", but the Phase 1 plan (outline section 11) does not deliver them. IN-18 has target_phase 4, and the "allocation register" is listed among Phase 4 India fields. The README says the register was "built early as INV-27 context" and that Phase 4 wires the issue guard to registerExternalBatchNumber. The ERP stub arrives in Phase 3 and the full ERP adapters in Phase 6. INV-27, the invariant this Phase 1 code proves, is about numbers never being reused, not about the allocation date.

   The suggested interim fix ("the zone of the site's rules") is not well-defined:
   - rules are per product and batch kind, and each stores its own caller-supplied zone, so a site can have rules with different zones;
   - a site that takes all its numbers from ERP may have no rules at all.

3. **Nothing is lost or forged.** recorded_at comes from the database clock (column default clock_timestamp()). The export always includes allocated_at as an exact UTC instant (register.ts exportBatchNumberRegister). The zone used is stored on the row and in the audit chain payload. The failure needs an authorised, permission-scoped caller (BATCH_NUMBER.REGISTER_EXTERNAL in site and product scope) to declare the wrong site zone. That is a misconfigured trusted integration, not a bypass. Even a deliberate choice of zone only moves the derived date by at most one day, and the true instant sits beside it in the same exported row.

4. **The IN-18 catalog test is still met.** It asks that numbers are never reissued after a void and that the export has allocation date, product identity and batch size. Both hold.

At most this is a Phase 4 hardening note: when site master data exists, take the register's zone from it, and consider showing the zone in the view. It is not a Phase 1 defect with a guarantee broken.

rejected.title: The lost-window incident is not created automatically (ADR 0007 decision 6), and this is not tracked as a follow-up
rejected.why:
Refuted. The factual part is correct: nothing raises the incident automatically. The live continuity.after_restore (0600_continuity_core.sql:742; no later migration redefines it) only moves counters and sequences. continuity.lost_window (0600:844) is referenced only by its grant (0600:924), restore.ts:135 lostWindow(), the continuity README and its test. 0900_integration_wiring.sql calls records.raise_incident only for time faults. But the gap has no failure path in Phase 1, so it does not meet the bar for a defect:

1. The failure scenario cannot happen in this phase. ADR 0007 decision 6 and outline 4.2 describe the incident as one "listing the batches active in the window, with re-entry through the late-entry or paper path." The phase plan (outline section 11) has no batch records, batch execution or late-entry/correction paths in Phase 1. Execution with correction/void paths arrives in Phase 3, and review and disposition in Phase 4. So the claimed failure, "batches whose history was lost can continue without the re-entry and QA review", has no batches to act on. The batch-linked incident depends on objects that later phases deliver. DI-12's batch linking, and "blocks disposition", are likewise later-phase features.

2. The restore is a manual, SOP-driven procedure that already requires a data-integrity incident. docs/operations/ha-and-restore.md section 5.2:
   - Step 1 opens a data-integrity incident or change record authorising the restore.
   - Step 10 has QA and production handle the lost window with lostWindow(restore event), with evidence "Incident, re-entry records".
   - Step 12 closes that incident only after QA review of steps 1-11.

   So the scenario's "no records.incident exists for the discarded history" requires ignoring the documented procedure. It is not a bypass the application role or an ordinary user can exploit. Running after_restore also needs CONTINUITY.RESTORE_OPERATE and an event approved with a RESTORE_APPROVED e-signature (0720), so a QA person is always part of the restore.

3. The linked controls and invariants are not violated:
   - INV-08 (outline section 5.3) is "anchors match, or a signed restore event covers the gap". That is implemented and tested, and it says nothing about an incident.
   - DI-45's behaviour and catalog_test (backups, separation, alarms, restore testing) do not mention a lost-window incident.
   - DI-12's automatic-incident list does not name restores and is framed around batches.

4. The item is tracked in PROGRESS.md: line 161 lists "lost_window -> records incident" among the B6 integration items. It is only missing from the later "Follow-ups carried into Phase 2" summary, and the status table in ha-and-restore.md section 7 is stale ("Wiring by the lead during Phase 1 integration").

At most this is a documentation and tracking nit: update section 7 and add the item to the Phase 2/3 carry list. It is not a real defect with a concrete failure path. Given the rule that unsure means refuted, refuted=true.

rejected.title: A person can declare the LMS qualification mirror fresh, unaudited, making stale mirrored qualifications count
rejected.why:
The code is as described: iam.record_mirror_heartbeat (0130_iam_qualifications_authority.sql:416) only calls require_permission('QUALIFICATION.RECORD') and upserts iam.mirror_heartbeat. No later migration redefines it. But in Phase 1 this is an intended, documented stub, not a defect you can exploit:

1. It is documented as a stub and as unaudited. The table comment at 0130:34 says "Operational heartbeat of each mirror (not GMP data; not audited)". The LMS source row at 0130:32 says "stub until the LMS adapter, Phase 6". packages/kernel/src/identity/README.md calls it "the mirror heartbeat stub". The real LMS adapter, with source time, feed heartbeat and stale-mirror fault injection, is Phase 6 work (outline section 11 Phase 6; outline 4.6). A heartbeat restricted to a SYSTEM service identity belongs with that adapter.

2. The heartbeat gives the coordinator no extra power. In Phase 1 there is no LMS feed. The only way an 'LMS'-sourced person_qualification row exists is that someone holding QUALIFICATION.RECORD entered it by hand with iam.record_qualification(..., p_source => 'LMS'). That same person can also record an INTERNAL qualification, which qualification_source_fresh always treats as fresh. They can withdraw a qualification too. So the heartbeat lets them do nothing they could not already do through the audited path. The step "possibly withdrawn in the LMS" cannot happen: there is no external LMS whose withdrawals could go unseen. Every withdrawal goes through iam.withdraw_qualification, which is audited and which the evaluation honours whatever the heartbeat says.

3. The call is not entirely without trace. require_permission runs evaluate_authority, which writes an iam.authority_evaluation row to a protected log. That row records the actor, the QUALIFICATION.RECORD permission and the correlation id, and it commits with the heartbeat.

4. The comparison with platform.record_drift_check does not fit. The drift monitor is a real Phase 1 service whose readings raise and clear data-integrity alarms. The LMS heartbeat has no real feeder until Phase 6. The test that ships with it, authority.test.ts ('[INV-26] mirrored qualification data outside its freshness bound fails closed'), deliberately drives the heartbeat as a training coordinator. It proves the fail-closed freshness check, which is what INV-26 and INV-38 require of the guard.

In short, this is hardening for a stub that belongs to a later phase, not a bypass or an invariant violation in Phase 1.

rejected.title: The occurred_at trust level is asserted by the caller, so a person-typed time labelled DEVICE_SYNCED skips the late-entry path
rejected.why:
The behaviour described is real. In 0530_platform_time_model.sql, ebmr_app has an INSERT grant on occurred_trust (line ~318), and platform.stub_step_entry_time_model (~line 277) passes new.occurred_trust unchanged into check_occurred_at, time_basis and assess_late_entry. No later migration redefines this trigger or checks trust against the actor source or the device; grep finds no other reference to stub_step_entry or DEVICE_SYNCED after 0530. So a USER_CLAIMED time relabelled DEVICE_SYNCED is not treated as a late entry. I still judge it not to be a Phase 1 defect, for these reasons:

1. What it depends on comes in a later phase. A trust level can only be derived from real provenance: the instrument's clock sync status, an enrolled gateway identity, and a data-point record of device and entry mode. None of that exists in Phase 1. iam.device (0140) has no clock-sync state. 0520 monitors only the server's time references. The threat model assigns fake instruments and source-time provenance to later phases: GW-1 to Phase 2/6, GW-2/GW-6 to Phase 2 and 6, GW-4 to Phase 2 and 3. ADR 0006 says instrument source times arrive through the site gateway (the Phase 2 gateway core). DI-28, which covers late entries, back-dating and the late-entry path, is target_phase 4 with build_status SPECIFIED, and its implemented_by is empty. Its control IDs (DI-28) therefore do not apply to Phase 1.

2. It is intended and documented. The B5 brief (docs/build-plan/phase-1/B5-platform.md) sets the Phase 1 scope: helper functions that take (occurred_at, trust, ...) as parameters, and a demo stub_step_entry whose bypass test only has to prove that the app cannot set recorded_at. Open question T2 in docs/decisions/phase-1-open-questions.md, listed in PROGRESS.md, leaves which trusts count as late to the owner and assumes device-buffered times come from devices. The 0530 grant comment says the application "can state what happened and when it claims it happened"; the trust label is part of that claim.

3. INV-16 is not violated. INV-16 requires that recorded_at comes from the database clock and that a claimed time is stored separately with a trust level. Both hold: recorded_at is forced by enforce_db_time, and occurred_at and occurred_trust are separate columns. Nothing is altered or lost without trace. The row is audited in the same transaction with the actor's person_id and source (0010 records 'source', e.g. UI), so a DEVICE_SYNCED claim from a UI operator is attributed and visible in the audit trail.

4. There is no production path in Phase 1. stub_step_entry is a demonstration table, and no Phase 1 GMP business table accepts a DEVICE_SYNCED time through a late-entry flow. The proposed fix (refuse DEVICE_SYNCED from UI/API) is also a design decision still to be made: a scale reading relayed through the gateway may be confirmed by an operator whose source is UI. That decision belongs to the Phase 2/3 data-point and gateway work.

This is at most a note on the design of later block tables, not a Phase 1 defect with a concrete bypass of a Phase 1 guarantee. Where this is borderline, I have refuted as the review rules require.

rejected.title: Protected-log writers callable without any actor let the application fabricate evidence and security alerts
rejected.why:
This is intended, documented behaviour. None of these rows feeds any decision, so there is no GMP bypass, no record change and no forged attribution. At most it is hardening with limited value.

1. **The grants are deliberate.** The functions are callable by the application on purpose, so it can log refusals after the failed command rolls back.
   - `packages/kernel/sql/0170_iam_signing_readiness.sql`, comment above `iam.segregation_evaluation`: "a refusal raises EBMR-IAM-041 with a JSON DETAIL so the caller can log it again after the command rolls back".
   - `packages/kernel/sql/0230_esig_sign.sql`, line 683: "Signing failures are logged after the failed command rolled back (the TypeScript signing wrapper calls this)".
   - The grants to `ebmr_app` are at 0170 line 500 and 0230 line 714.
   - The callers are `packages/kernel/src/esig/signing.ts` (`logSigningFailure`) and `packages/kernel/src/identity/authority.ts` (`logRefusal`). They call these functions from the pool, outside any command. That is why no actor can be required: the command that held the actor has rolled back.

2. **`iam.evaluate_authority` cannot fabricate anything.** The database computes every stored field from its own grant, qualification and status data. It also records the actor's correlation id and `requested_by_account`. A stored evaluation is a true record of what was asked and what the database answered. The evidence package and `esig.signature_problems` (0240 line 61) read only the evaluation whose id the signature carries, so extra evaluations never reach a signature's evidence.

3. **The `evaluate_segregation` rows are true for their inputs.** `allowed` is computed from the rule, person and excluded set that the row itself stores.
   - They attach to a signature's evidence package only by correlation id. The application chooses that id by design (build outline, Capture section: "the application sets the actor context (... correlation ID ...)"). It is not unique, and legitimate later commands can share it.
   - To inject a row into S's package, the attacker needs a real `begin_command`. That writes an `iam.command_log` row with the correlation id, account, session and time.
   - The injected row's `evaluated_at` is after S's `recorded_at`, because the evidence package orders these rows by `evaluated_at`.
   - `signature_state` and `signature_problems` never read `iam.segregation_evaluation`, so S stays valid.
   - The row is added, not forged: it is traceable, and it changes no record or signature.

4. **`record_signing_failure` only adds notice rows and alerts.**
   - Account lockout is computed from `iam.authn_attempt`, which only `ebmr_authn` writes (`iam.consecutive_failures`, 0160). A fabricated failure therefore cannot lock anyone out or change anyone's rights.
   - It produces a notice row and an alert that has no matching `authn_attempt`, which the security unit would see when investigating.
   - Genuine failed signing authentications raise their own SIGNING_FAILED alerts through `ebmr_authn` (0160 line 433).

5. **ADR-0012's guarantees are not touched.** Its list of what a compromised application must not do is: jump a state machine, forge or transplant a signature, sign without real authentication, or rewrite recorded data. Adding an evaluation or alert row does none of these.

6. **The suggested fix would not remove the capability.** A leaked application credential can already run `begin_command` as any user with an active session on a personal device, because `validate_actor_context` checks no session secret. Requiring a validated actor would therefore not stop the application from writing these rows.

7. **Ordinary users cannot trigger this.** The application code calls these functions only with the DETAIL the database itself returned.

rejected.title: IT administrators own the 21 CFR 11.100(c) enforcement switch and an unvalidated site zone used by every signature
rejected.why:
I refute this finding. The first half describes intended, documented design, and the second half describes a reversible misconfiguration that fails closed and does not bypass any rule.

1) esig.us_certification_mode belonging to IAM.POLICY_MANAGE is intentional.
- The 11.100(c) letter is recorded by iam.record_us_esig_certification in 0170. That function needs IAM.CERTIFICATION_RECORD, a GOVERNANCE permission held by PROCESS_OWNER. Neither the letter nor its gate was ever placed with the quality unit.
- DI-18 lists "configuration" among the system-administration permissions. Its guard list limits iam.assert_not_administrator to GMP data write paths (market rule tables, site values, policies, records, and so on). IAM policies are not on that list.
- The DI-15 test in packages/kernel/test/identity/accounts.test.ts:227-230 deliberately switches the mode as the administrator ('expert chose the catalog position').
- FLAG is the catalog's own requirement. DI-15 behaviour says "The system flags a missing letter for US-market tenants but does not block execution", and type_detail calls tracking of the letter a DESIGN_CHOICE and an organisational duty. BLOCK is only a proposed_modify, and the expert decision is still PENDING (outline section 13 item 9; the comment at 0170:361-364).
- So an administrator switching to FLAG gives exactly the behaviour the catalog asks for, and breaks no control. The change is also attributed and audited: set_by_person, set_by_account and a reason are recorded, and iam.policy_value is registered as an audited table at 0100:343. The edit is not traceless.
- The failure scenario also cannot happen in Phase 1. Nothing outside 0170 calls iam.assert_us_esig_certification, and batch issue (PLANNED -> ISSUED, outline 5.x) belongs to a later phase. No US-market batch can be issued in this codebase with or without the letter. Wiring the gate, and deciding who owns it, is later-phase work that depends on the pending expert decision.

2) site.zone accepting an invalid zone.
- iam.set_policy (0130:432) does not validate TEXT keys that have no allowed_values. So an administrator could store 'Mars/Base'.
- The result fails closed. Actor contexts created by the identity module (0160:531) would carry the bad zone. Platform time-model writes run platform.assert_time_zone (0530:274) and raise EBMR-PLAT-017. esig.sign's zone and offset handling would error too. Nothing is signed or recorded with a wrong or missing attribution. No GMP rule is bypassed, and no record is changed without a trace.
- The change itself is attributed and audited, and the same role can revert it at once.
- This amounts to a system administrator being able to cause a denial of service through misconfiguration. Administrators can already do that in many ways (disabling accounts, locking devices). It is a hardening suggestion, not a defect with a concrete path to a Part 11, data-integrity or privilege-boundary breach.
- The finding's own scenario covers only the invalid zone. It does not show a valid but wrong zone leading to a violation.

Neither half shows a real violation of DI-15 or DI-18 in Phase 1.

gaps: COVERAGE GAP (spot-checked, finding 1): nobody checked how the records and continuity/audit modules work together. The records reviewer skipped continuity and the continuity reviewer skipped records purge. PROGRESS.md line 133 (B4 integration items) says verification 'must use records.verify_chain/verify_anchor (purge-aware) combined with B6 restore-event coverage'. That was never done: continuity.external_anchor_problems, continuity.verify_external_anchors, checkAgainstLedger and src/audit/verify.ts verifyAnchor are not purge-aware. The item is also missing from 'Follow-ups carried into Phase 2'.

ATTACK CLASS NOT TRIED (spot-checked, finding 2): the application's own session settings inside SECURITY DEFINER code. Every definer function pins only search_path; nothing pins TimeZone, IntervalStyle, DateStyle or bytea_output. to_jsonb(row) in the audit trigger, the true-copy export and the purge digest follow the session TimeZone. What I checked and found sound: all event times use clock_timestamp(), so a long-held transaction cannot backdate anything; every esig content provider renders instants explicitly in UTC; restore_event_content is UTC-safe. Minor: iam 0170:385 compares p_submitted_on > current_date, which follows the session zone. Not verified: the app can SET synchronous_commit=local/off for its own commits, which defeats the RPO-0 claim in docs/operations/ha-and-restore.md §2. Failover is treated as a restore, so the loss is detected rather than silent.

CLASS NOT COVERED (finding 3): security-event logging that relies on the application. iam.require_permission refusals are logged only by the TS withGuardedCommand/logRefusal after rollback. Signing refusals (misuse codes IAM-091/093/094, ESIG-036/038) reach esig.signing_failure and the SIGNING_FAILED alert only if the app calls logSigningFailure → esig.record_signing_failure, and that function has no actor check. F72 covers only the platform authorize path.

CONTROL catalog_test PARTS WITH NO CODE OR TEST, although the control is marked IMPLEMENTED and CI counts it covered: DI-23 'the verification job alarms and names the entry'. verifyAllChains/verifyChain (src/audit/verify.ts) and esig.verify_signatures only return rows. Nothing schedules them, stores the result or raises a critical alarm, and the DI-23 tests assert detection only. Outline 5.3 says 'production runs the same [invariant] queries on a schedule', but no invariant query is wired to a schedule or an alarm. DI-13 'USB storage on a kiosk is blocked' exists only as an attestation record.

CI TRACE GATE NOT REVIEWED (tools/register/src/trace.ts): CONTROL_TAG = /\[((?:DI|PR|ST|IN)-\d{2})\]/ does not match [INV-xx]. The Phase-1 exit criterion 'INV-03, 06-11, 16, 22, 26-29, 40, 47 with bypass tests' is therefore not machine-checked. A control also counts as covered by any passing test whose name contains its tag, whether or not the catalog_test is exercised.

INVARIANT QUERIES: outline 5.3 says every invariant has a query that must return zero rows. Zero-row queries exist only for INV-03/09/10/27 (esig.invariant_violations), INV-11 (iam directory scan, 0180), INV-16 (platform.time_model_violations), INV-22 (records.inv22_violations) and INV-27 (continuity.number_invariant_violations, site.batch_number_invariant_violations), plus the state-machine queries. None exists for INV-06, 07, 08 (verify functions exist, but no zero-row query), 26, 28, 29, 40 or 47. Only F85 touched this area.

TEST FIXTURES HIDE DATA-TYPE CLASSES: the true-copy and retention tests use stub tables (stub_tc.entry/reading, stub_b4.*) without timestamptz, interval or bytea columns. The test '[INV-08] a bundle of a real chain ... verifies offline' therefore never exercises the column types that every production audited table has. I found 80+ audited kernel tables with timestamptz columns via pg_attribute.

NOT REVIEWED BY ANYONE: the DI-01 register content in packages/kernel/src/records/register.ts (BASELINE_RECORD_TYPES: official medium, retention keys, feeds_acceptance_limit); docs/security/threat-model.md, asvs-l2-review.md and security-baseline.md (the Phase-1 exit requires the design review, and nobody compared the claimed mitigations with the code); the exports in src/index.ts; tools/register.

TRANSACTION-CONTROL ATTACKS only partly covered (targeted races only): savepoint and ROLLBACK TO interplay with command markers, and the app's choice of isolation level for every writer. I checked the two deferred constraint triggers (esig_signature_sealed, idempotency_completed): SET CONSTRAINTS can only move the check earlier, so there is no bypass.

NULL-PROPAGATION IN PL/pgSQL GUARDS ('if not f(...)' or 'if not x = any(...)' with a NULL operand, which skips the refusal) was not searched systematically by the module reviewers. I sampled the 13 'if not <function>(' sites plus iam.delegation_valid and found no reachable defect. The search is not exhaustive.
NO CROSS-MODULE CONCURRENCY FUZZING was done. The cross-cutting reviewer set aside the admin-versus-GMP role-permission race and the link-versus-purge race without testing them.

WORKTREE NOT CLEAN: /home/user/ebmr-review/packages/kernel/test/review-tmp/ holds 55 untracked probe files (f1..f81.test.ts) written by the verification stage. The include glob in vitest.config.ts (packages/*/test/**) runs them, and the trace tool reads their [DI-xx] tags. Several coverage notes still say 'git status clean'. Remove the directory before any test or CI run on this worktree. My own probes are only in the scratchpad (scratchpad/critic), and their databases were dropped.

new_findings.title: A lawful retention purge turns every earlier external anchor into a permanent PROBLEM: continuity anchor verification and the start-up ledger check are not purge-aware
new_findings.function: continuity.external_anchor_problems (used by continuity.verify_external_anchors / compare_external_anchors; TS checkAgainstLedger in src/continuity/restore.ts:168; src/audit/verify.ts verifyAnchor)
new_findings.description: kernel.create_anchor puts every chain head into each anchor, and the anchor job copies each anchor to the external ledger every few minutes. records.purge deletes the purged chain's audit_event rows and its audit_chain_head row, and keeps the event hashes in records.tombstone. records.verify_anchor is purge-aware. continuity.external_anchor_problems is not: it looks up kernel.audit_event only (line 486), so the purged head is reported as 'differs from external anchor'. verify_external_anchors reports COVERED only when the anchor is absent from the database and an approved restore event names it. A purged chain in an anchor still held in the database can therefore never be covered. checkAgainstLedger, which the continuity README runs at start-up and after failover ('any ERROR ... keep GMP operation closed'), returns ANCHOR_MISMATCH ERROR permanently. At any later restore, compare_external_anchors classifies these anchors UNEXPLAINED. src/audit/verify.ts verifyAnchor also calls the non-purge-aware kernel.verify_anchor. This relates to the B4 integration note in PROGRESS.md line 133, which was not carried into 'Follow-ups carried into Phase 2'. It is worse than that note describes: it breaks INV-08 and the continuity start-up gate, not only the nightly verification.
new_findings.failure_scenario: Confirmed with a scratch vitest probe on a fresh database built from this worktree's migrations. (1) Operator inserts stub_b4.batch_entry for batch B, corrects it with a reason and inserts a batch_reading. QA creates the retention schedule (IN+US, manufactured 2008-01-10, expiry 2010-01-31). (2) Anchor job: exportAnchor(db.app, ledger) → anchor 1, which holds batch:B at seq 3. checkAgainstLedger → ok=true. (3) QA Manager signs RECORD_DISPOSAL_APPROVED and approves the disposal; the retention job runs records.purge('batch:B') → tombstone. (4) records.verify_anchor(1) → no problems (the purge is legitimate). verifyExternalAnchors → anchor 1 status PROBLEM, 'chain batch:B at seq 3 differs from external anchor 1'. checkAgainstLedger → ok=false with ANCHOR_MISMATCH ERROR. continuity.compare_external_anchors([anchor 1]) → in_database=true, status UNEXPLAINED. An anchor exported after the purge MATCHes. Every anchor exported during the record's retention life is affected. Operators must then either keep GMP operation closed or learn to ignore ANCHOR_MISMATCH, which hides real tampering or an unrecorded restore.
new_findings.suggested_fix: In an integration migration (>= 0900), redefine continuity.external_anchor_problems to resolve an anchored head of a purged chain against records.tombstone.chain_event_hashes, as records.verify_anchor does. Switch src/audit/verify.ts verifyAnchor/verifyAllChains to the purge-aware records.verify_anchor/verify_chain. Add a regression test: export anchor → purge → checkAgainstLedger ok and verifyExternalAnchors MATCH.

new_findings.title: Audit row hash and true-copy canonical form follow the session TimeZone: an unchanged record fails true-copy verification when the writing and exporting zones differ
new_findings.function: kernel.audit_row_change (with src/records/true-copy.ts:132 buildTrueCopyBundle and verifyRecordsPart lines 447-448; records.purge digest at 0440:315)
new_findings.description: kernel.audit_row_change builds v_row := to_jsonb(new) (line 282). It stores row_hash = sha256(v_row::text) for insert-only tables and the jsonb old/new values for mutable tables. to_jsonb(timestamptz) renders each instant with the writing session's TimeZone offset, and interval columns such as platform.stub_step_entry.site_utc_offset follow IntervalStyle. buildTrueCopyBundle renders each row again with to_jsonb(x)::text in the exporting session. verifyRecordsPart then compares that text string-for-string with the INSERT row_hash, or with the state rebuilt from the audit events. Only search_path is pinned in the SECURITY DEFINER functions. Nothing pins TimeZone: not the ops templates, not db/command.ts, not true-copy.ts. The app can set TimeZone freely because it is a user-level setting. Almost every audited table has timestamptz columns. The existing true-copy tests use stub tables with no time columns, so they never see this. The purge tombstone's rowsDigestSha256 is described as the 'same row hash as the audit trigger uses', and it has the same dependency.
new_findings.failure_scenario: Confirmed with a scratch probe. Server TimeZone is Etc/UTC. records.raise_incident is run through db.app. buildTrueCopyBundle(db.app, 'incident:<id>') → ok. The same, unchanged incident exported through an ebmr_app pool opened with options '-c TimeZone=Asia/Kolkata' → offline.ok=false, 'records.incident row <id>: row differs from the hash recorded when it was inserted'. An incident written by an app session in Asia/Kolkata and exported in the default zone fails the same way. Realistic path: an Indian installation initialised in Asia/Kolkata is restored or migrated to a UTC host during a multi-year retention, or an export client sets PGTZ, or the app sets its session zone. Every archived true copy of older records then reports tampering. register_true_copy and purge ignore the offline verdict (F34), so such copies still become the disposal archive, and a genuine tamper report cannot be told apart from this noise.
new_findings.suggested_fix: Make the canonical form independent of session settings. Add SET TimeZone='UTC', IntervalStyle='iso_8601', DateStyle='ISO' and bytea_output='hex' to kernel.audit_row_change, records.purge and every definer that hashes or serialises rows. Have buildTrueCopyBundle run SET LOCAL of the same settings in its snapshot transaction. Alternatively, render instants with an explicit UTC formatter. Add a true-copy test with timestamptz and interval columns written and exported under different zones.

new_findings.title: esig.record_signing_failure lets the application, with no validated actor, forge HIGH SIGNING_FAILED alerts and failure-log rows naming any signer, while real misuse is logged only if the application chooses to
new_findings.function: esig.record_signing_failure (TS caller logSigningFailure in src/esig/signing.ts:160; same pattern in src/identity/authority.ts withGuardedCommand/logRefusal)
new_findings.description: record_signing_failure is granted to ebmr_app. It takes any challenge id (esig.challenge is readable by the app) and any well-formed EBMR code. It never calls iam.assert_validated_actor and never checks that a signing attempt on that challenge actually failed. For the misuse codes (IAM-093 proxy signing, IAM-094, IAM-091 reuse, ESIG-036, ESIG-038) it inserts esig.signing_failure attributed to the challenge's signer_person and raises a HIGH iam.security_alert naming that person. In the other direction, esig.sign rolls back all of its work on refusal, so a misuse attempt reaches the security unit only if the TS wrapper calls this function afterwards. The same is true of authority refusals (withGuardedCommand/logRefusal; DI-18 'refused and logged'). ADR-0012 makes the database the enforcement point, yet DI-19 misuse detection (11.300(d)) depends on the application in both directions.
new_findings.failure_scenario: Confirmed with a scratch probe. A QA person created a signing challenge. A bare ebmr_app connection, with ebmr.ctx empty (no begin_command), then ran: select esig.record_signing_failure('<challenge id>', 'EBMR-IAM-093', 'forged: proxy signing attempt'). The result was an esig.signing_failure row with signer_person = the QA person, and an iam.security_alert of kind SIGNING_FAILED, severity HIGH, person_id = the QA person, details {code: EBMR-IAM-093, record: record_type_version:BATCH_PROCESSING_RECORD:1}. This is a false proxy-signing accusation made by nobody. Reverse case: a compromised app replays another person's auth event into esig.sign, gets EBMR-IAM-093, rolls back and skips logSigningFailure. No failure row and no alert exist.
new_findings.suggested_fix: Record refusals inside the database whether or not the app cooperates. One option is for esig.sign and iam.require_permission to write the failure through an autonomous path (an owner-run dblink/background-worker logger or an equivalent) before re-raising. Restrict record_signing_failure to a validated actor whose account, session and device match the challenge. Derive the failure code from server-side state, not from the caller, or drop the function from the app grants.

new_findings.title: DI-23 is marked IMPLEMENTED and CI counts it covered, but its alarm half has no code or test, and the trace gate cannot see the INV bypass tests at all
new_findings.function: verifyAllChains (and tools/register/src/trace.ts CONTROL_TAG, buildTrueCopyBundle-free DI-23 tests in test/audit/audit-trail.test.ts)
new_findings.description: DI-23's behaviour and catalog_test require that 'a scheduled verification job checks the chain, and a break raises a critical alarm ... the verification job alarms and names the entry'. verifyAllChains, verifyChain and esig.verify_signatures only return arrays. Nothing schedules them, stores their result or raises an alarm (there is no continuity/iam/platform alarm call). The DI-23 tests assert detection and naming only. tools/register/src/trace.ts marks a control covered as soon as any passing test name contains its tag. Its regex /\[((?:DI|PR|ST|IN)-\d{2})\]/ never matches [INV-xx], so the Phase-1 exit criterion 'INV-03, 06-11, 16, 22, 26-29, 40, 47 with bypass tests' is not enforced by CI either.
new_findings.failure_scenario: Run the DI-23 test scenario: a superuser rewrites an audit_event payload and recomputes its hash. kernel.verify_chain returns the problem only when someone calls it. No job exists, and no alarm or incident is raised, yet `pnpm trace` reports DI-23 as passing. Separately, deleting every [INV-..] bypass test leaves `pnpm ci` green, because trace.ts ignores INV tags.
new_findings.suggested_fix: Add the verification job: scheduled verifyAllChains (purge-aware), verify_signatures and the invariant queries, with persisted results and a critical alarm through continuity.raise_alarm or an iam alert, plus a test that a tampered row raises the alarm. Extend CONTROL_TAG to INV-\d{2} and fail the trace when a Phase-1 exit invariant has no passing bypass test run under the ebmr_app pool.
